en: Record of the Profound Eulogy on the Heart Sutra of Prajñā, Volume One.
Compiled by the Bhikṣu Shouchian of Longxing Monastery in Zhending Prefecture during the Great Song Dynasty.
The eulogy states: "Now, sentient beings are obscured by the habitual tendencies of their conditioning."
The commentary notes that only the first two lines constitute the cause of deluded attachment; the subsequent text consists entirely of deluded attachments, both general and specific.
The phrase "now for the sake of" refers to the benefit for a single period during the time of composition, similar to what is stated in the preface to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*:
"Now I compose," etc.; the general meaning is identical. As for the term "sentient beings" (*sattva*), this refers to those for whom [the work] is intended—those whose consciousnesses are deluded.
Love is called "sentiment" (*sneha*). That which possesses this sentiment is called a "sentient being" (*sattva*). Regarding the term "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*):
"tendency" (*saṃyojana*) means to bind; it also refers to that which binds and fetters. "Habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*) means seeds; it also refers to present practice. There are nine such types:
they consist of the six root views (from which [the first three] are taken) together with envy and avarice. These three especially increase the binding of sentient beings.

Therefore, it is established separately. It may not consist of only nine; generally speaking, "knots and habits" refers to all fetters and afflictions (*saṃyojana* and *anuśaya*). "Obscuring" means to hinder.
[This refers to those who] superficially believe and accept heterodox teachings while slandering the Mahāyāna.

This note generally demonstrates the belief in the heterodox and the destruction of the orthodox. Below, it specifically demonstrates how deluded attachments arise in competition. The old commentary asks:
"How does delusion regarding the truth give rise to the false? How does one obtain benefit according to one's capacity?"
The *Śū* (Commentary) states that [certain people] give rise to revulsion and fear regarding the emptiness and existence of the sūtras.

The *Zhù* (Sub-commentary) explains that they do not understand the underlying intent (*sandhāya-bhāṣita*) of the root sūtra. Following the literal words, they grasp at the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) as being collectively empty or existent;

since this results in contradiction, they give rise to revulsion and fear. If one knows that when it is said "existence" is taught, although it is spoken of generally as existing, it refers only to the dependent and perfected natures (*paratantra* and *pariniṣpanna*).
Emptiness. This emptiness merely empties away the *parikalpita* (imagined nature), whereby it becomes a single flavor (*ekarasa*) free from discord and contention.
The commentary establishes the rare and essential [teachings], up to the point where false and confused instruction is bestowed upon those in training.
Regarding those who are mired in deluded attachments: at times they harbor doubts that remain unresolved; at other times they delight in liberation and hope for its pursuit.

Yet, both teacher and disciple have failed to attain the Middle Way. Since the teacher has imparted erroneous instruction, how could the disciple study correctly? Instead, they grasp at extreme views.

What has been demonstrated above concerns the general confusion regarding emptiness and existence. Below, the specific delusions and errors in this regard will be detailed; note carefully the characters *xi* (希) and *xi* (悕).
The *Shu* (Commentary) expresses fear regarding the textual instructions (*wen-hui*), stating that [the author] was unable to comprehend them.

The *Zhu* (Sub-commentary) explains that he feared the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and initially refused to study it; although he delighted in this scripture, he could not comprehend it. The following passage distinguishes this lack of comprehension.
The Commentary [states] that from the ultimate and conventional truths (up to) "closely gives rise to grasping and rejecting.
The sub-commentary (*zhù*) below this distinguishes what was not understood above. There are two gates: first, the two truths; second, mind and objects.

In the mundane world, there is the "emptiness of the conventional" (*saṃvṛti-śūnyatā*); this is the school of Bhāviveka. In the Hīnayāna schools, there is the "reality of the ultimate" (*paramārtha-satya*) and the "emptiness of the conventional";

this is also [the position of] Bhāviveka. [The view that] abandons the mind and grasps objects belongs to Bhāviveka; [the view that] abandons objects and grasps the mind belongs to Sthiramati. The "Mind-Only" (*cittamātra*) [of Sthiramati] is not yet the Middle Way; this is the teaching of the present Śūnyavāda school.

It asserts that [all things] arise solely from the mind without depending on external seeking. The remaining [positions] are to be assigned according to their respective schools. All of the above are [the views of] those who... (object of study).
This constitutes a fundamental error. Alternatively, this section does not belong to the preceding text; the previous discussion was incomplete, referring only to this single passage.
What follows below distinguishes the benefits, while the commentary (*śū*) ensures that the true and erroneous meanings of the True Dharma are fully distinguished.

The first note states that the character "wei" (為) extends throughout this section. It means to cause sentient beings to understand what is true and what is erroneous—that is, to recognize the true as true and the erroneous as erroneous;
both are termed the "True Dharma. "Fen" (分) means to discern, either through knowing or through understanding.
Sentient beings who believe and study [this] shall all obtain benefit.
The Commentary (*ṭīkā*) states that based on the above, one should distinguish between the true and the erroneous; by believing and studying them accordingly, one obtains profit and happiness.
How could the claim of the former masters—that one obtains benefit only partially depending on the two extremes—be more clearly demonstrative of benefit than the preceding passage?
The *Shu* (Commentary) briefly extols the Middle Way based on what was previously received;

the *Zhu* (Annotation) connects with the above at length. This is the general purport: in order to cause those who are deluded and attached to distinguish between the true and the false, so that they may gain benefit through faith and study, it extols the Middle Way based on what was previously received. To show that this is not his own personal view, he says "previously received. This—
These two lines precisely describe the qualities that the praiser is capable of possessing. Why, then, does some judge them as belonging to the subsequent section?
If that were so, what dharma would the praiser have as the object of the praise just explained? To clarify the actual subject of the praise, I shall briefly cite it according to its meaning.
The wise should understand that what follows is a detailed exposition of the teaching, which sets forth two intended meanings.
This is explained in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* (up to the section on the three natures).

In the commentary on the three periods, the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* is cited. First, the sequence is established: after explaining the absence of nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), the first line and the remainder collectively summarize the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

Subsequently, following the section on the arising of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the three absences of nature are explained individually: first, the absence of nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*); second, the absence of nature in terms of arising (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*);
and third, the absence of nature in terms of the ultimate (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*). "Nature" (*svabhāva*) here refers to the imagined (*parikalpita*) and the dependent (*paratantra*).
It is also his perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). The repetition of the term "nature" (*svabhāva*) and so forth is as explained extensively elsewhere.
[The commentary] states: "At that time, Paramārthasamudgata... reached the place of firm abiding.

The sub-commentary notes that while this is addressed specifically to the Śrāvakas, in reality it benefits all vehicles (*yāna*), as all obtain its advantages; thus it is spoken in contrast [to other teachings].

Although the notion of a permanent self is indeed extraordinary, it does not manifest the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Because the true nature is concealed, the meaning of the teaching remains insufficient;

thus, disputes still persist. The meanings of the wheels of truth (*satya-cakra*) and so forth are as explained in other places. Why, then, were these doctrines of the three times and so on established?
As explained elsewhere in the commentary, [the teaching] is intended solely for those who have reached the stage of "establishing a firm footing.

The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) likewise maintains that it is directed toward the correct [vehicle], being intended solely for those proceeding toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). In reality, however, it encompasses all three vehicles; thus, it is a general description given with intentional ambiguity (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) regarding the whole.

The essence and meaning of all phenomena are both non-existent, thereby revealing the eternally quiescent nature of original nirvāṇa. Although this transcends the teachings of existence, its name is even more extraordinary;
yet, as the dependent and perfected natures do not appear and the underlying principle remains unclarified, it still invites controversy—how can this be a place of secure footing?

Question: Who is it that is "heading toward the state of a Great Being" (*mahāpuruṣagati*)? Answer: It refers to Subhūti and others. Question: Since they have not yet turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], how can they be said to be "heading toward"?

Answer: They are called "heading toward" because they are currently being led toward it; thus, they are designated as "heading toward. Although there are teachings [to this effect], the Great Practice (*mahācaryā*) has not yet been manifested, and therefore it is not spoken of explicitly.
Even though those of the Sudden Vehicle (*tongren*) are heading toward it, it is not primarily for them, because the three periods [of time] are established [for them]. [This is] complete.
Upon examining the *Prajñāpāramitā* [sūtras], there is no place where gradual awakening or the arousal of the great mind (*mahācitta*) occurs. Reflect on this and consider it carefully.
This commentary now proceeds from "setting out" (*prasthāna*) to the "place of rest."
The commentary refers to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. It correctly clarifies that the name [of this teaching] applies universally to all vehicles (*yāna*);

while one [vehicle] is primary and the others are secondary, although it is the same as the previous [teachings], when discussing the explicit exposition of the doctrine, it relies solely on what is primarily applicable. Nevertheless, it must also fully clarify the objects (*viṣaya*) and so forth of all vehicles;

therefore, it is called "universally for" (*pùwéi*). This differs from the first two [teachings], which are only partially applicable. Although all vehicles receive benefit, the doctrine is not explicitly taught [to them].

To speak of it by way of the power of wisdom for those of remaining capacities, it is based on a brief realization of the extensive; it is not by the power of the teaching, and thus its application differs and cannot be called "universal.
Because both emptiness and existence are manifested together, there is no room for contradiction. This supreme ultimate truth is called the "True Definitive Meaning" (*nītārtha*).
Since there is no further challenge or refutation, there is no basis for dispute.
Commentary on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* (up to the section titled "The Retention of Turning and Illumination").

The upper portion relies on the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* to fully explain the three periods; the lower portion extends down to the point where discord has not yet arisen, further citing other teachings to explain the aforementioned meaning.
This citation from the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* explains the three distinct wheels, or alternatively cites two sūtras to belong [to this category].

Distinguishing the three periods: subsequently, from the various lower [stages] onward, it is revealed that [the teaching] is of a single flavor, though distinctions are established according to the capacities of sentient beings.

The masters of old asked: "How are the major divisions of the *Kāśyapaparivarta* (The Chapter of Kāśyapa) structured? This scripture establishes the sequence of "turning," "illuminating," and "maintaining" based on their predominance: "turning" refers to the illumination of emptiness, while both [turning and illuminating] are taken together as "maintaining.
Alternatively, these may be understood as the general names acquired at the outset.
The commentary (*śāstra*) explains that this [verse] both negates and affirms, as it simultaneously subverts and expresses.

The *ṭīkā* on the sūtra contains the character "wheel" (*cakra*). This first phrase provides the explanation; alternatively, these two phrases together explain the meaning of "wheel," because it negates and subverts while expressing and turning.
The former [phrase] is the subversion, thus expressing existence while negating emptiness; the latter is the refutation of existence, thus expressing emptiness while negating existence.

The third pair may be considered as both refuting and expressing; alternatively, this [third] alone explains the name "upholding" (*dhāraṇī*), because the preceding two primarily clarify that which cannot be named.
The first reveals the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) but does not speak of refuting emptiness; the second never explicitly expresses it.
The Commentary states: "From all sentient beings... to the middle way, the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
The Sub-commentary explains that this reveals the single flavor (*ekarasa*). First, it identifies the faculties as the disease; through delusion, they invite suffering.

The Great Sage, the Dharma King, forcibly bestows the medicine of the Dharma, causing those of the three vehicles to sever their hindrances according to their needs, so that each may personally realize the middle way, the single-flavored true reality. This...
This is about teaching according to principle; as for the principle itself, there is no distinction. If one does not realize the Middle Way, how can one obtain benefit?

It is simply that there are differences in depth and distinctions between the partial and the perfect; therefore, it is said that "one obtains [benefit] accordingly. The *Kechao* asks: what is meant by "resolving difficulties"?
Therefore, there is a verse which says: [omitted] "neither self nor non-self.
This single verse serves as a commentary to prove that the thousandfold differences of what is taught all return to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The true mark is precisely that which is realized through the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). Some take this verse to prove the three periods; regarding the first period:

Because the precepts are not being recited, this statement refers to the "self. This discourse concerns the true and eternal, or it speaks of the conventional self; the absence of self is like the eternal.
These two cases are mentioned for now as examples, by which all others may be understood. Above, it reveals the single flavor; below, it accommodates various capacities.
The Commentary continues from "other sutras further state" (up to) "each attains understanding," etc.

The Note states: This is the teaching in terms of the Dharma; although it is fundamentally of one flavor, it manifests distinctions according to the capacities of beings. The meaning of this "one flavor" and so forth is as analyzed in the usual [commentaries].
The Commentary states that [the Dharma] is like a celestial drum (up to) "like seeking the treasure of rain.
These two metaphors provide a layered explanation. The single flavor adapts to the capacities of beings; the meaning is as explained previously.
The Commentary states that although it is taught in response to sentient beings (up to) "no discord or contention has yet arisen."
The preceding section, from "by all those below," reveals the single flavor (*ekarasa*) of the Dharma. This subsequent section reveals that there is no discord or contention among persons.

As for the topical outline (*kośa*), it is determined by the major headings. This first part concludes the preceding [section] while simultaneously giving rise to what follows; it may also be considered a major division.

However, as the text arises closely [following the previous], it is like the addition and modification of the character *ji* (既). *Ji* means "already"; it signifies that [the explanation] has already been completed.
The section from "After the Buddha’s Nirvāṇa" (疏佛涅槃後) to "Initially Sealing Attachment to Existence" (初封著有) involves the following:

the commentary (*zhù*) first clarifies the illness [of attachment]; the subsequent "allowing" (*zòng*) encompasses both benefit and harm; and there are four meanings: confusion and disorder, contentious dispute, sealing and fixation, and firm attachment.
This is the heading.
The *Śāstra* contains a verse which says (up to): "Selecting and taking up the true reality.
The *Commentary* notes: "These are the words of the teaching; they explain the principle of the Four Truths as the true reality. The *Zonglun shu* states: "The rest are slanders..."
Regarding the principles and the various sectarian tenets, right and wrong are not fixed. The principle of the Four Noble Truths is like genuine gold;
one should not, because of their mutual disagreements and disputes, reject the various schools and declare them all to be false. This passage clarifies the act of selection.
The character "采" (cǎi) is identical to "採" (cǎi).

The commentary states that from "the holy Nāgārjuna and others" up to "thoroughly elucidating the True Doctrine," the subsequent two lines beginning with "this first manifests virtue" and "is not like Mahādeva" are problematic; they do not apply. Following this, the two lines beginning with "later sentient beings" also give rise to error. They are not [correct].
This refers to the Bodhisattva.
As the commentary states in a verse (up to): "Non-arising is like a flower in the sky.

The note explains that this is also a scriptural teaching; both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) each have their own measure, and each takes the preceding phrase as its thesis (*pakṣa*).

The second line provides the reason and the analogy. In the preceding section on conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-pramāṇa*), the analogy was presented first and the reason afterwards, as extensively explained elsewhere.
The commentary states: "That which is conventional (*saṃvṛti*)... [up to] all are empty."

The commentary here mentions only two gates, as it resembles Bhāviveka; however, I now suspect there may be another as well, since the ultimate truth is also taught as emptiness in a cryptic manner—this should be considered.
Although this [text] states that "this true emptiness" (疏雖此真空) up to "the principle is the nature of emptiness" (理皆空性), [it remains so].

This note addresses the case where both [positions] are non-existent, discussing the nature that transcends words; it may also apply to Bhāviveka. Therefore, in the *Kuiyao* (Essentials of the Dharma), an analogy is presented to demonstrate the fault of "neither being established for both.
The subsequent refutation relies on the conventional expression, which is precisely the aforementioned ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The commentary states: Sentient beings, because of this, subsequently give rise to the view of emptiness (*śūnyatādṛṣṭi*).
The sub-commentary notes: Although Bodhisattvas, out of compassion, eliminate existence and speak of emptiness, it is like heat increasing when cold is applied; how can one help it?
The Commentary by Bodhisattva Asaṅga (up to the point where he) simultaneously eliminates the two types of grasping.
This is annotated as the Middle Way below; it is exclusively attainment and not loss. Although there are differences in faculties, the teaching has not yet clarified them.
The commentary explains this in verse: [up to] "this accords with the Middle Way.
The first line refers to the *paratantra* (dependent nature); the second line, to the *parikalpita* (imagined nature).

The following two lines reveal the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature) and how it exists in mutual dependence with the *paratantra*. The subsequent two lines cite scripture to establish this proof; the final two lines provide the conclusion.
This is an exclamation regarding what has been clarified. As for the phrase "existence, non-existence, and because of existence," the character "hence" (故) has three functions;

one should examine its usage according to the meaning. Regarding the term "Middle Way," it refers to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). To bring one's principle into accord with right knowledge is called "conforming to the Way. The rest is as explained in the *Shishu* (Commentary on the Śrīmālā-sūtra).
I cannot cite further examples here.

That commentary states that from the conventional [truth] up to these two types of emptiness, the sub-commentary notes that "provisionally existent and substantially non-existent" is the conventional name for the superior [truth]. Since this refers only to the emptiness of the present, it merely adds to the school of Emptiness (*śūnyavāda*).

Look at me. Furthermore, one sees the distinction within the word "only" (kevala). "Only" implies exclusion and maintenance; "only" refers to the two attachments to emptiness, while the dependent and perfected [natures] still remain.
Regarding the four lines of text below, they all describe the Middle and the Extremes. How should the commentator arrange these sections above and below?

It should be said that this reveals both the emptiness of persons and phenomena through the two modes of the secret and the manifest. These two are either entirely absent, or they may be present together.
The following passage provides a general synthesis and reconciliation; the analysis thereof is as follows.
Although the Commentary states that the Buddha [taught] "emptiness" and "existence" in order to refute [extreme views], this contains four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

First, existence is explained in terms of its general characteristics; this refers to the dependent and perfected natures (*paratantra* and *pariniṣpanna*). Second, emptiness is explained in terms of its general characteristics.

The first [position] asserts universal emptiness; the third asserts that both are neither, as these two rely on the abandonment of the expressive medium (*prajñapti*). The fourth asserts both existence and emptiness, as this relies on the provisional employment of the expressive medium.
By means of understanding the former three, one returns to the fourth. Why is this so? As stated in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*:

Since both existence and emptiness are discussed as the literary theme, although it is said that "both are negated," this is for the purpose of providing scriptural evidence; thus, it serves to overturn that very evidence.
Therefore, Maitreya says (up to the point where he) designates it as "non-existent."
The commentary below merely establishes that there is existence and emptiness; this precisely accords with the Middle Way’s two aspects of existence and two aspects of emptiness.
The sub-commentary does not state that all dharmas of existence and emptiness are themselves empty or existent.

The commentary above establishes the pair [of existence and emptiness] to clarify the text itself; below, it returns to the pair of "neither" (non-duality) to manifest the correspondence with the cited proofs.
Regarding these terms "emptiness" and "existence," the wording is not sequential: "existence" does not mean fixed existence, and "emptiness" does not mean fixed emptiness.

Therefore, while the text may follow a formal sequence, the character "non-" (fei) extends throughout. It is not that because one speaks of existence all phenomena are empty, nor that because one speaks of emptiness all phenomena exist.
Since there is both emptiness and existence, it is not the case that emptiness exists [as a substantial entity].
The commentary (*shū*) observes this intention of the Sage [up to the point where it states] "provisionally speaking of emptiness and existence.
The preceding text all describes the ancient scriptures; from here below, the commentator explains the intent behind the concluding praise in contrast to what preceded it.

The "Root and Branch" section appears in the *Dàwén* (Great Questions). First it provides an exegesis and subsequently returns to the source. This exegesis does not contradict the sacred intent of the three periods [of the Buddha’s teaching], for the Dharma is of a single flavor.
Later scholars (up to this point) have regarded this as an erroneous interpretation.
The commentary on this explanation states that later students have deviated from the truth and harbor perverse attachments.
This sub-commentary now extols the meaning of the sutra; those of wisdom should understand it.
The preceding commentary extensively elucidates the intended meaning of the teachings of the three periods; it is specifically for the sake of providing the basis for praising [this work].

This is because it reveals how the two schools interpret this sutra. Otherwise, what would be the purpose of such an extensive narration of the three periods? How could one subsequently categorize it?
It would be like drawing ripples after a rope has been cut, or adorning the head with a crown after it has been broken. Alas, alas!
Question: Why do the three schools merely cite two [interpretations] when explaining the sutras? Answer: Because the sutras speak of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

There are other passages that state, "The profound assistance lacks order," but this is incorrect. When authors compose their works, they produce the text at a single moment; it is not a fixed, singular standard.
Regarding the commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā* (up to the point "belonging to the subject as its designation"):

examine this title; it contains four pairs of categories. First, the pair of the general and the specific, and the internal and external. Second, the pair of the restricted and the universal, such as king and minister.
Third, the pair of practice and fruit, and raft and shore. This present case is the pair of the general and the specific, and the internal and external. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* is general...

As for "like the body," this sūtra is the most essential; it is named "Mind" (*citta*). Although this is called a "sūtra," it is actually a definitive judgment on the word "mind," with the character "sūtra" added as a prefix.
In contrast to the preceding text, this constitutes the fourth pair of the signifier and the signified (*vācaka-vācya*).

Alternatively, this pairing may not exist, as the preceding title contains the term "possessing wealth" (*adhikaraṇa-samāsa*) because it refers to the *Mahā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. My intention in praising [this] is thus. Therefore, the *Cittasūtra* (Heart Sūtra) should be read as follows:

The fourth section distinguishes the Mahāyāna from the Hīnayāna Piṭaka. Regarding the character "also" (也), its formation through the combination and separation of radicals has already been explained.
The following text provides a detailed analysis of the destination [of rebirth], consisting of six categories and eight transformations, as is commonly understood.
Although this sutra refers to it simply as "mind" (*citta*), the commentary states in full that it is also called *prajñāpāramitā*.
This is to manifest the distinctiveness of its specific correspondence; thus, it does not receive that [latter] name.
This is not a *karmadhāraya* compound.
It explains the meaning of "prajñā-wisdom" (*prajñā-prajñā*).
This phrase is annotated as a parallel correspondence with the "raft and the shore" below; it corresponds to the second pair.
The commentary states that there are three ancient expositions (up to the point where it says "referring to the true teaching").
Within the *Zangshu* (Commentary on the Tripiṭaka), these three bodies [of the teaching] exist. Now, when referring to the ancient expositions, I do not know which scripture they originate from.
The Commentary now explains that there are five [categories] (up to) "referring to all phenomena.
The Sub-commentary now explains the objective sphere (*ālambana*): it takes what is proximate and not remote; otherwise, it would follow that it applies to all defiled phenomena. Question:

Why does the subsequent section state that it "encompasses all phenomena"? Answer: Regarding the inclusion of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena, this refers to only a small portion of "all. Question: [Regarding] the uncontaminated...

Is it not the case that there are also remote objects of cognition (*parokṣālambana*)? Answer: The four parts [of consciousness] are mutually related; since there are no direct objects not subsumed [within them], they exhaustively encompass all phenomena (*dharma*).
Question: How can the words for "true reality" (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) not be an object of cognition? Answer: Because one excludes those [words] and grasps what remains, there is no confusion.
Alternatively, the latter [the true reality] is merely the principle of the two kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) inherent in all phenomena; it is not a truly distinct entity.
The commentary states that one must cultivate both merit and wisdom until understanding is thoroughly realized.
The sub-commentary explains that five factors are required for completion: the retinue, the object, the words, the true reality (*dharmatā*), and contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā*).

These are assigned in sequence to demonstrate that Prajñā is never separate from them; therefore, five are necessary. Cultivation, illumination, investigation, and thorough examination are all functions of wisdom (*jñāna*). As it says:
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Because it is the self-nature; because it is associated with consciousness; because it is transformed by consciousness; because it is a state of consciousness;

and because it is the true nature of consciousness. Question: Why does this differ in order from what was cited previously? Answer: The previous [citations] were based on proceeding from the fundamental toward the derivative;
this [text], however, relies on the inclusive returning to the primary, wherein contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is established as the primary [subject]. The others...
If the four truths proceed from the distant toward the near, the sequence is as follows. Alternatively, the latter two phrases concern the characters and the true nature (*dharmatā*).

The four phrases merely explain what must be supplemented by the other four. Regarding the term "arising," it is used in conjunction with the preceding [phrase]. As for the contemplation of the true essence, it does not require further explanation to be established.
The nature of wisdom (*svabhāva-prajñā*) and the wisdom that serves as its support (*upastambha-prajñā*) are both termed *prajñā*.
In the preceding section, these five were explained individually; here, they are collectively shown to be equally named *prajñā*.

This wisdom is the primary [factor], and thus it is established by its own essential name (*svabhāva-nāman*); the others are auxiliary, and consequently they receive the designation of "support" (*upastambha*). Alternatively, one may explain that the other four [factors] attain [the name].

The name [Prajñā] refers to its essential nature (*so-yi*). Principle (*li*) constitutes the essence of wisdom (*hui-xing*), while the remaining three [faculties] serve as its resources (*zi*). Since all are derived from wisdom, they are termed *prajñā*. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"The nature of consciousness (*shi-xing*) and the characteristics of consciousness (*shi-xiang*) are both not separate from the mind. Here, the subsequent understanding is superior.
The following statement that "wisdom is the foremost" implies that the other natures or resources are all *prajñā*.
The *Śāstra* states that it "can eliminate the obstacle of habitual tendencies" (up to) "encompassing all phenomena.
The commentary (*Ṭīkā*) on the following text clarifies that this [treatise] stands alone as superior by virtue of possessing four meanings, just as wisdom (*prajñā*) subsumes the others.
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says, this demonstrates its superiority in terms of ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).
The term *pāra* means "the other shore.
This is combined with *maitrī*, forming the third pair.
According to ancient explanations, there are two [aspects], namely *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.
The Commentary frequently explains this because the fruit and the shore are clearly manifested. Furthermore, within Bodhi, are not all other [factors] subsumed?
The Subcommentary now explains that there are five [types], up to the five fruits.

It is focused upon the fruit of enlightenment (*bodhiphala*). This opens up the previous four [categories]. If one relies on the two turnings [of the wheel of Dharma], they are fully subsumed within the reality (*tattva*).

Question: What is the difference between the "knowable" (*jñeya*) and the "previous objects" (*viṣaya*)? Answer: The former is the cause and the latter is the fruit; within the fruit, its own essential nature (*svabhāva*) may be subsumed. Question:
What distinguishes this principle from the previous "true aspect" (*lakṣaṇa*)? Answer: The former pertains to the fruit itself, whereas this refers solely to the underlying principle (*yukti*).

Alternatively, this may also apply. Question: How does this differ from the aforementioned *prajñā*? Answer: Because the former pertains to the cause while this pertains solely to the fruit, they are not the same.
This refers to the practices of generosity and so forth that benefit others within the state of fruition. Question: These practices also exist within the lower *maitrī* (loving-kindness).

What is the difference between the "agent" (*kartṛ*) and the "object" (*karman*) here? Answer: In relation to the cause, it is termed the "object"; in comparison to the other [stages], it is the "agent. Thus, it is already [established].

"Reaching" (*prāpta*) means "to arrive. This is not contradictory; it will be explained further below. Regarding *śūnyatā*, the term "śūnya" carries the meanings of both "separation" (*viyoga*) and "reaching" (*prāpti*).

The commentary [on the *Mahāyāna-saṃgraha*] takes it only in the sense of "reaching," meaning to go forward and arrive. Now, however, it includes the sense of "separation," meaning that which is to be transcended.
The Commentary states that this name is established because of practicing *prajñā* (up to "...therefore this name is established").
The first phrase of the Sub-commentary provides a general summary of "by means of practicing. The second phrase provides a general explanation of the meaning of "leaving behind" (*vīti*).

The following five phrases then correspond respectively to the essence of the five perfections (*pāramitā*) to provide a detailed explanation of the meaning of "reaching" (*gata*). The first phrase functions as a thread running through all of them.

This is because one practices *prajñā*. The preceding [phrase] serves as the basis; the character “ascend” (*sheng*) correctly explains the meaning of “leaving,” while the character “arrive” (*dao*) refers to what follows.
These two are distinct textual units. This explanation clarifies the ability to arrive by citing the shore reached. The following section discusses essence and function:
it establishes the ability to arrive in contrast to the essence of *prajñā*, and the ability to leave is its function. Some say:
Regarding *pāramitā*: it is not the case that this refers to reaching the opposite shore through a lack of understanding, nor is it correct to divide the essence and function within the fruit itself.
[The *Śāstra*] states: "However, as for the practices cultivated... up to *pāramitā*.

This commentary, although it speaks of both [the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Sūtra*], maintains that in the sense of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the seven meanings do not reside "on the other shore" (*pāram*).
Therefore, it establishes the sub-sections according to the *Sūtra*; this reasoning is also sound.
Commentary: 1. Abiding in the bodhisattva lineage; up to 7. not being interspersed by the two obstacles. Note:
"Nature" (*xing*) should follow the feminine [gender]. Use [the terms] above and below in detail. 4. Regarding the activities that assist and deliver according to circumstances.
5. These are the three wheels. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* lists four; "assistance" consists of two sets of three: the object given and the fruit, each combining the giver and the receiver. Therefore—

Two or three [factors] are involved. Alternatively, it may be combined with the first fruit (*srotāpanna*); otherwise, there would be a contradiction. The seven [verses] refer to the two obstacles, namely the regret at the three times;
these are simultaneous obstacles. The commentary states:
"If one practices wisdom and so forth... [it is] not reaching the other shore (*pāramitā*)."

The foundation is covered by the floor-steps; the walls and mats face outward in emptiness. From beginning to end, there is no change, and only then is the great hall completed; otherwise, it is not accomplished.
[Commentary: This refers to the first kalpa (up to) the Great Pāramitā.

The commentary states that what is proximate to the fruit is called "proximate" (*āsanna*); what has already been reached is called "great" (*mahat*). Since "neighboring" (*ānantarya*) is also termed "reached," these three are each established based on their respective fundamental causes.
The sub-commentary notes that within the state of Buddhahood, there are no further distinct designations.
The commentary places it in the third name; this refers to that which has already arrived. Those ten thousand kalpas correspond to the first name.
The sub-commentary (*shu*) states that because this concerns the cause and fruit of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it cites the general name.

The commentary on the names of the Buddhas has already been completed, as explained previously. However, since their essence and characteristics may overlap, it is possible that although these are here cited by their general names, the intention is to take only the causes—just as with the case of the *adhipati-pratyaya* (dominant condition), which is not conflated with others—and thus they remain universally "wondrous. As for form (*rūpa*), it should be understood in its comprehensive sense.
The term "mind" (*citta*) is a designation for that which is firm, substantial, wondrous, and supreme.

This commentary now sets forth the meaning of "mind," which generally comprises three types: first, that which is designated as "mind" because it takes objects as its cognitive focus; second, that which is designated as "mind" because it accumulates and arises through aggregation;

and third, that which is designated as "mind" because it is firm, substantial, wondrous, and supreme. Of these, the meaning of the first—the mind as cognitive focus—is easily understood; as for the latter two...

How is the meaning of its mind perceived? Since neither the meaning of the words nor their etymological definitions are perceived, one should understand that the latter two are not literal definitions of the words, but are named by way of analogy. The commentators apply the dharma to the analogy.

To explain this according to its meaning: first, regarding the sense of "accumulation" (*cita*). Just as in the world there must be a place where accumulated objects rest, so too there must be a place where the mind accumulates and arises;
it is for this reason that it receives this name. Furthermore, that which is accumulated and arises must necessarily be the mind;
thus it is called *citta*. Now, regarding the sense of "solidity" (*drdha*): just as in the world one selects wood, requiring that it be firm and solid, so too must the mind be firm and solid.
This is also most excellent. Furthermore, it is like the heart, which governs the five viscera; it is the most essential and subtle organ, protected by the various external organs.
It is that which first receives [the consciousness] and later relinquishes it; it is firm and constant. If one does not provide this interpretation, how could one avoid the objection:

"Why is it that that which does not accumulate [karma] is called 'mind' (*manas*) and so forth? Therefore, this interpretation is necessary. Although there are many meanings above, they are also attached to the central mind.
"Training" (xùn) is explained as "instruction. Here, however, only the third meaning is employed.
The *Shu* (Commentary) states that the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* was taught according to the capacities of beings, while this [present] sūtra was separately expounded.
The *Zhu* (Annotation) explains the intent behind this separate teaching of the present sūtra. Based on this, it is simply the intention of the compilers.
Of the three parts of the *Shu* (Commentary), two—the two prefaces—are missing.

Of the three parts of the *Zhu* (Annotation), two are missing; both prefaces are likewise omitted. Regarding the "two prefaces," these refer to the Preface of Testimony and Faith (*zhèngxìn*) and the Preface of the Arousing [of the Teaching] (*fājī*), which are the general and specific prefaces (*tōngbié xù*).
When it says they are "missing," this means they exist within the *Dà jīng* (Mahāvaipulya Sūtra).
The *Śū* (Commentary) meticulously synthesizes the subtle and profound [from] "up to" "designating the true mind as its title.
The *Zhù* (Sub-commentary) here correctly explains the two meanings of "firm" (*jiān*) and "subtle" (*miào*). The first two phrases indicate the meaning of being most subtle;

the final two phrases conclude with the meaning of being firm and solid. The remaining text applies universally to explain these two meanings, which do not exceed the scope of object (*viṣaya*) and wisdom (*jñāna*). Therefore—

It encompasses them exhaustively. "Micro" (wei) means subtle; "upright" (zhen) means firm. "Discerning" (zhenguan) refers to selection; "synthesizing" (zongrou) refers to integration; and "comprehensively governing" (tongshe) refers to total inclusion.
This commentary on the Sūtra [extends] to the ultimate patterns of ordinary, deluded beings.

The commentary states: The preceding phrase accords with principle; the following phrase accords with the faculties [of beings]. The preceding phrase is "encompassing" (*she*); to encompass is to gather these wondrous meanings. The following phrase contains three meanings:
"constant" (*chang*) refers to the Way that serves as the track for a hundred kings; "pattern" (*fan*) means the law (*fa*); and "ultimate" (*ji*) also carries the sense of "pervading.
As for "the thousand-petaled ordinary being," it refers to the fact that all are deluded regarding their own nature.
The Commentary (*Śū*) intends to cause [the practitioner] to cultivate and realize [this], and thus employs "mind" (*citta*) and "eye" (*cakṣus*).

This clarifying statement contains three meanings: first, that which is realized is explained based on its support; second, both are firm and subtle; and third, the Buddha likewise relies on these [two] before proceeding to expound them.
"Cultivation" (*xiū*) refers to the act of cultivating; "cultivation" (*xiū*) means to extend or prolong. It also commonly implies the sense of "to practice. Therefore...
Both are applicable.
The commentary follows the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, and other scriptures.
It provides two teachings and one analogy, followed by three proofs for the three meanings. Those meanings are manifold, as distinguished in the *Shuyao*; this is merely a brief [explanation].
A separate proof is also not contradictory. [The commentary] states:
"The Proponents of Ultimate Emptiness (Śūnyatāvādin) say... up to "...attaining the two benefits.

The annotation explains that because the ultimate meaning is entirely empty, they are called "Proponents of Ultimate Emptiness. Question: Regarding the Proponents of Ultimate Emptiness, although their tenets are explained separately, the topical outline (kośa) [treats them as one].

The judgment asks: How do the first two and the third differ? The answer is: The *Śūnyatāsaptati* (Treatise on Emptiness), fearing it might deviate from the fundamental tenet, does not explicitly provide an exhortation or demonstration;

rather, both [the first two sections] function to reveal emptiness, and thus they are merely concise and detailed respectively. This should be understood accordingly: although the Sūtra speaks of emptiness, it does not negate the practice of cultivation.
First demonstrating and then subverting—how could this contradict the principle? Therefore, there are three sections. Now, regarding the question of the third section:
What is the difference between the two schools? Answer: This shall be explained below. The *Great Sūtra* states (up to): "one does not see a bodhisattva. Note:
This is a citation from the sūtra. "Real existence" is attachment; this is conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). "Not seeing" is emptiness (*śūnyatā*); this is ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Regarding the meaning of the truth (*arthasatya*): the *Sūtra* instructs that one should not see [the person], yet it speaks of the emptiness of persons (*pudgalaśūnyatā*).

The commentary explains this with one sentence and concludes the manifestation with two sentences; the topical outline (*kośa*) appears obscure. Although the Sūtra mentions the person, how [is this to be understood]?
[The opponent] objects: "It is not seeing. [The author] replies: "Not seeing is called contemplation (*vipaśyanā*);
therefore, it is indeed a refutation. The Commentary states: "As for 'as appropriate' (*yathāyogam*), it refers to the subsequent perfect realization free from suffering.
The Sub-commentary notes: "'As appropriate' means being in accordance with the principle (*yathātattvam*). Furthermore, "as appropriate" is not a fixed definition; it applies to all four [truths].

Because it is a phrase, it is not definitively empty. Regarding the exhortation to practice, there is no distinction in the textual sections; regarding the presentation of capacities and the exposition of principles, the textual sections differ;

and regarding the learning of virtues and the expressions of praise, the text likewise appears in different sequences. Furthermore, it is explained that "exhortation" (*kuan-shi*) is actually a general designation.
This marks the practice of persons; these constitute two types. Within the midst of practice, there is both attainment and detachment; therefore, they are divided into two.

Regarding the three [categories] above, these are all intended as exhortations and demonstrations—this is the general purport. Question: The scriptural passage on "refining and removing obstacles" is extremely obscure.
What is the purpose of this topical analysis? Answer: The meaning of the scripture is profound and far-reaching; its significance is as follows.
The commentary states that there are three types of refinement (*parikarma*), beginning with the first refinement.

[Question]: Regarding the encouragement and instruction for the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), why does the subsequent text not mention it? Should it not be included solely in this sentence? [Answer]: It is because the capacity for cultivation already implies both the instruction and the encouragement.
The arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is taught as being manifest; it is not that it does not pervade what follows.

There is one who takes the three phrases beginning with the present heading as corresponding to the first section, and the final phrase as corresponding to the second section. Now, taking the single phrase "there are three kinds of refining" (*trimanana*) and reading it together with what follows, it fully reveals the initial refining.
Alternatively, regarding the upper portion of the "refining," one may take one phrase by implication to exhort and demonstrate the arousal of the mind for the purpose of refining.
There are three types of polishing (*parimārjana*). This section below provides specific indications: three phrases and one phrase, each being the first of a triad.

This marks the person [to be encouraged] and exhorts them to practice polishing. Since bodhi is profound and vast, [the author] uses others to draw a comparison for his own practice; thus, he cites the Bodhisattvas to illustrate his own case, as there was no regression in the preceding sutra.
The *Śāstra* states that upon hearing of bodhi, [some] give rise to despondency and retreat.

The *Commentary* explains: the first four lines cite the retreat to mark the need for refinement; the next nine lines cite others; the final four lines use them as a comparison for oneself. The verse says:
"Infinite sentient beings throughout the ten directions have, in every thought-moment, already realized the fruit of the Sugata. Since they are all great men (*puruṣa*),"
I am also thus. One should not disparage oneself and become disheartened.
Regarding the commentary on "observing" (*guan*), it examines the meaning [up to] the sublime function of deliverance.

The upper section, based on "refining and polishing" (*lianmo*), provides a general explanation which is abbreviated; the lower section, based on "exhortation and instruction," explains it in detail through specific distinctions. "Observing" (*guan*) refers to...
Sovereign. Wisdom and compassion constitute its essence. The following passage concerns those who have traveled from the Western [Land] to this [region].
The commentary [states]: "All those... are named Avalokiteśvara."
The upper part provides the heading; the lower part provides the explanation. Regarding the first four lines, one should pray for a manifestation in the present life.

As for the subsequent text, it concerns those who do not request the descent of the flying wheel (*cakravartin*); these are those in states of no leisure (*akṣaṇa*) or perilous suffering, which are the places from which they are to be rescued—namely, the eight states of no leisure where there is no opportunity to cultivate virtue, or specifically referring to the evil destinies (*durgati*) where there is no leisure due to the experience of suffering. The descent of the four wheels and so forth will be explained extensively later.
The Commentary further states: "As for 'the observer' (to) 'accomplishing the ten masteries' (*vaśitā*).
The preceding explanation clarifies the name based on the essence and function of benefiting others; this explanation designates the name based on the causes and fruits of self-benefit.

Regarding "mastery through observation," it may be interpreted as a *tatpuruṣa* compound when contrasted with the bodhisattvas mentioned below, whereas here it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. This constitutes the second of the four phrases used as headings.
This constitutes the explanation of the phrases. Since one practices the six perfections, why speak of wisdom alone? The latter two phrases apply universally, simultaneously indicating the fruit.
Alternatively, the latter four phrases connect with the preceding to indicate what follows, as categorized in the outline.
Commentary: First, mastery over life (*āyur-vaśitā*) [up to] that which is obtained through wisdom (*prajñā*). Note:

The first three are obtained through giving (*dāna*), for there is no distinction in the wealth of the Dharma. The next two are obtained through ethical discipline (*śīla*); "action" and "cessation" arise in their respective order.

Mastery means being like a king and so forth. Regarding mastery over resolve (*adhimukti-vaśitā*): one investigates [all things] as being like an illusion, and having reached a definitive resolution, one is able to transform them. The last...
The second pair follows the respective order: [the first] is the unimpededness of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and the others are as stated in the text.
Regarding the "stages" (*sthāna*) in the commentary, all refer to the stage of the "Successor to the Position" (*kṣetra-jina*).

[If one were to say otherwise,] both the wording and the meaning would be lost. As for the annotator’s division of sections, it is overly fragmented; he does not understand the underlying intent. One should state that this passage cites the stages, the purpose being to emphasize the contemplation of their function.

There is nothing hidden that it does not illuminate. Why, then, do the ancient translations refer only to Avalokiteśvara? Or perhaps the title of the section is "Correctly Distinguishing the Exegesis," which subsequently refutes the ancient [tradition].
Regarding the commentary on the term "Bodhisattva" (from "The Bodhisattva... down to "...briefly speaking of the Bodhisattva").
The commentary notes that because wholesome qualities arise according to the respective directions, the Sanskrit term has been abbreviated.
Regarding the *Sūtra*’s statement "Bodhi is Prajñā" (up to) "benefit and peace":

the commentary states that some say these are distinct names for the beginning and the end [of the path] regarding the Bodhisattva. How could one cite Ci'en [Xuanzang] as agreeing with the *dharmadhāraya* interpretation? If one relies on...
In the original [text], it should have been a *tatpuruṣa* compound expressing opposition; however, here it is simply a *karmadhāraya*.

The subsequent statement says that these two bring about benefit and happiness because they are capable of discernment through skillful means; thus, with respect to the welfare of others, the commentary treats it as a *tatpuruṣa*.

It is as stated in the *Mingde* (Attaining Clarity). Alternatively, it is like the sixth and seventh perfections being called "fundamental wisdom" (*mūla-jñāna*), because even from afar they can bestow peace and happiness.
According to the *Huayan jing xuanshu shu* (Commentary on the Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), these two functions rely upon the same single wisdom.
Having thus analyzed their separation and combination, one further establishes the possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*), for this is essential for the person [practitioner].
The Commentary further states that "bodhi" [refers to the fruit], hence the term "bodhisattva.

The preceding note referred to *prajñā* as the wisdom of the cause (*hetu-jñāna*), whereas this refers to the wisdom of the fruit (*phala-jñāna*); therefore, they are not the same. This constitutes a contradiction in their functions.
Furthermore, there is a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) analysis, which is easily understood as usual.
The commentary further states that *sattva* [refers to] ... thus it is named "Bodhisattva.
Since the term *bodhi* is identical to the second interpretation provided previously, it will not be mentioned again here. It is treated as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound).

However, because it is simply "vigorous effort," there is yet another sense of "possessing wealth" (*dhanin*), or it may be understood as a designation for a person; thus, no further analysis is required.
The Commentary further states: "As for the practitioner... [omitted] ...therefore they are called Bodhisattvas.
The annotation on this explanation is easy to understand.
The Commentary mentions that they possess both compassion and wisdom; therefore, it specifically designates only these two.

The preceding commentary provides a general explanation. What follows applies specifically to this [deity]. Although compassion is universal, he dwells in the West to save those here; thus, there is a particular affinity.
The *Sūtra* states: "In some places he occupies a superior station" (up to) "is universally Avalokiteśvara."

The commentary [of Vasubandhu] states that it either extends through the ten stages (*bhūmi*) or is restricted to the eighth stage alone. *Miaohui* explains "contemplation" (*guan*), while *Chengjiu* explains "mastery" (*zizai*).
*Juzhi* does not deviate from the two preceding interpretations; it merely provides a broader scope.
The *shū* (commentary) points this out and instructs one to gaze upon it, saying "contemplate" (*kuan*).

This annotation explains the character "contemplate": it means to direct the eyes toward the object of the occasion, precisely commanding one to arouse the bodhicitta by contemplating what lies above.
That which is contemplated is none other than the Sovereign Bodhisattva; this is the same as the previous explanation. It points to all Sovereign Bodhisattvas, commanding [one to contemplate them].
The *Jiguanjian* (Examination of Contemplation) seems obscure in its categorization.
The *Shu* (Commentary) states that from "not dwelling in the Western [Pure Land]" until "it does not separately manifest," the sub-commentary (*zhu*) refutes the two preceding interpretations;
it appears to treat what was severed as being severed, yet it is incorrect. Nevertheless, although the *Mahāyāna Sūtra* (the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) does not separately manifest [this],...

Furthermore, the holy one who transmits the Dharma was also present in this assembly; since he inspires wholesome states according to the capacities of beings, what fault is there in designating [the teaching] in this way?
The commentary states: "The Victorious Emptiness" (Śūnyatā-jaya) says that because Prajñā is named "Emptiness," [it is so designated].

The commentary cites the locus of *prajñā*; since this is precisely emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it therefore negates phenomena. Next, the term "prajñā" appears; below it, the four characters "pāramitā" should be supplied as a complement.
From "the emptiness of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) downward, the character "hence" (*gu*) should be connected. This principle [applies] to the subsequent matters.
In some cases, the substance and the meaning differ; in others, both the substance and the name differ; and in others, it serves as a concluding phrase for the commentary.
As stated in the *Śū* (Commentary) "according to what is appropriate," this refers to the second stage of refining the mind (*citta-parimārjana*).
The note "above the dharma being practiced" constitutes the first section. The five characters below it constitute the second section.

Since the myriad practices are difficult to cultivate, one must humble oneself, reflect, and increase one's training; this is also what was previously practiced, which serves to cause one to reflect upon oneself.
The commentary states that the Bodhisattva [from "up to"] should not retreat or be disheartened.
The first four lines of the note cite retreat to mark the training. The next eight lines express self-reproach. The subsequent five lines involve self-examination.

Nevertheless, one should reflect by comparing oneself with others. The verse says: "Though you have traversed many eons in the evil realms, you were able to transcend them despite your fruitless toil and suffering.
Since you can attain enlightenment through a small amount of ascetic practice, you ought not to succumb to despondency regarding this great benefit."

The Commentary states that from "Śāriputra" up to "exhorting him to practice refinement," the Sub-commentary notes that this specifically cites those who have previously resolved upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), so that the meaning of "retrogression and refinement" is made manifest. Question: Subhūti and others had not yet resolved upon the Great Mind;
why does Śāriputra say the same thing about them? Answer: This statement refers to those who had previously resolved [upon the Great Mind], but at that time, they regressed.

[It has already been said. This [resolve] has not yet arisen again. What contradiction is there? Question: If that is so, why was it said, "Fearing he might now regress, observe his training and fortification"?

Answer: This refers to a preliminary stage; it is not the actual training at this very moment. By calling out Śāriputra’s name and exhorting him, it causes Śāriputra to bring to mind and manifest the resolve when he later generates the thought of enlightenment, so that he may reflect upon his own training and fortification; it does not refer to the present moment.
Now, as for the question: "If it is 'now,' one should not say 'fearing now. 'Now' refers to the present time; why then speak of 'later'? Answer:
In contrast to the past Buddhas, this particular Buddha's time is designated as "now. This does not mean that the time of the teaching is "now" while the subsequent time is "later.
It refers to the present Buddha, who, when he has finished preaching the teachings during his third period, is also called "now. Alternatively, [it may refer to the current era].
This refers to the present body. Fearing a future regression, he has secretly indicated this in advance. Many rely on this text;

however, its claim that those who attain gradual enlightenment have already resolved their minds contradicts the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and thus it cannot be relied upon.
Regarding the commentary’s statement from “as for the practitioner” up to “is precisely what is called practice”:
the note explains that although one practices the practice of emptiness, this is still conventional reality; it is only within conventional reality that there is abandonment and realization.
The Commentary states: "If one relies on the ultimate truth... this is called 'activity' (*saṃskāra*). The Sub-commentary notes:

Since it is definitively non-existent, how can there be the extreme of eternalism? What, then, is meant by "activity"? The intention is that it is so called because it causes [the realization] of total non-existence; therefore, it is termed "activity."
The Commentary states: "Vimalakīrti says... because there is no recollection. The Sub-commentary notes:

"If one relies on the correct interpretation, this refers to the absence of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). Since this master [Vasubandhu] asserts that [the object] has no substantial entity (*svabhāva*), he falls into partiality and dogmatic attachment."
The commentary on the Great Sūtra also states (up to): "Because there is no nature. The note says:
According to the correct interpretation, when the non-discriminating mind does not engage in self-discrimination, it is called "not seeing.

Alternatively, this may be an indirect indication (*paryudāsa*) that the sense of "activity" (*caryā*) exists therein. The subsequent phrase excludes the activity of an imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); therefore, it is called "non-existent" (*asat*). This...
The Master directly negates not only practice, but the very substance of non-practice is likewise non-existent.
Alternatively, he may negate both view and practice; for "view" is itself "contemplation."
The Commentary now states: "As for the practitioner... [up to] ...it does not have the meaning of 'practice'.
This is the explanation of the Madhyamaka school itself; it truly has no essence, as has already been explained previously.
The Commentary further states: "Or perhaps it is taken in a hidden sense... [up to] ...it is not considered practice."
In the previous commentary, although the two truths were still distinguished, there remained that which was not practiced;
because one does not practice conventional cultivation, abandonment, and so forth within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), this non-practice was termed "practice.
In the present interpretation, however, there is likewise nothing omitted, yet it is called "practice" precisely because there is nothing to be practiced. As for that which is not practiced:
Furthermore, there is nothing that exists. It is not the case that only that which possesses activity is called "activity"; that which does not engage in activity is likewise not "activity. Question:

What is meant by "taking up the hidden meaning" (*guǐqǔ yìyì*) as an interpretation? Answer: It refers to taking up the words from the Middle Doctrine (*zhōngzōng*) that state both [extremes] are abandoned.
This is explained by returning to emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Alternatively, the following line may be understood as praising the fact that all practices are practiced without exception. The meaning is:
if there is nothing practiced among all practices, there is not a single practice that is not practiced. If there is something practiced...

There is something insufficient [in this]. If one values only the "leaving behind," how is this different from "superior emptiness"? This is because the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* cited previously also speaks of those who do not see and do not practice.
Furthermore, the Commentary provides an alternative interpretation (extending to): "this is called practice."
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that one should practice "non-recollection" as a form of mental attention (*manasikāra*). That treatise first requires one to withdraw the mind and collect it;

once the mind has been stilled, one gradually advances in cultivation. This master [however] merely requires one to sever all recollective thought; since there is no further progress in this way, his view is incorrect.

This means that within this stage, one first contemplates that the four factors—name and so forth—which constitute the "grasped object," are all transformations of one's own mind, existing only as provisional designations and being ultimately unfindable in reality.

Because one has for the first time attained the precursor sign of the sun of wisdom, it is called the stage of "Light" (*ālokalabdha*); that is, it is the precursor sign of the fire of the Path that is about to be attained.

Therefore, it is also called "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). Based on the concentration of Increasing Clarity (*vṛddhāloka*), one gives rise to superior reflection and contemplates that there is nothing to be grasped; this is established as the stage of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).

This means that within this stage, one repeatedly contemplates the four factors—name and so forth—which constitute the grasped object, realizing that they are all transformations of one's own mind, existing only as provisional designations, and that in reality they cannot be found.

Now, since it is called a "stage," although the seventy stages differ, their names and meanings are largely the same. Question: In what way do they differ? Answer:

The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are defined in terms of the abandonment of hindrances; therefore, the Tathāgata stage is excluded. The seven stages are based directly upon meritorious practice (*guṅxing*);

therefore, they include both the first and the last. Question: Since it has been stated that these involve the abandonment of hindrances, why are they referred to as "fruits" (*phala*)? Answer: This is also because, through prior cultivation, one acquires this capacity.
Alternatively, within this context, cause and effect are not distinguished; even within the discussion of the "stages" (*bhūmi*), their "abiding" is also included.

Because these rely on the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*), there is a distinction between the broad and the narrow. Question: Is it not the case that enjoying a dwelling is a great acquisition, and being supported and growing therein is surely progress?
If so, do the names and meanings of cause and effect not appear inverted? Answer: This is because it is taught that Bodhisattvas do not accept [worldly] blessings (*puṇya*).
Virtue consists solely in the practice of the Dharma, and the same applies to one’s dwelling. Such progress is due to prior cultivation;
thus, one perceives the meaning of the Bodhisattva’s unceasing cycle of rebirth. As for the "Stage of Supreme Joy" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), it refers to the extensive nature of the first stage.

It is not only the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); there is also the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). It is only upon emerging from the path of seeing that one realizes this with joy; it is from this that the name is established.

Such conceptual differentiation does not exist within the path of seeing itself. As the treatise states: "The first is the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), because for the first time one attains the nature of the noble ones (*āryatva*)."

1. The Ground of Joy (*Pramuditā-bhūmi*): Because one possesses the realization of the two kinds of emptiness and is able to benefit oneself and others through great joy. 2. The Ground of Purity (*Vimalā-bhūmi*):

Because one possesses pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) and is far removed from the defilements of afflictions that give rise to even subtle transgressions. 3. The Ground of Radiance (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*):

Because one achieves superior meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and the great dhāraṇīs, and is able to emit the light of boundless, wondrous wisdom. 4. The Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*): Abiding in...
The supreme factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) burn the fuel of afflictions because the flames of wisdom increase.

The fifth stage, the Extremely Difficult to Conquer (sudurjayā), is so called because it is extremely difficult to conquer, as it unites and brings into correspondence the two types of knowledge—the ultimate and the conventional—whose modes of activity are mutually contradictory.

The sixth stage, the Manifest (abhimukhī), is so called because one abides in the knowledge of dependent origination, which draws forth and causes the manifestation of the most supreme non-conceptual prajñā. The seventh [stage], the Far-Reaching...

The Stage of Practice (*caryā-bhūmi*) extends up to the final limit of the effortful application in the Abode of Signlessness (*animitta-vihāra*), for it transcends the worldly paths and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

The Eighth, the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), is so called because non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) continues spontaneously and uninterruptedly, such that neither signs, functions, nor afflictions (*kleśa*) can cause it to waver.

Ninth is the Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*). Because one has accomplished the four subtle and sublime analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and is able to skillfully expound the Dharma throughout the ten directions.

Tenth is the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*Dharmameghā-bhūmi*). Because it is a great cloud of Dharma-knowledge that contains the waters of manifold virtues, obscuring the coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) as vast as space, and filling the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

These three are established in mutual relation; "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) is itself meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Although this [term] lacks the character for "wisdom" (*prajñā*), it encompasses all its attendants.
The commentary states: "Although these three are common [to other contexts], they are most excellent when applied to Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*)."
A note on these three types: they encompass all myriad practices (*sarva-caryā*). Since it is not yet known upon which contemplation this present [text] relies, this passage exists.
Within this passage, first the essential points are clarified, and subsequently the meaning of the names is explained.
Regarding the first part, this section connects with the preceding by contrasting it with others, serving as a formal heading. As for the categories (*koṭi*), what are such divisions of the "sons"?
The Commentary [discusses] gradual and sudden enlightenment (up to the point where it says): "Because this principle is profound.
The Sub-commentary further explains and establishes this, clarifying the reasons for its partial adoption while also manifesting its broad pervasiveness and dispelling lingering doubts. Question:
How is this reconciled with the Hīnayāna? Answer: It is discussed from the perspective of the Mahāyāna.
The *Commentary on the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains [the passage] up to "the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

This commentary notes that this teaching refers to the bodhisattva’s mindfulness and vows; therefore, it is taken as proof. As for the statement "everything that exists in the three realms is created by the mind," this is because they exist due to the mind.
The following two phrases clarify that these apply universally throughout the three realms. The subsequent section refers specifically to the Buddha.
The two subsequent lines follow the reverse order and correspond to the same two meanings as before.
"By means of the mind as the agent" and "by means of the mind as the cultivation" indicate that the Buddha and the body are not separate from the mind; thus they are termed "identical.
The passage beginning with "the mind does not know itself" reveals that such a vision is free from discrimination and devoid of deluded thought. It is said that all [phenomena] arise from ignorance.
As for "emerging": the aforementioned grasping at characteristics all arises from ignorance. The following two phrases do not connect sequentially to the preceding phrase;
rather, they conclude the general summary by clarifying whether these grasped or ungrasped characteristics are manifest or not. This is precisely entering the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) is the foremost.
This note serves as a conclusion. The ancient commentary asks: "Why is this not consistent with the preceding heading?
The Sub-commentary (*Śū*) states: "Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the mind" (up to) "...encompassing all remaining phenomena."
This note indicates the heading. The inclusion of phenomena has already been seen.
The commentary uses the term "only" (*kevala*) to exclude [other factors], hence it is called "Vijñaptimātra" (Cognition-Only).

This note provides a brief general explanation; below follows a detailed and extensive explanation. Regarding the causal nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they are briefly termed "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*). Alternatively, it may be...
And as for "nature" (*svabhāva*).
The commentary does not mean that everything [down to] "are not non-existent";

rather, this section below provides a specific explanation of how all phenomena are subsumed. The positive and negative implications can be understood accordingly. There was an error in the previous topical outline (*kośa*).
The commentary calculates that the nature of what is grasped at (parikalpita-svabhāva), up to [the other two natures], are all not separate from the mind.

The upper note establishes that they must exist; the lower note explains that they are subsumed within the mind. Since the three natures are inseparable and encompass everything, the previous classification was erroneous.
The commentary states that as a verse says (up to): "...and the characteristics of the object are established.

The note explains that the first four lines reveal that the object is not real, while the latter four lines clarify that it appears in accordance with the mind for the four classes of sentient beings.
Because they are perceived as distinct in a single location, they are not real. Regarding the phrase "identical objects," this refers to being in the same place.

Although their essential natures (svabhāva) are distinct, if they were substantially existent (dravyasat), how could they appear in the same location? The *Viṃśatikā* states: "The fact that cognition arises differently in a single location proves that there is only consciousness.
The final four lines provide an analogy to demonstrate that [the appearance of objects] is merely a transformation of the mind.
The Commentary (*shū*) states that since these [points] occur in various places [up to this point], they shall be briefly concluded here.
The Sub-commentary (*zhù*) notes that this refers to other teachings.
The Commentary now examines the sacred teachings [up to this point], which do not exceed five types.
This commentary addresses the fivefold relationship between the subject that contemplates and the object contemplated.

The sub-commentary states: "First, 'discarding the false and preserving the real' (referring to the passage from '...because in principle there is no sentient being') explains this in terms of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Because existence and non-existence differ, the dependent nature (*paratantra*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) are explained together. 'Sentiment' (*qing*) refers to grasping; 'principle' (*li*) refers to..."
[The title] is titled "Zheng" (Correct). In the *Śāstra*, the verse by Bodhisattva Asaṅga states: "[... this is the entry into the three natures. The previous commentary was erroneous;

therefore, the character [should not be read with the preceding line]. The character "wu" (no) should be annotated [as belonging to the following line]. The first verse consists of the four types of thorough investigation (*paryeṣaṇā*).

The second line concerns the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). At the level of inferior *vitarka*, one contemplates that the grasped object (*grāhya*) lacks mutual connection and designates it as "adventitious," which corresponds to the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
In the meditative state, the Bodhisattva contemplates that the reflected image is nothing but mind itself. The first line concerns the stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).

Regarding the superior-grade investigation: one again contemplates the apprehended object and also contemplates the objects of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*). Once these signs have been eliminated, one carefully contemplates one's own mental conceptions (*svasaṃjñā*).
These two mentioned here refer to the aforementioned names and meanings, as well as their intrinsic natures and specific differences, which are not separate from names and meanings.
Therefore, it is not stated separately. Some point this out as the differentiation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*). "Measure" (*pramāṇa*) refers to mind and perception (*saṃjñā*).

That there is only mind and only perception clarifies that [these] do not truly exist; what follows clarifies their conventional existence, which applies to both of the two aforementioned positions. This is the meaning of the three lines of the subsequent verse.

Fourth is the knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*). Under the two phrases of "patience through receptivity" (*kṣānti*), one first seals the apprehended object (*grāhya*). Thus abiding in the internal mind, one knows that the apprehended object does not exist.
Regarding the statement "there is only conceptualization" (*vikalpa-mātra*), both name (*nāman*) and referent (*artha*) each have three types: general and specific.
