This refers to the two or three [aspects]. Since those constitute six, they exist only as conceptual constructions (*parikalpita*), which means they are non-existent in essence. Alternatively, this may include the dependent nature (*paratantra*).

Next, during the middle and superior stages of patience (*kṣānti*), one contemplates and seals that the apprehended object (*grāhya*) is non-existent; consequently, the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*) is also non-existent.

This corresponds to the subsequent statement that "the apprehending subject is also non-existent. The final phrase concludes [the section]: one seals the locus of observation by contemplating the ultimate reality (*tattva*), or one contemplates the state of non-existence. That is to say...
By seeing the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), one enters the three natures. This is the phrase of "non-attainment" that is not subsequently touched.
As for the commentary’s refutation, it employs the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bhāvanā*) to eliminate both emptiness and existence.
The commentary states that there is understanding based on existence within emptiness; this refers to the simultaneous expression of both.
The sub-commentary states that if existence is absent, emptiness is also absent;
this enters into the simultaneous negation of both. The former provides the heading, while the latter establishes the proof.
The Commentary states that from "that emptiness and existence" up to "are all equally determined," this note establishes a dual manifestation.
The Commentary proves that in the stage of True Contemplation (up to "is difficult to conceive"), it is because [the state] is inconceivable.

This commentary addresses this "neither-nor" [position]. Alternatively, together with the preceding section, both constitute a "neither-one-nor-the-other. While the previous [section] used illusion to negate the pure [nature], this relies on its own specific designation (*sva-abhidhāna*).
The Sub-commentary states that one must contemplate emptiness [until realizing that] the true essence is not empty.

This commentary resolves the contradiction. [The objection states: "It arises immediately following the preceding [thought], yet it speaks only of 'contemplating emptiness'; therefore, there is a contradiction.

The intent of the commentary is that while the gate of the emptiness of the parikalpita (imagined nature) reveals the truth, the statement "contemplating emptiness" is spoken from the perspective of that specific gate.
The Commentary [states]: "These words 'consciousness-only' (yǐwéishí) [should be understood as extending] up to 'should also be eliminated.
The Sub-commentary [notes]: Fearing that an outsider might ask, 'Is not the adherence to the Middle Way the correct contemplation? this passage provides a comprehensive response."
The Commentary states that all [sections] from [the beginning] up to this point are subsumed within this contemplation.

The Sub-commentary notes that the eleven subsequent sections all discuss the retention and rejection [of objects], as well as the presence and absence of the objective sphere; therefore, they are subsumed under this section.

This includes everything—existence and non-existence, retention and rejection. Since the initial discussion of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) does not fail to encompass the rest, it is applied accordingly as appropriate.
The "Threefold Unborn Patience" (*tri-anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) refers to: the unborn nature of reality, the spontaneous absence of arising, and the non-arising of delusion and suffering.

Regarding the "Four *Siddhāntas*," this is translated as "the objects of reliance. There are four such objects of reliance: first, the worldly (*loka-vyavahāra*); second, that which is for the benefit of others (*pudgala-vaineya*).
Third is the antidote; fourth is the ultimate meaning; and fourth is the *udāna*. This term has two pronunciations. When pronounced lightly, it is translated as "collected offering" (*jishi*):
by means of few words, many dharmas and meanings are collected and offered to all sentient beings; this refers to the initial verse of the compilation and commentary.

When pronounced heavily, it is translated as "essential summary" (*yao-lue*), which is what is being discussed here: "All that is contaminated is suffering; all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all dharmas..."
Non-self and the tranquility of nirvana—these are the four essentials. In other contexts, they are not necessarily limited to these four alone. The five patiences are, in order:

the patience of subduing, the patience of faith, the patience of conformity, the patience of non-arising, and the patience of cessation; these correspond respectively to the stages prior to the [ten] bhūmis.
The first three [consciousnesses], the next three sets of three, and the final one are assigned to the Buddha.
The commentary states: "To abandon the redundant and retain the pure consciousness" (up to) "it does not say 'only objects'."

The commentary on the "thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita*) has already been dispatched; this merely abandons the name. Above, one begins to cite [the text], but what has not yet appeared is set aside and retained.
The sub-commentary (*śū*) establishes the term "only" (*kevala*), leading up to the statement "only consciousness" (*vijñaptimātra*).
The commentary states that what is erroneously conflated consists of both the substantial nature (*dravya*) and the imagined nature (*parikalpita*).

Furthermore, the sub-commentary notes that from the passage "all foolish commoners" up to "is taught as consciousness-only," it is specifically the imagined nature that is the object of such conflation.
The *Commentary* quotes the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, stating [up to] "the triple world is mind-only," as a scriptural citation for the preceding section.
Since it speaks of both mind and objects, it serves as proof for this present gate.
The *Commentary* further quotes the *Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda Sūtra*, stating [up to] "all are subsumed within this contemplation."

This note serves to subsume the remainder; it is not a citation of scriptural authority. It merely manifests the state of mind and its objects, rather than manifesting their actual existence or their negation.
Therefore, within this section, the two preceding sūtras also apply to both existence and negation.
Commentary: "Bringing the branches back to the root consciousness" (up to) "because in the Dharma of the Final Age they do not exist. Annotation:
This brings the branches of the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) and *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect) back to the root of the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-cognizing aspect).
Commentary: Therefore, the Thirty Verses on Consciousness-Only states (up to) "these transformations are only three."
The commentary on the first one and a half verses briefly addresses external objections and provides a concise definition of the characteristics of consciousness (*vijñapti*).

Here, however, there is only one verse, with two further lines below it stating: "the ripening [consciousness], the deliberating [consciousness], and the consciousness that discriminates objects. The present section specifically employs the meaning of the third line;
the remaining text follows as a consequence and is therefore not cited in its entirety. An opponent objects: "If there is only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), how is it so?"

The world and the various holy teachings speak of a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*). Now, the first two lines answer objections and refute attachments [by showing that these] exist only as conventional designations and do not exist as separate, real entities.
The third line briefly indicates the tenet of this treatise: those conventional selves and phenomena.
It is established solely based on the two divisions that arise through the transformation of consciousness. As for the fourth phrase, it belongs to the heading;

therefore, the accompanying prose merely explains the character "transformation" (*pariṇāma*). The *Commentary on the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "[... up to "because it arises from self-cognition."

Regarding the commentary on this passage concerning the basis (*āśraya*) and the based (*āśrita*), only one interpretation is cited here. Within the school of Dharmapāla, it is held that the self-attesting essence (*svasaṃvitti-svabhāva*) transforms to give rise to the two divisions of the other-dependent nature:

the aspect (*nimitta*) and the vision (*darśana*). Therefore, the derivative functions are subsumed and returned to the fundamental essence, which is the self-verifying division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).
The *Commentary on the Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* explains [the passage] up to "manifested by consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) as that which is transformed.

"Manifested" (*xian*) means "transformed" (*bian*). This term "object-condition" (*ālambana*) correctly refers to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*). It is said that the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) takes its own image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) as its object;

this is explained through a successive progression. Furthermore, it is appropriate to say that this is the ultimate returning to the fundamental substance. It is not [the case that] the self-... [text ends].

The aspect of realization directly takes the two extremes as its object and only then subsumes them back [into the middle]. This is not the same as the meaning of "transformation," which can directly transform the two;
the term "transformation" (pariṇāma) is broad in its application because it refers to a process of transformation.
The commentary (*śūtra*) subsumes the characteristics of the perceived object (*nimitta-dṛṣṭi*) and returns them to the fundamental consciousness;
thus, these two phrases are annotated as being applicable to all the passages from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* cited previously.
The phenomena and principles explained in the commentary are all encompassed within this section.
This note summarizes the remainder; it does not explicitly state the negation, but merely speaks of observing conditions. Therefore, the aspects and views are contained within this gate.
As for those that explicitly state the negation, they are found in the first gate; there is no fault in their being common to both.
The Commentary (Sūtra): Section Four, "Concealing the Inferior and Revealing the Superior Consciousness" (extending to) "Revealing Only the Superior Dharma.

The Sub-commentary (Note): This proceeds from the shallow to the profound. First, it eliminates the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*); second, it discards the names of objects; third, it subsumes the aspects (*nimitta*) and the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) so as to return them to self-realization (*svasaṃvitti*).

This is because [the aspects and seeing-part] still appear as distinct from the self-realization of the subject and object. This section subsumes the inferior into the superior and conceals [the former].
The term "mental factors" (caitta) does not exclude their substance;
therefore, Maitreya stated that there are no separate defiled or wholesome dharmas.

Having already established in the first sentence that the transformation of the mind consists of two parts, and that these two parts are not real but are termed "semblances," he explains that it transforms them.
Because it appears as such, it is called "the mind transforming and appearing as [objects]. The next two phrases refer to the mental factors (caitta), which depend upon the mind;

since they are of the same nature as the two divisions [of subject and object], they are also called "transforming and appearing. Furthermore, they are not real, because they arise depending upon the mind.
The Commentary states that the words of Vimalakīrti (up to) "are all subsumed within this contemplation.
The Sub-commentary notes: "This is the inclusion of all other minds directed toward objects; they are all subsumed within this gate.
The Commentary states: "5. Discarding marks to realize the nature of consciousness" (up to) "one should seek to realize it."
The preceding was contemplation based on phenomena; this is contemplation based on principle. This [contemplation] dispels the essence, yet it is not the same as the former.
That [former] dispelled it because there was no essence; this merely dispels it because it is not perceived.
The *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) on the verses of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Knowing [the rope] as a snake is deluded cognition.

The commentary notes that the snake is a metaphor for the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), the rope for the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), and the hemp fibers for the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).

"Fragments" refers to the fragments of hemp. The first phrase reveals the basis—the grasping at the *paratantra*. Next, seeing the *paratantra* means one realizes the *parikalpita*. Finally, seeing the hemp fragments serves as the analogy.

Realizing the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), one does not perceive the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as one does the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). This is based on true contemplation (*bhūta-darśana*).
This differs slightly in its intended meaning from the sequence of realization and vision presented in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Verses).
The Commentary states that the teachings of other sutras regarding the mind (up to the point mentioned) are all subsumed within this contemplation.

The Sub-commentary notes that these collectively subsume the remainder; however, those that manifest the locus of reality are all subsumed within this gate, as there is nothing therein that contradicts it.
Regarding the second text, there are ten gates: the emptiness of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is the empty Tathāgatagarbha; the empty Tathāgatagarbha.

There are two ways of explaining [this]. Here, we adopt the explanation of the *tathāgatagarbha* as revealed by the contemplation of emptiness. The passage beginning with "free from all conceptual discrimination" provides the general explanation.
The commentary states: "Thus what has been explained... [up to] 'comprehensively subsumes everything'."
Commentary: Focusing on emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is exclusively non-existence. In the external world there is substance, yet its function possesses the characteristic of being visible;

this is hidden from the self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*) of the subject. Since both the characteristic and the object are eliminated, it is progressively subtle. Above this, whether based on what is negated or what arises, there is likewise progressive subtlety.

In reality, this permeates all five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), yet it is purely internal. Fundamentally, it is merely self-realization; the latter two [aspects] can be understood accordingly. Therefore, it is progressively subtle.
The *Śū* (Commentary) states that from "through hearing, reflection, and cultivation" up to "the meaning is common to the former two.

The *Zhù* (Annotation) notes that although three [stages] were previously established, their essence (*tǐ*) and function (*yòng*) had not yet been distinguished; therefore, they are now distinguished again.

Furthermore, the previous [section] mentioned them in relation to the stage of entry (*rùwèi*), so the text did not repeat them. Within this [section], there are two parts: first, the essence; second, the meaning. Within the latter, there are the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and...

Regarding the untainted (*anāsrava*): within the tainted (*sāsrava*), it includes both that acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*) and that produced through application (*prāyogika*); and regarding the three realms (*tridhātu*). Regarding the untainted: from the perspective of its essential nature (*svabhāva*), it is so described;

yet from the perspective of its functional meaning (*artha*), it also extends to those produced through hearing and reflection (*śruta-maya* and *cintā-maya*). It is also like the process of adding or correcting.
Commentary: These various forms of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only), up to [the point mentioned], are still not yet the truly supreme.
The sub-commentary states that looking down upon the seeds and so forth, one should proceed from this stage. The preceding contemplation of *vijñaptimātra* constitutes the dharma to be studied;

from this point downward, one enters the stages where one becomes capable of such study. Accordingly, these serve as the objects of study. Furthermore, consider that the words [of the previous section] were not yet fully sufficient.

Regarding the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*): this is not yet the stage of actual cultivation, but rather the stage of resolute belief and understanding (*adhimukti-avasthā*). It excludes the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
The Commentary [states] that from the stage of preparatory application up to the stage of universal knowledge (*parijñā*), [the object] does not exist.

The four types of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) mentioned here refer to the four preparatory stages (*prayoga*), each being a single *samādhi*, such as the "increasing illumination" (*vṛddhāloka*) and so forth; the rest is explained as usual.

In this context, the preceding sections on "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) are explained together because they are termed "investigation" (*paryeṣaṇā*). Subsequently, the two latter [stages] are explained together with "knowledge as it truly is" (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*).
The Commentary states: "Therefore, the Honored One of Sage Compassion" (up to) "subsequently touching upon non-apprehension.

The commentary notes that two phrases refer to the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and two phrases refer to the stage of the Summit (*mūrdhan*). Both involve contemplating the apprehended object (*grāhya*). Regarding the character *shàng* (上), there is a difference in the intended reading;

in the treatise it is the character *xiàng* (相). Alternatively, the character is not erroneous. A conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) regarding an object is called "conceptualization of an object" (*artha-saṃjñā*); this also entails no fault. (2)

At the stage of "patience regarding the words" (*pada-kṣānti*), one realizes that the apprehended object (*grāhya*) is non-existent. Next, at the stages of medium and superior patience, one contemplates the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*).

At the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), both types of apprehension are unified. In the final phrase, the immediate precursor is raised, whereby one enters the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The Commentary [states]: "This stage of the Bodhisattva... has not yet realized the truth.
The Sub-commentary notes that this distinguishes it from the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), concluding the previous section and introducing the next.
The Commentary further explains that within the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*)... one only then attains the name of "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*).
The commentary below concerns the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). The four lines correspond to the first two lines of the verse;

the remaining lines correspond to the phrase "at that time abiding in consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*), or alternatively, to the first six lines of the verse. The preceding three lines of the verse have already been explained, while the concluding line has not yet been interpreted.

This section also explains the meaning of the term: *tong* (通) means "to embody" (*tattva*), and *da* (達) means "to realize" (*adhigama*). To embody and realize *tathatā* (suchness) is therefore called "thorough realization" (*prativedha*). Hereafter...
These four lines further explain and establish what preceded them regarding the preparatory practice (*prayoga*).
Therefore, the root verse states: "Because one is free from the marks of the two graspings" (*dvaya-grāha-nimitta-vigamāt*).

The commentary notes that one first realizes true contemplation (*tattva-darśana*) while still in the stage of preparatory application; because the two marks [of subject and object] still exist, it is said that one does not yet truly abide in the state of mere-consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).

Therefore, it is said: "If at any time, within the object of cognition, non-conceptual wisdom is entirely devoid of both the two aspects of existence and emptiness, that time is called truly abiding in consciousness-only; this is the stage of thorough penetration."
The subsequent phrase provides a concluding explanation, turning back to examine the subject and object.
The commentary (*shu*) establishes that true consciousness [extends] from "having been realized" up to "though it exists, it is not real.

The sub-commentary (*zhu*) here establishes the characteristics of the seeing and the seen; this is easy to understand from the prose (*changxing*). Within the verse (*songwen*), one knows the root and understands the branches, as it says:
When realizing and seeing those factors such as time, they differ from their previous functions. The latter three phrases are connected.
In this section of the commentary, [it says] "up to" attaining unsurpassed enlightenment.

The commentary on this consists of four sections, with further subdivisions numbering in the hundreds; it would be impossible to record them all in full. The classification [of this section] as "Explanation of Names" (Shiming) is incorrect;
it should be titled "Virtues and Merits" (Gongde), for by this title everything can be fully subsumed.

In the *Śāstra* (Commentary), from the section on the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) up to "arising of superior practice," the *Ṭīkā* (Sub-commentary) explains this as distinguishing the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). It analyzes it separately into four sections: with effort (*anābhoga*) and without effort (*sābhoga*), and mastery (*vaśitā*) and non-mastery (*avaśitā*).

Regarding the phrase "possessing superior practice" (*sa-viśeṣa-caryā*): "possessing" (*sa*) refers to the contemplation of reality (*yathābhūta-parīkṣā*); "practice within that" (*tad-antargatā caryā*) consists of acting for the benefit of others.
It is victorious. That is, within true contemplation (*tathatā-darśana*), one is able to give rise [to it] immediately. Emptiness is precisely true contemplation.
According to the Commentary, at the stage of ultimate realization, one gives rise to consciousness that takes both the ultimate and the conventional as its objects.
This commentary on the stage of the Tathāgata shows that all stages ultimately converge upon the contemplation of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
Herein, the temporal stage does not include the resultant stage (*phala-avasthā*), as this is explained incidentally.
The commentary states that there are two types of cultivation (up to): "However, they possess both seeds and manifestations.
The note should divide the sub-text according to the following passage; the old outline’s major divisions do not capture the intended meaning.
Regarding the commentary’s statement "as for cultivation" (up to) "grows to full completion":
this note clarifies the ritual procedure of cultivation as well as its characteristics and functions. To cause [the qualities] to increase is the meaning of "cultivation.
This gives rise to the following text.

Regarding the commentary’s statement from “Those who possess mastery” (至) to “cannot cultivate the higher stages,” the sub-commentary notes that this refers to whether one can or cannot increase [the cultivation]. Since there is a superior path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) which is attained through collateral cultivation,
to further divide this into sub-sections as a major heading would constitute an error.
The Commentary [states] "this is the cultivation of *vijñapti-mātra* (up to) because it is the cultivation of *vijñapti-mātra*.

The Sub-commentary [notes] that this is stated as a "comprehensive inclusion" (*saṃgraha*) in the sense of being inseparable, and not based on the characteristics of the cultivation itself; otherwise, there would be a contradiction.
The Commentary asks: "What are the characteristics of the fruits of this abbreviated practice?
Since this question is general, the following two sections [of the Commentary] address it.
The Commentary states: "Regarding those who practice with outflows... they may attain everything."
The commentary should state that the first [section] relies on distinct functions, while the latter relies on mutual support; thus, dividing it into three segments does not present any difficulty.
This reference to "outflows" (āsrava) does not include everything; rather, it refers to the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*) and the seven stages prior to the eighth.
The Commentary states that having briefly explained the abbreviated cultivation, it now asks:

"How is extensive cultivation practiced? The sub-commentary clarifies that the section above elucidates abbreviated cultivation, taking *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) as its primary tenet; the section below distinguishes extensive cultivation, taking the *Yogācārabhūmi* as its foundation.

Because both the text and its meaning are extensive, it is called "extensive cultivation"; it does not mean that a brief [treatise] is extensively explained, which would be termed "abbreviated-extensive."
The commentary (*śāstra*) likewise contains these three [sections] (up to) the three types of persons who train.
It cites the text of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, which consists of twenty-eight chapters divided into four sections: the first eighteen chapters constitute the *Yogasthāna* (The Basis of Yoga);
the next four chapters constitute the *Anudharmayoga* (Conformity with the Dharma); the following five chapters constitute the *Niṣṭhāyoga* (Ultimate Yoga); and finally...

This first section consists of sequential yoga (*anupūrvayoga*). At the beginning, there are three "retentions" (*dhāraṇī*): the lineage (*gotra*) and the generation of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), each having one chapter;

the retention of the practice of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya-pratipatti*), which has sixteen chapters; the five chapters on the points of training (*śikṣāpada*); and one chapter on the methods of training (*śikṣā-dharma*). These constitute thirty-eight [chapters].
The ten chapters concerning the person capable of training concern the objects to be known (*jñeya-viṣaya*), which should be understood as they truly are. As...
Regarding "the dharmas to be studied" as explained below: this refers to the rules of training.

For example, when going to receive the precepts, how one goes there and arrives there, and what the proper deportment and ritual procedures are—these are the methods by which one can train. The person who is able to train is demonstrated by the following practice, as explained below.
In the commentary, it first states "one should know" (up to) "the one who is able to train.

The sub-commentary asks: what is to be known, and by what means is it known? Regarding the phrase "relying on that," it means relying on those principles or relying on the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*);
by training in such principles, one becomes one who is truly able to train—this refers to the practitioner (*śaikṣa*). At [the point]...
In the "Discrimination among Humans," it is necessarily required that one study the Dharma concurrently;
therefore, all three are subsumed under the practices of a Bodhisattva.
The commentary states that the first two rely on learning, which is itself practice.
In the initial section on the objects of study, there are briefly five kinds.

Since the commentary states that the Bodhisattva takes great compassion as primary, they first know the distinctions among the lineages (*gotra*) of those to be converted and should then bring them to maturity.

This refers only to maturing others; next, one knows the practice of beneficial conduct (*artha-caryā*), which likewise refers only to others, before finally realizing one’s own sphere and severing [defilements].
Regarding the distinctions in cultivation: having understood the objects of knowledge, one knows for oneself the power and the fruit attained;
thus there are five types, in this specific sequence, neither more nor less. According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, regarding the points of training, there are seven dharmas and five categories:
the first two dharmas constitute one category, namely, the benefit of self and others; the second is the category of the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*); the third is the category of power...
In the "Chapter on Powers" (Bala-paṭala), the fourth chapter, "The Maturation of the Two Dharmas," matures both oneself and others.

The fifth chapter, "Enlightenment" (Bodhi-paṭala), is different in what way? Answer: The treatise [in the previous context] relies upon maturation for the sake of maturing one's own welfare, which is proximate to enlightenment.

Now, it relies upon benefiting others, establishing those who are to be converted by others. Because this occurs prior to benefiting others, it has been moved to the preceding section; thus, there is no contradiction.
Commentary: Regarding the first section on the places where beings are transformed (up to "matured as appropriate"):
the note refers to the thirty-seventh [chapter], the Chapter on Maturation (*paripāka*). Among the two dharmas and six gates therein, the "two dharmas" are:
first, maturing one's own Buddha-dharma; second, maturing other sentient beings. Here, we deal only with the latter. For what reason? Precisely...
Because it is for the sake of benefiting others, and because it brings about one’s own maturation through the gateway of majestic power (*prabhāva*), this [topic] is abbreviated here.

Thus, at the conclusion of the section on majestic power, the commentary briefly indicates that it accomplishes one’s own Buddha-dharmas. Regarding the six gateways: first, the maturation of oneself and others;
second, the persons to be matured; third, the distinctions of maturation; fourth, the means of maturation; fifth, the person who effects maturation; sixth, [the result].

[The beings] have already been matured; now, this [text] merely concerns that which is to be accomplished. That [passage] lists the four castes (*catur-varṇa*); the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*) are without fixed caste (*agotra*).

This statement is not definitive; it should be understood according to other sources. Regarding those who are capable of being delivered and those who are not, one must first understand them as they should be delivered.
What is called "maturation" (*paripācana*) means causing virtue to increase, encompassing both oneself and others. Now, however—
"Taking up" refers to bringing others to maturity.

Regarding the commentary's statement "one should diligently cultivate [the practices] for the benefit of others," although the practice of benefiting others actually encompasses both types of benefit (self and others), it mentions benefiting others here specifically; this should be understood according to the previous section on accomplishment.
There are also sentient beings who belong neither to the category of benefiting oneself nor to the category of benefiting others.

According to the thirty-fifth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the "Chapter on Benefiting Oneself and Others," there are ten types of benefit; here, however, only the first two are addressed. These are: (1) purely benefiting oneself and purely benefiting others;

and (2) benefiting oneself while simultaneously benefiting others, and benefiting others while simultaneously benefiting oneself. Regarding purely benefiting oneself, one should exclusively abandon [such actions]; regarding benefiting others, both [types] are permitted.
That which should be cultivated and that which should be abandoned are both for the benefit of others; that which is solely for cultivation is as described in the present text.

That which is purely for self-benefit consists of seven points, with two phrases constituting each point. Although one may engage in study and practice, if it is done solely for oneself, it is termed "miserliness regarding the Dharma" (*dharmamātsarya*).
Wealth, status, wife, servants, property, and the like are termed "defiled fruits. To view these with attachment and clinging constitutes [the first point].
He was then released, only to become his own slave once more. In such cases as these, the Bodhisattva severs [the cycle] exclusively for the sake of benefiting others.

Within this pure benefit for others, there are two meanings, which may be understood from the text. One should cultivate both types of benefit, encompassing both gates; however, they cannot be recorded in full detail here.
Commentary: Section Three on the Topic of True Reality (up to) "to be cultivated and abandoned as appropriate.
Note: That which accords with principle and corresponds to reality is called "true reality" (*tattva*). Based upon the two natures, four types of true reality are established;

all true realities do not transcend these. Regarding the nature as it is (*yathāvadbhāva*) and the nature in its full extent (*yāvadbhāva*), [the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] fascicle thirty-six states: "All..."

Regarding the "reality of phenomena" (*dharmatattva*) and the "all-nature of all phenomena," there are two interpretations of the former: first, based on the distinction between the objects of focus in their original and subsequent states;

second, based on the distinction between principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), wherein principle extends to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Regarding the latter, there are two interpretations: first, in terms of the essence and meaning of all phenomena;
second, in terms of how the essence of suchness (*tathatā*) encompasses everything. Furthermore, there are seven other gateways which cannot be recorded in full here. As for the four realities:
First, worldly established reality (*loka-prasiddha-tattva*): this refers to that which is transmitted from one to another among worldly people;
for instance, [the notion] that "this is earth" and so forth is also called reality because it accords with convention. Second, logical reality (*yukti-tattva*):

while abiding in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), there are things established by means of the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and fourfold reasoning; because they do not contradict reason, they are called reality. Third...
The reality that is the object of knowledge purified of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa-viśuddhi-jñāna-gocara-tattva*) is precisely the Four Noble Truths.

It is the sphere of activity attained by those of the Two Vehicles through the abandonment of delusions; according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it takes the principle of the knowledge of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*) as its essence.

The reality that is the object of knowledge purified of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa-viśuddhi-jñāna-gocara-tattva*) is taken by Bodhisattvas and others as the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). These two differ in that, regarding the Truths, [the former] possesses...
Because it is the Path, it does not admit of outflows (*sāsrava*).

Regarding the four bases of power (*pratihārya-sthāna*)—namely, the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā-pratihārya*)—the commentary notes that these powers are categorized within the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*). Of these, there are three in the first group and five in the latter. As for the first three, the first is the Noble [Path].
There are two categories of dharmas. Third is the power of co-nascence. Now, the latter five are cited: first, supernormal powers; second, dharmas;

third, co-nascence; fourth, common; and fifth, uncommon. Regarding what is called the "power of supernormal faculties," this is the first [category], namely the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*).
Commentary: From "The Six Perfections" (to) "named the power of the Dharma.

Note: The character "shàn" (good) in the transmission is an error; it should be the character "míng" (name). This explains that each of the six perfections possesses four characteristics, which are named the power of the Dharma:
first, the characteristic of abandoning what is to be countered; second, the characteristic of accomplishing the provisions; [third], benefiting sentient beings.
Characteristics. Fourth is the characteristic of the future fruit. In the text regarding giving, only the first and last are mentioned.
The second characteristic is the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment and the maturation of sentient beings. The third characteristic also has three aspects:
being joyful before giving, being pure while giving, and having no regret after giving—this absence of regret at the three times is called self-benefit. It eliminates... [text ends]

Alleviating the sufferings of others is the very way to benefit them; this is the fourth characteristic. In future lives, one will obtain great wealth, treasures, followers, and retinues; the remaining five [characteristics] should be understood accordingly.

The six perfections are established within the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). The first [perfection] is the characteristic of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings, which is the means of attraction through generosity (*dāna*).
The subsequent four are the means of attraction through common purpose (*samānārthatā*); wisdom permeates all four means of attraction. As for the remainder...
Consider this according to the *Śāstra*. The commentary states: "For the benefit of sentient beings... [up to] innate power.

The note explains that there are four meanings here, all of which are termed "innate" (*sahaja*) because they are accomplished without deliberate mental application (*amanasikāra*). Regarding the second...
First, one is able to endure from birth, not through deliberate reflection. The four types of birth are entrusted to the eight phases [of a Buddha's life] which follow.
The Treatise states that when he was a bodhisattva, all birds, beasts, and even wriggling insects placed their utmost trust in him.

As for the "eight phases," they are: first, dwelling in heaven; second, entering the womb; third, dwelling in the womb; fourth, emerging from the womb; fifth, leaving home; sixth, attaining [enlightenment]; seventh, turning the wheel of the Dharma; eighth, entering parinirvāṇa.

The Path; seventh, turning the wheel of Dharma; eighth, parinirvāṇa. There is also the addition of "subduing Māra," while the "dwelling in heaven" is excluded because [the Buddha] does not remain below.

The Commentary states that from "the sentient beings of the dharma-realm" up to "accomplishing one's own Buddha-dharma," the latter two [of the three types of power] possess three characteristics not shared with the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). First, the subtle characteristic:
thoroughly knowing immeasurable skillful means and benefits. Second, the characteristic of categories: fully accomplishing the aforementioned three types of majestic power throughout the three times.
Regarding the characteristics of the realms (*dhātu-lakṣaṇa*): the entire world of sentient and insentient beings constitutes its objective sphere (*viṣaya*).

Excluding the three aforementioned characteristics, the coarse characteristic is termed "common. This text, however, contains only the three uncommon characteristics; these three phrases constitute the beginning: place, time, and the vessel of the Dharma.
The three meanings may be understood as follows. The second is supernormal power (*abhijñā*); for brevity, it does not mention the [magical] creation of phenomena or that which arises simultaneously.

From "the transformation of objects" (*nirmāṇa-viṣaya*) onwards constitutes the third characteristic. Within the exhortation at the conclusion, the personal accomplishment is included; such is its origination, according to the treatise.
The Commentary on the Five Stages of Bodhi (up to) "the fruit which one hopes to realize.
The Note is in the middle of the eighteen [sections]. The two abandonments and the two knowledges constitute the essence of the two fruits of transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Herein, they are treated as the objects to be known; the subsequent factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) are taken as the causes.
The Commentary (*śāstra*) thus [discusses] these five points up to "diligent cultivation and realization.
The Sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains the sequence here while also showing the reasons for their inclusion or exclusion; this differs from the main treatise (*śāstra*), as previously reconciled.
Based on this, "spontaneous accomplishment" and "self-benefit" are appended to the section on "powerful efficacy" (*prabhāva*), because the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are present therein.

The commentary, from "Having understood the training rules" up to "the dharmas to be studied," annotates the thirty-eighth chapter, the *Bala-gotra-paṭala*. It contains seven sections. First, one must first resolve upon faith regarding eight points;
thereafter, one seeks the Dharma. Having obtained it, one correctly expounds it; thereafter, one practices it oneself. Having practiced it, one teaches others. Thus one cultivates.

Having skillfully severed evil, one then employs the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the three types of action (*trikarma*) to benefit others. Question: Regarding these dharmas to be studied, what is meant by the "seed-lineage of power" (*balagotra*)?
Answer: The *Za lun tong* (Compendium of Concordant Treatises) states: "Power refers to the ten powers (*daśabala*). This is precisely the seed-lineage of the ten powers.

While the previous chapter on "Seed-Lineage" (*Gotraparivarta*) explained all [aspects] in general, it did not specifically clarify the cultivation of the seed-lineage of the ten powers; this [chapter] now clarifies that specifically.

Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Lineage of Powers" (*balagotra-varga*). Question: Why is it specifically the lineage of powers? Answer: Because the Ten Powers (*daśabala*) largely consist of this [wisdom], and one seeks awakening through them.
Furthermore, consider that within the primary objects of pursuit in the lower treatise, there are three aspects of inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*); the first is the primary cause and effect.

The power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible is the lineage; the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma—both what has been done and what has not yet been done—is the lineage.
Regarding the remaining eight powers within the context of instruction, one must contemplate their underlying reasons.
In the commentary, from the beginning regarding the Three Jewels up to "decisive joy," there are eight points:
first, the Three Jewels; second, power; third, reality; fourth, the causal stage; fifth, the resultant stage;
sixth, the stage of the benefits to be attained—namely, enlightenment; seventh, the means for this; and eighth, virtuous speech.
Well said. Regarding these eight points, one should seek the Dharma with pure faith and resolute conviction;
following this sequence, one should seek it with right diligence.
As for that which is to be sought, it refers to the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*). Among these five, the first three each have two aspects. The first is the science of medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*).
The four characteristics. The *Abhidharma* (Karma-prakāśa) is immeasurable, as described in the *Juyao*.
The commentary (*shu*) should state: "How does one seek [the teachings] up to loving virtue and loving the Dharma?

The sub-commentary (*zhu*) explains the mode of seeking. Below this, it merely describes the seeking within the *Adhyātma-vidyā* (Inner Science). By analogy, this constitutes "loving and valuing" (*ai-zhong*).

Seeking to hear [the Dharma]. The four lines serve as the heading; the two analogies demonstrate the characteristics. Lun says: "The two analogies are used for comparison to clarify the locus. The two analogies are thus understood.
Below the section on "the footless," the text continues with the subsequent analogy and concludes the passage according to the dharma.

The ancients explained this as "going to listen for seven reasons," while the following section discusses "seeing the teacher for seven reasons. Lun says: "This is to further clarify the gravity [of the occasion]. There is a judgment already established.

To revere the Dharma above all and seek to hear it, while subsequently showing respect to the teacher—this judgment is excellent. Within the section on revering the Dharma, the preceding passage correctly clarifies this reverence;
the subsequent passage, which possesses the correct intention (*āśaya*), is this very text. Now, because of such loving reverence, there is no sense of satiety and so forth.
Therefore, other examples do not serve as metaphors. The two characters share a single meaning.
The commentary proceeds to the passage concerning the Venerable Master (until the phrase "the thought of delight").

The annotation states that from "having made a judgment" onwards, the text spanning approximately five lines is entirely for the purpose of honoring the teacher; this section is divided into two parts.

The first is the mind endowed with merit, comprising approximately three lines. Following the phrase "in accordance with the occasion," there is the mind free from defilement. Now, having examined the root treatise (*śāstra*).
The five kinds of thoughts of delight and the five kinds of thoughts of difference are found in the "Chapter on Cultivation" (*Sannikarṣa-varga*).
This chapter contains only a mind free from dispute and a mind free from arrogance, as well as that which is solely for the sake of goodness.

If one judges according to the previous [classification], it merely classifies the text of that "Chapter on Cultivation" and has never classified the text of the present chapter. Now, from this perspective, it is directly judged as follows:
Three. First, regarding reliance on the weighty Dharma, as may be understood from what precedes. Second, respecting the teacher. Third, the time of listening.

Within the section on respecting the teacher, first the avoidance of faults is clarified, followed by the cultivation of virtue. In the former, there are two parts; first, being free from a mind of interrogation or challenge.

This is because it follows a pleasant and agreeable intention, and subsequently lacks a mind of haughtiness; it is the reverse of a contrary intention. Therefore, the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) has cited it in this manner.
Otherwise, for what reason would there be such an intermingling? Only the passage beginning with "having acted as a wondrous jewel" and below [is relevant].

Regarding the five pleasant and agreeable intentions, the *Forty-four [Thousand Dharmas]* states: "First is the jewel, because its meaning is difficult to fathom; second is the eye, because it is obtained simultaneously."

First, it is the nature of the cause of wisdom (*prajñā*), because it has the sense of being the cause for wisdom. Second, it is illumination, because it has the sense of already having attained the eye of wisdom and so forth to shine upon all things.

Third, it is the fruit, because it has the sense of being the causal nature capable of attaining the sublime fruit. Fourth, it is faultless (*anavadya*), because regarding that which has not yet been attained, it correctly possesses the sense of being the causal nature of faultlessness.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states that one generates deep respect (up to) the notion of having a different intention.

The commentary on the first two phrases is found within the relevant chapter. Because one does not disparage others, there is no fault of arrogance. This reverses the "inferiority" of having a different intention;
the subsequent text, beginning with "not breaking the precepts," constitutes the five types of thoughts of having a different intention, which are found among the forty-four [types of thoughts].
There are ten characters in this interval; two characters constitute a single meaning.
In the *Śū* (Commentary), it says "merely for the sake of seeking goodness" (至) and "seeking the True Dharma" (而求正法).

In the *Zhù* (Annotation), it states that the phrase "fearing [rebirth] and seeking the True Dharma" belongs to the preceding section; thus, "this is merely for the sake of goodness" also reaches back to connect with what precedes.
The Commentary states: "One should be reverent" (up to) "...seeking [the teaching] with a compliant mind.
The Sub-commentary explains these two meanings below: being free from defilement and being free from distraction. Regarding the time of listening, one is free from such faults;
relying on the treatise, one proceeds further, arising from what preceded. This freedom from defilement arises based on the former two; as for distraction, it relies solely on the former.
One is born as a virtuous being. Because one does not disparage oneself out of reverence for the Buddha, one does not belittle oneself; furthermore, one reflects upon this correspondence.
Within the discussion on freedom from defilement (*vairāgya*), there are three types. Here, the second type—freedom from contempt—is absent. Among these, the first is freedom from pride (*māna*).
Within that, there are six meanings, all of which are present here. The first two lines constitute this [point].
There are three meanings. Two characters share one meaning; "listening" and "hearing" pervade all three. The following two phrases also contain three meanings.

The two characters "do not" and "arise" pervade the subsequent "harmful interference," which is the fourth meaning. Furthermore, they also pervade the character "accordant," which is the fifth meaning.
"Not to comply" means not to bend or conform to human sentiments. Furthermore, "do not give rise [to such thoughts]" governs the three characters that follow;
this is the sixth meaning.
The commentary states: "One should not disparage even one's own person."
Note: This is the third [point], distancing oneself from cowardice.
The commentary (shū) states: "Solely for the sake of seeking the Dharma" [up to] "sweeping away and maintaining.
Note: This is the distancing from distraction (*vikṣepa*). It has five meanings: the first phrase has one meaning, while the remaining [phrases] each have two characters. The final two [points]...
Regarding the mind:
[the commentary asks] for what purpose does one seek?
The note explains that "purpose" (yi) means "benefit" (li). For what benefit, then, does one seek the True Dharma?

The Commentary, from the section on the Inner Science (*adhyātma-vidyā*) up to "the provisions are swiftly fulfilled," notes that when Bodhisattvas seek these treatises on the five fields of knowledge (*pañca-vidyā-sthāna*), it is for the purpose of benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings;
this is their intended meaning. Nevertheless, they must study them in succession. As the Treatise says: "In this way, regarding the treatises revealed in the field of the inner science..."
The characteristics of correct cause and effect are such that what has been done is not lost, and what has not been done is not obtained.

By practicing with diligent application, one causes the lineage of the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and impossible and one's own karma to gradually become purified and gradually increase.

In the sub-commentary (*śāstra*), the passage from "one should next act for others" up to "according to their needs for benefit and happiness" consists of two phrases as the heading and two phrases as the response. Upon examining the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are three questions and three responses;
this corresponds to the answers to the first and the last questions, as the treatise also first provides the answers to those two. The treatise states:
When a bodhisattva teaches the sublime Dharma to others, what should be taught? How should it be taught? For what purpose is it taught?

The first question concerns that which is taught; the second concerns the method of instruction; the third concerns the benefit. Herein, the teaching of the five fields of knowledge (*pañca-vidyā-sthāna*) answers the first question regarding the Dharma to be taught.
Teaching in accordance with what is appropriate for the welfare and happiness [of beings] answers the third question regarding the benefit.

Regarding "benefit" (*artha*): the treatise states that this refers to that which Bodhisattvas should correctly seek; it is precisely what has been explained. Seeking for this purpose, and for this very purpose, they teach it to others.
This can be understood by correlating it with the questions. Both [cases] rely on the aforementioned seeking and the teaching of the Dharma.

Therefore, the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) are taught. As for the benefits of the five sciences, since each was previously explained, the term "according to what is appropriate" (*yathāyogam*) is used. [This concludes] the former [section].
There is an error in the classification. Question: Why are these called the "dharmas to be studied"? Answer: Because they are said to be "learning" (śikṣā) as well;
furthermore, up to the three types of action (trikarma), they constitute the essential core of learning, and moreover, they are all that is required—namely, the dharmas.
The Commentary asks: "How is it explained?
The Sub-commentary notes that this is the method for explaining the intermediate questions.
The Commentary states that from "one should abide" up to "is called explaining in accordance" [constitutes the response].
This commentary addresses the questions within this response. The treatise contains two types of questions: general and specific.
The first concerns that which one should preach to others in accordance with [the teaching]; the second concerns that which one should preach to others with purity.

This is the first section. Within the text of the treatise, there are fifteen characteristics: first, timeliness; second, reverence for the Dharma; third, sequential order; fourth, continuity; fifth...
1. Conforming; 2. Joy; 3. Affectionate delight; 4. Serene gladness; 5. Exultant courage;
6. Non-rejection; 7. Appropriateness; 8. Accordance; 9. Absence of confusion; 10. Conformity with the Dharma.

Fifteen points on conforming to the assembly. Now, five characteristics are cited regarding conduct in accordance with the Dharma (*yathādharma-vinaya*); this is the first period, for it is the principle and meaning.
Not possessing proper decorum is contrary to principle. One does not sit upon a high seat; this is the second point, out of respect for the Dharma. Furthermore, there are three other [points]:
one does not speak while standing when others are seated; one does not walk in front [of others]; and one does not cover one’s head. All [these]...
Such are these matters; as stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there are twenty rules concerning the preaching of the Dharma.
In the present text, because it reaches the point of "extreme veneration," all subsequent passages serve to explain this characteristic and should be explained without interruption.

Regarding the third sequence: it refers to explaining for others in a sequential manner without any gaps. One should not act like a teacher who receives offerings, nor should one exhibit signs of stinginess. This is the sequence.

The four [types of] continuity. The current text is not in sequential order. The *Śāstra* states: "Furthermore, regarding the True Dharma, one does not give rise to stinginess, nor does one act as a teacher who holds it back.
Therefore, the current text is not in sequential order. The meaning of this characteristic is as follows: a person who is stingy with the Dharma has a cessation of its teaching.
As for the term "acting as a teacher" (*shifeng*), Lun says that "fist" (*quan*) signifies grasping and not letting go; this is precisely the characteristic of stinginess. This is also explained.

One should not harbor the intention of acting as a master or teacher. Furthermore, the *Qieyun* states: "Quánquán" means anxiety. Following what the assembly delights in, the sequence is marked and explained.

Fifth, regarding "following the assembly," the treatise marks and follows this sequence; however, it is spoken according to the order of marking and explaining so that the assembly may hear with pleasure.
Below there are further passages concerning "benefits" (*yìlì*) and so forth, at the end of which it is stated in all cases: "according to what is appropriate for the assembly."
To proclaim [the Dharma] for their sake is called "teaching in accordance" (*anuloma-vyākaraṇa*); this is the concluding phrase. Some say that the seven meanings have not been fully examined.

Furthermore, the explanation of the characteristic of being free from stinginess connects with the two preceding meanings; because one is likewise free from stinginess according to the sequence of the assembly.
Thus he was led in this manner. The text is not without intention.
The commentary states that [the Buddha] preached the Dharma even to those who harbored enmity.
The note says this is the second reliance on pure teaching. The treatise has five characteristics: first, a mind of loving-kindness; second, benefit...

(3) a mind of increasing benefit; (4) a mind of compassion; (5) a mind that neither praises nor disparages; and (6) a mind not for the sake of fame or profit. These are easily seen when correlated with the preceding [five].
Combined with the former fifteen, there are twenty in total, as listed in the treatise.
The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) next states "should practice" (up to) "unmistaken practice.
The commentary contains five characteristics: the three types of action constitute three; the fourth is right reflection; and the fifth is non-distraction.

Regarding the first three, the character *wen* (聞, to hear) is a transcription error for the character *wen* (問, to inquire). This refers to the two gates of permission (*kṣānti*) and prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), which are commonly spoken of as "doing" and "not doing."

Because it is performed intentionally, the *Śāstra* states that it "proceeds without inversion," which means it proceeds in accordance with the Buddha’s prescriptions and prohibitions. It transforms the three types of action (*trikarma*).
Since "transforming" (*parāvṛtti*) implies arising, it also refers to their cessation; therefore, it encompasses both abstention and performance.
The *Śāstra* states: "Dwelling alone in quietude... [until] unmoved by heterodox views.

The commentary notes that this corresponds to the fourth characteristic of right reflection (*samyak-cintā*). The treatise contains eight points, but here only six are briefly presented, omitting two.
Dwelling alone in quietude and reflecting upon the teachings one has heard is the first point; this generally describes the nature of reflection, setting it apart from [other mental activities].
"Beyond the inconceivable and uninterrupted" is the second meaning. Because of the two types of preparatory application (*prayoga*), there is no slackening or laxity;
below that, there is no third. This is based solely on the meaning and not on the literal text.
Furthermore, there is no fourth: his mind does not fall into confusion, delusion, or disarray. "Beyond the unknown" is the fifth meaning. "Beyond the unreached" is the sixth.
Because they understand only a small portion of the six meanings, and because their own limited wisdom cannot penetrate the most profound dharmas, they look up to the Tathāgata and say:
"Such dharmas are the domain of the Buddha; they are not within my sphere."

One does not give rise to slander and is free from all faults and transgressions. Within the text, the phrase "fearing the lack of the eye of wisdom" (*prajñācakṣur-abhāva*) is itself a fault and transgression;
one should rectify the mind and believe with resolve. To well understand the hidden intent (*saṃdhi*) is the seventh meaning, because one relies on the meaning rather than the literal expression.
To well understand the hidden intent so that one is unshakable by divergent explanations is the eighth meaning. This is due to...
Because he is skilled in the discourse on the conventional and the discourse on the ultimate, regarding the true meaning, no entity or phenomenon can overturn or disturb him;
all divergent theories are subsumed by him. If one follows the logical classification, from "the unknown" (*ajñāta*) downwards, this constitutes the restatement (*anuvāda*).
Previously there were eight [points]. The first two are as stated in the text. Regarding the following six meanings, one observes them through reasoning and enters into realization accordingly.
As for their minor aspects, one merely follows through faith and understanding; one relies on the meaning rather than the literal text.
One understands correctly the "dark" (mṛdu) and "great" (adhimātra) teachings and is truly able to enter into realization. Through initial reflection and repeated mental attention, one causes...
One attains firmness, as in the subsequent six [verses]. Two phrases have one meaning.

In the commentary on the passage from "the ineffable realm" to "vipaśyanā," it is noted that this corresponds to the fifth characteristic, non-distraction. Because of the cultivation of non-distraction, śamatha and vipaśyanā are clarified.
The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) next provides instructions (up to the point of "arrogance," etc.), annotating eight types of instruction.

The full text is contained in the treatise (*śāstra*). Regarding the first four, they concern the practitioners (*yogin*) who are the objects of observation: first, the mind; second, the faculties (*indriya*).
There are three types of intention (*āśaya*) and four latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); these [practices] are free from latent tendencies. Some say that the prefix *anu-* (in *anuśaya*) subsumes them.

The latter four clearly explain the practices to be taught: first, the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-viṣaya-sthiti-citta-bhāvanā*), which are also not explicitly present here, though they may be included within the "as appropriate" (*yathāyogam*) teachings;

second, the avoidance of the extreme of eternalism (*śāśvata-anta*); third, the avoidance of the extreme of annihilationism (*uccheda-anta*). These words "abiding in the middle" (*madhyama-pratipad*) encompass these.

Second: abandoning the overweening pride (*adhimāna*) of those who understand the mind through meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This refers to the faculties of faith and so forth. Excluding concentration, there are the other four;
or, concentration may be included as well. "Intention" (*āśaya*) is that which is desired. What are the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that follow its practice?
They are greed and so forth. What is the illness? The treatise says: "In this way, a bodhisattva, either by receiving correct instruction from another, or by [bestowing]..."
His unerring instruction enables the remaining eight powers of the lineage to gradually attain purification and gradual growth;
namely, the power of knowledge regarding dhyānas, liberations, concentrations, and meditative attainments, and the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties of beings.

The power of knowledge regarding the various elements (*nānādhātu-jñānabala*); the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading to all destinations (*sarvatragāminīpratipad-jñānabala*); the power of knowledge regarding the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñānabala*); the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth (*cyutyupapāda-jñānabala*); and the power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñānabala*). These constitute the lineage (*gotra*).
The commentary next explains the instruction (upadeśa), [extending] to "causing them to rejoice and increase their practice.
The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) lists five kinds of instruction: first, the prohibition of what is faulty; second, the permission of what is faultless;

third, admonishing and causing repentance for occasional transgressions; fourth, the possibility of expulsion for repeated transgressions; and fifth, praising right practice. Regarding the character "huì" (repentance), the treatise states it is *kaukṛtya*.
Regarding the characters: "宜" (yí) should follow the character "誨" (huì); or, if one exhorts them to repent, the character "悔" (huǐ) may be used.

"Arising from being unstained and distinct" means arising from being unstained and turbid, in the sense of being without change or transformation. "Lower offenses committed temporarily" refers to such acts as defiling other families; once reformed, one is again received back into the community.
"Higher offenses" refers to the four cases of non-cohabitation (*asaṃvāsa*).
In the commentary, the three types of action are established next (up to the point) "because there is no other teaching.
The note states that there are four kinds: first, the skillful means of following and gathering; second, the skillful means of being able to gather; third, the skillful means of causing entry;

and fourth, the skillful means of conforming and turning. These are precisely the four bases of sympathy (*saṃgrahavastu*). They consist of extracting [beings] from the unwholesome and exhorting them to settle in the wholesome. That is to say...

This is beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*). The following is collaborative action (*samānārthatā*). "No one else speaks" means not causing others to be reproached; it refers simply to exhorting others, rather than practicing it oneself.
[The] Commentary [continues]: Next, the cultivation of the *pāramitās*.
The commentary distinguishes the ability to practice and study, and sets forth ten chapters to manifest the person [who practices]. This [work] contains only the first nine;

the "Chapter on Merit" is excluded because it constitutes the fruit and is therefore appended to the end of the preceding nine. Furthermore, within the subsequent "Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment," the five immeasurables are appended.
At the end of the thirty-ninth [chapter], the six perfections and the four means of attraction each have nine aspects. The summary verse (*uddāna*) says:

The nature [of generosity], its universality, its difficulty, its universal accessibility, its excellence, its fulfillment of every kind of request, and its purity for happiness in both worlds—these nine characteristics constitute the brief explanation.
For the various practices such as ethical discipline and so forth, one merely changes the final phrase.
Question: In what sense are the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) called "benefiting oneself"? Although it is said that they increase accordingly, their characteristics have not yet been seen.
Answer: Because it is taught that for all six, there is one's own fruit; namely, reaching the other shore (pāramitā) and possessing maturation (vipāka).

Question: Why are these two categories called "superior progress" (viśeṣa-gamana)? Answer: They also increase accordingly. They are called "direct vision within the middle," because they are viewed in relation to the higher practices. [Regarding] offerings...

Cultivating intimacy is the superior stage; thus, even the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are merely provisional studies for this superior stage. The further advancement of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) is easy to understand.
"Sparse giving" refers to the stage of relinquishment, consisting of the three non-greedy actions (*trividha-akuśala-karman*).

This note concerns the first of the nine gates. Formerly, there was an error in the classification; in reality, these two factors—non-greed (*alobha*) and volition (*cetanā*)—are provisionally associated with both sound and form.
The Commentary states: "In general, when practicing giving... all should be bestowed. The Note says:
"This corresponds to the second [category] among the 'All-Givings' (*sarvadāna*). The Treatise relies on the meaning of 'increasing' (*vṛddhi*);

whereas the preceding section contains only one [type], this section contains two, namely, internal and external objects. Now, this text is abbreviated and merely sets forth these two gates: what should and should not be given, and skillfulness."

The wise practice giving. This concerns what is appropriate and what is inappropriate; first briefly, then extensively. The brief explanation refers to the general meaning of what is appropriate and inappropriate, while the extensive explanation points out specifically who is appropriate or inappropriate.
The previous classification contained errors. Now, this section briefly distinguishes the meaning of what is appropriate and inappropriate, which does not exceed four categories.
The great purpose of practicing giving is for the sake of benefiting others, and not for the sake of worldly pleasure; therefore, although...
Four propositions. Two propositions [indicate] that one should give; two propositions [indicate] that one should not.
Commentary: "If one hopes for wealth and goods... (up to) "...should act with mastery as appropriate. Note: This refers to the preceding treatise.
It states within the section on the internal and external: "Furthermore, all bodhisattvas also, by means of two characteristics, [act] externally..."
Regarding the objects of giving: one gives to all sentient beings. First, for those who seek enjoyment, one allows them to have whatever they require.

Second, for those who seek mastery, one gives everything while severing all [attachment] in the mind. This passage was originally placed earlier, but it has been moved to the end because it corresponds correctly with the latter two lines.
It merely differs in its external phrasing; furthermore, it should correspond with the latter two of the four lines.

Because they are combined in the act of giving. Otherwise, why would they not be sequential in this way? The distinction between these two is that in the first case, one has not yet relinquished [the object], but merely causes it to be used;
in the latter case, one gives it directly to the recipient and no longer maintains any attachment to it oneself.

The Commentary states: If one seeks weapons such as knives for the purpose of harming oneself or others, this is included among the "Inappropriate Objects. There are two types: first, inappropriate external objects; second, internal lack of skillful means.
The following section concerns those who are enemies, relatives, and so forth. Regarding the initial portion of the treatise, there were fifteen points, but now there are only twelve.
Here, the seventh point—refraining from giving to one's elders—is absent, as is the ninth—suppressing gifts to one's kinsmen—and the twelfth—giving things that are not lawful;
these will be pointed out later. This present section is the first: weapons and the like are harmful and should not be given.
Furthermore,
the commentary states that these are not one's own property.
The note identifies this as the second [point].
Acting as a matchmaker for others;
this is the third [offense]. Acting as a matchmaker for another’s wife;
eating food that contains insects, and so forth.
The commentary states that this is the fourth [point].
The sub-commentary (*śū*) says: "Meaningless objects of pleasure" (up to) "seeking enmity and resentment.

The commentary states that this is the fifth [point]: meaningless objects of pleasure. The first phrase is the general statement; the subsequent text provides the specific details, which are briefly cited here.

There are five types. Methods such as hunting and so forth are called "methods of killing and harming. Here, "method" (dharma) refers to a rule or principle; because they accord with one's desires and produce pleasure, they are also called "instruments of pleasure.

The following cases should be understood by analogy. The second type consists of improper religious practices and sacrifices to celestial deities. Apart from these sacrifices to celestial deities, [the remaining types are as follows].
Other shrines dedicated to spirits and deities are termed "perverse transformations. Places where water and land beings are harmed or killed are categorized as one type based on their location.

Regarding enmity and resentment, if one does not grant what the other desires, or if the enemy itself becomes an object of pleasure—as previously explained—or if one takes up the implements of that enemy or adversary, if these five categories were expanded, they would be as follows:
[This completes] nineteen [sections].
Regarding the commentary on "The illness of one's hopes is not appropriate" (up to) "grief and anxiety will cause harm":
this is the sixth [section]. That which is sought is not appropriate. The first phrase is easily understood; the second phrase means that after being full, one is still greedy.
Regarding the "frequent seeking" [of death]: the latter part of the verse concerns the sorrowful seeking of self-killing and so forth. If these three are expanded, they constitute fourteen [types].
Next, the seventh [category], concerning parents, teachers, and elders, is absent from this current text.
The *Śāstra* (commentary) suppresses and excludes base objects.
The note states that this is the eighth [category], following the arrangement of the *Treatise*. According to the *Śāstra*, it is the seventh:

for example, being in a royal position, one seizes the wives of ministers or commoners to serve as objects of giving. Next, below this is the ninth: suppressing the giving of one's own kinsmen, even down to servants and slaves.
Do not suppress giving; this is also absent herein.
The commentary states that the stage of seeking evil with pleasure is the tenth. If there is one who is violent and wicked who comes to seek the throne, one should not grant it to them.
The commentary explains that this refers to giving away what has been seized from others.
Note 11: It refers to seizing and coercing the wealth of one's kinsmen, or seizing and coercing the property of one's parents, even down to the possessions of slaves and servants.
Regarding the twelfth category below, "illegitimate objects," these are likewise not present here.
The commentary states that "sudden and violent loss" (sūdzabau dam) refers to the remaining [cases] where one violates the training rules (*śikṣāpada*).
This note identifies these as the latter three. In the treatise, "sudden and violent loss" and the preceding "unlawful [acquisition]" (*adharma*) constitute a single section.
The treatise says: "All bodhisattvas, by means of the True Dharma, accumulate wealth without sudden violence and practice giving."
One does not practice giving through unlawful means, nor through sudden violence, nor by coercing or harming others.
While this may at first appear to be a single point, it also pertains to human relations and the principles of classification.

Regarding external objects, unlawful objects, or objects obtained through sudden violence that harm all the wealth of others—violating the prohibitions of the Vinaya scriptures—is termed a transgression of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*). This...
The latter point concerns the meaning of the treatise based on the renunciant life.
The commentary addresses the discriminative mind arising from [the categories of] enemies and kin;
the preceding notes merely discussed the impropriety regarding external objects, whereas what follows further discusses how the mind itself is irrational, which does not concern [external things].
From the "substance" (*vastu*) down to "skillful wisdom" (*kauśalya*), there are twenty-nine items in total, all of which constitute skillful means (*upāya*).
Now, excluding "skillful wisdom," there are twenty-eight; however, here only twenty-four are cited. These will be pointed out below.
This is the first instance where enemies and kin are treated unequally; it lacks a mind of equanimity and should not be done.
The commentary permits giving more to the superior and less to the inferior.
This second [point] and the third [point] do not follow the order of the treatise.
The commentary states that one might harbor divergent views and give rise to a mind of resentment and turbidity;
this refers to the fourth meaning. "Divergent views and resentment" means that after giving, one praises the gift and speaks of the debt of gratitude toward the recipient.
This annotates the fifth meaning: praising oneself and speaking of one's own kindness.
"Liao" (撩) means to cast away what has been discarded.
This annotates the sixth [offense], disrespectfully casting things aside. The character "yan" (掩) is a scribal error; it should be "liao" (撩). This is recorded with emphasis.
"Qiè. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to grasp an object with the hand," or "to pick up and arrange. Here, we take the first definition. [The commentary states:
"Sloping toward the wicked and seeking with aversion.
The note says: "This is the seventh. 'Seeking' refers to coarse and evil conduct; since one should feel compassion, do not give rise to such perverse actions, nor..."
A weary mind. Furthermore, even if the seeker acts with misconduct, the donor never, for even a moment, gives rise to a wrong course of action or a mind of weariness while practicing generosity.
Moreover, even if that seeker acts with anger, resentment, and so forth, the donor does not grow weary;
this applies throughout the preceding and following sections.
The intent of the commentary is that one gives rise to perverse giving.
This eighth note concerns those with perverse views who give while performing acts such as killing;
the commentary maintains that these are virtuous and pure.

The commentary states that this is the ninth [dedication]. "Purity" means being free from [defilements]; it pertains to both the mundane and the supramundane. Next, the tenth [dedication] below is dedicated toward worldly fruits, which is not present here.
This was cited by another [author] in the sub-commentary (*śāstra*).
This eleventh [point] is annotated as being "induced by external conditions" and "ignorant of cause and effect," for it depends on the inducement of others.
The Master of the Commentary (Sushishi), fearing his own poverty,
annotated this twelfth [point] as not being out of compassion.
The commentary states: "Giving away leftovers and impurities" (up to) "holding [them] to bestow as charity.
The note says this is the thirteenth type: giving that does not accord with proper decorum (*yī*). "Decorum" refers to ritual protocol;

it is not a matter of personal preference. Within this, there are two parts: first, clarifying the giving of leftovers and impurities to those who have left the household life; second, surreptitiously giving onions and the like to those who do not eat them.
This, however, refers to external objects that do not conform to the ritual protocol; it follows the principle of "the few following the many" within this category.
