The commentary states: this is the fifth stage of patience for a person (*pudgala-kṣānti*). This treatise identifies five characteristics: first, being free from enemies; second, being free from discord;
third, possessing much joy and happiness; fourth, having no regrets at the time of death; and fifth, being reborn in a favorable realm. Now..."
This is not in the correct order; it is easy to see when it is properly aligned. To realize unsurpassed enlightenment, one should discuss joy and bliss. The following belongs to the general text.
Furthermore, regarding "one who cannot endure any bitter fruit," this is the opposite of seeing benefit and instead seeing loss; this is not seen above this section of the treatise.
The four dharmas below are present within the general discussion of the treatise because they reveal superior benefits, such as acting for oneself and so forth. Moreover—
To explain these words as proving the realization of unsurpassed awakening, one should refer to the introduction and conclusion of the treatise. The treatise states:

"It means that all bodhisattvas first perceive various benefits within their patience... (etc.). Having perceived these benefits, they are personally capable of enduring; whereas perceiving the fruits of suffering is the reverse of this introduction and conclusion.
Furthermore, because there is abundant joy and delight, the word "also" (*api*) is placed [in the text].
The commentary states that "diligence" refers to the three types of courageous activity (*trikarma-vīrya*).
The sub-commentary maintains that there are forty-two [factors]. This is the first category; including its attendants, it constitutes the three types of activity.
The Commentary states that this is briefly divided into three [sections] (up to) "having no slight cowardice or inferiority.
The Sub-commentary notes that all these sections are also first divided into two: lay and monastic. Within the text, there are three parts; the first is the heading.
The first section provides an illustration as a heading. Next is the explanation. The section from "I now" down to "the suffering becomes thin" uses a difficult case to illustrate an easy one.
The subsequent section is the praise; it uses an inferior case to illustrate a superior one. This is the portion beginning with "In this."
The commentary (*śāstra*) subsumes "exertion in gathering wholesome qualities" [up to] "swiftly realizing bodhi.

The annotation consists of three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation; and third, the praise. From "World-Honored One" onwards is the praise. Within the explanation there are seven points:
first, immovability; second, firmness; third, immeasurability; fourth, correspondence with skillful means; fifth, non-perversion; sixth, constancy; and seventh...

Free from pride. Within this, there are three [types]: the first two and the last one. The treatise states: "Firmness is due to earnestness (*ādara*). The rest continues until... The commentary explains:
"The three types of beneficial diligence" (extending to) "various forms of exertion."
The commentary states that these constitute the eleven types within the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārthakriyā-śīla*).

The sub-commentary explains that from "thus distancing oneself" up to "cultivating without error" refers to difficult-to-practice diligence (*duṣkaravīrya*), which also has three kinds: the first two phrases form one [type], and the subsequent two phrases form another.
The subsequent text constitutes a single unit.
The commentary states that [this] can cause the defiled dharmas (up to) the three types of wisdom to increase.
The sub-commentary notes that these "all-gateways" also consist of four kinds: the departure from defilement, the induction of purity, the three types of action, and the three types of wisdom.
The commentary states: "Without relinquishing and without retreating, one acts with diligent vigor.

The sub-commentary notes: "There are five types of noble beings (*satpuruṣa*). The two characters [of 'noble being'] have a single meaning; however, the two characters 'and acts' are applied throughout the preceding context."
The Commentary states: "Possessing power and diligence" (extending to) "protecting oneself and benefiting others.
This refers to all aspects [of application]. There are six preceding and seven succeeding [factors]. First, regarding the six preceding ones: first, uninterrupted; second, earnest.

[The stages are: 1. the three types of flow, 2. the four preparatory practices, 3. the immovable, and 4. the insatiable. These five kinds are listed here; however, one should discuss the preceding six.
Regarding the scriptural citations, how can citing five serve as proof for six? Answer: The main text is similar [to the treatise], yet not identical in every detail.
Alternatively, it may not be a direct citation. According to the treatise, these five are established by means of the six. The treatise states: "The Bodhisattva..."
Having accomplished these six kinds of all-encompassing diligence (*sarvākāra-vīrya*) and having aroused diligent effort, it is for this reason that it is said:
"possessing power and possessing exertion" (and so forth). This is precisely the armor-like application (*saṃnāha-prayoga*), which is neither inferior nor regressive.
There is no [further] division. Those fourfold explanations should be fully examined and correlated. Regarding the subsequent seven types: first, that which is associated with desire;
second, equanimity; third, superior progress; fourth, diligent seeking; fifth, cultivation and study; sixth, benefiting others; seventh, excellent protection.

These are all contained within this text. From "intense" (*tīvra*) downward is as follows. The first two are understandable. The third and fourth are out of order; "unwearied" (*akheda*) is the fourth. Next...
The second line constitutes the third [category]. Protecting oneself is the sixth; benefiting others is the seventh. The final two are not in their sequential order.
As for "fulfilling requests" and so forth, they are not cited here as their meaning is minor.
The commentary states that meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is precisely one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
This is noted under the section on "essential nature" in fascicle 43, which cites wisdom as being dependent upon concentration.
The commentary further explains that there are three types [of concentration], up to all forms of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
This second section is also first divided into two: the mundane and the supramundane. It is further divided into three;
within the third, there are eleven aspects, which are the same as those for diligence mentioned previously.
The Commentary states: "From relying on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)... to performing what ought to be done.

The Sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains that one subsequently seeks meditative concentration, which likewise has eight types. Taking "non-ritual" as the general category, it applies to two or three [of the eight], or perhaps to the first six;
however, the treatise (*śāstra*) addresses only the first. These range from the first, the pacification of calamities (*śāntika*), up to the eighth, performing what ought to be done. First.
The first six [sections] each have three characters; the final two each have four characters. The sequence of giving material wealth, food, and the Dharma is not fixed.
The commentary explains the supernatural powers (ṛddhi) and the prophecy (vyākaraṇa), up to the phrase "extinguishing all sufferings."

Within the commentary on the bliss of the two worlds (*dvitīya-loka-sukha*), there are also nine aspects (*navākāra*). The first three concern the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*). The fourth is the manifestation of the miserable realms (*durgati*);

here it is called "transformation. The fifth is the ability to bestow eloquence (*pratibhāna*). The sixth is the ability to bestow right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). The seventh is the composition of non-erroneous treatises (*aviparīta-śāstra*).

The eighth is the creation of various crafts and skills (*śilpa-kalā*); these four aforementioned types are included within the phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*). The ninth is the emission of light to pacify suffering (*duḥkha-praśamana*). This concludes the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya*.
The characters are regulated. The transmission is precise.
The commentary is also able to eternally eliminate all heavy obstructions.
There are ten kinds of purity; these are stated collectively as: mundane purity, supramundane purity, purity of application, and purity of the faculties.

Original purity; superior progress purity; mastery over the three minds; realizing again after having relinquished; mastery over supernormal transformations; freedom from views; freedom from hindrances;
these are fully detailed as in the treatise.
The commentary states that discernment (*prajñā*) is the analytical investigation of objects according to reality.
The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) also contains forty-three [sections]. This is the first gate of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
The commentary states that there are three kinds [of this], up to "equanimity leading to awakening."
Within the commentary on "All-Wisdom," there are also first two divisions: mundane and supramundane; subsequently, there are three divisions.
Next, regarding the first [division], the wisdom that takes ultimate reality as its object, the treatise states that one is about to correctly awaken to non-self and the true truths.

[The question is: Why is it not the same here, where one simply takes awakening as the object? The explanation says: This refers to the initial stage of cultivation, where only "about to awaken" is mentioned. Its...
The correct [explanation] and my own [view] will be examined and considered later in the section on the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
Regarding the second [point], from the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) up to the awakening through the accumulation of wisdom (*jñānasaṃbhāra*), [it is as follows].

This is the commentary on the subject matter. Regarding the "three aggregates": first, the aggregate of dharmas that lead to what is beneficial; second, the aggregate of dharmas that lead to what is not beneficial;
and third, the aggregate of dharmas that lead to neither the beneficial nor the non-beneficial. As for the term "suchness" (*tathatā*), it means knowing things as they truly are.
By embracing the aforementioned eight [factors], one fulfills the provisions (*sambhāra*) and achieves Buddhahood. Thus it is stated in the treatise.
Regarding "delivering sentient beings":
the commentary (Sū) states three times "sentient beings" (up to "practicing together with sublime wisdom").

The sub-commentary (Zhù) notes that there are eleven of these, which constitute the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārthakriyā-śīla*); the mention of "one" is illustrative and stands for the rest.
The commentary on the section concerning the study of the inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*) [extends] to "rejoicing and diligent cultivation.
The wisdom regarding the happiness of the two worlds also has nine types: the five sciences constitute five; based on the wisdom of the inner science, the latter four arise.
These demonstrate to the ignorant, guide the indolent, encourage the timid, and celebrate cultivation. The treatise states that, in general, these are based upon the five sciences.
The commentary next explains the practice of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).

The sub-commentary (*zhù*) likewise contains forty-three [sections]. Following the previous discussion on generosity and so forth, there are also nine gates; however, these are absent from the section on "common purpose" (*samānārthatā*).
Commentary: First, generosity (*dāna*) has already been explained above.
The commentary on the treatise is the same as before; therefore, there are not nine [types].
Regarding the second [type] in the sub-commentary, "loving speech" (*priyavāda*)—up to—"words that lead to the meaning.

The commentary states: "Loving speech by its very nature (*svabhāva*). That which possesses the four meanings constitutes its nature. "Provisionally, it refers to sound," which is to say, it is volition (*cetanā*).
The Commentary [states]: "Avoiding frowning" (up to) "constantly providing superior benefit.
The Sub-commentary [explains] that all loving speech is first divided into three types, and subsequently condensed into two; this differs from the [classification of the] perfections (*pāramitā*).

Regarding the condensation into two: first, speech that accords with worldly etiquette; second, speech that conforms to the correct teaching. Regarding the previous division into three: first, consoling speech.

The second is rejoicing; the third is superior benefit. The former two accord with worldly convention, while the latter one accords with the teaching. Here, there is no abbreviation of the two [worldly modes], but rather an expansion into three.
Consolation refers to words of inquiry after one's well-being; rejoicing refers to awakening the other to that which they find joy in.

The treatise contains two [sections]: "Prosperity" (*ṛddhi*) and "Wholesome Qualities" (*kuśala-dharma*). The current text reveals these through implication; the former refers to prosperity, while the latter refers to wholesome qualities. The full text should read:

"Seeing that there is prosperity and an increase in wholesome qualities, one does not yet know it oneself; perceiving that there is prosperity and an increase in wholesome qualities, one expresses joy.
Here, "perceiving" (*buddha*) means being alerted (*prabodha*). Prosperity refers to wealth and so forth, while wholesome qualities refer to—
Regarding the dharmic precepts and so forth, their superior benefit is the teaching of the Buddha’s Dharma.

In the commentary on the passage from "toward one's own enemies" to "practicing difficult loving speech," it is noted that there are three types of difficult practice: first, toward enemies; second, toward the deluded; and third, toward those who are deceitful and fraudulent. Of these, the first and the last...
There are two types [of speech]. One fully employs three modes of expression: consoling, gladdening, and providing superior benefit. The foolish employ only that which provides superior benefit.

Regarding the phrase "toward a true field of merit," this refers to those who are being flattered and deceived; even toward such sentient beings of evil conduct, one should cultivate loving speech in this manner.
Therefore, this is difficult to practice.
The *Śāstra* (Sūtra/Sub-commentary) intends to eliminate hindrances and obscurations... [up to] "discussing and determining.
The *Commentary* states that these various gates are of four kinds; two phrases constitute one unit, which is easy to understand upon investigation. Regarding the phrase "first":

The "agent" refers to what should have been done previously; that is, the preliminary preparation (*pūrvaprayoga*). Below [the term] "virtuous person" (*satpurusa*) and "all aspects" (*sarvākāra*), the commentary states that based on the four pure modes of speech (*caturvidha-vāk-śuddhi*), the eight noble modes of speech (*aṣṭavidha-āryavāk*) arise.

The commentary states that this refers to seeking [truth] through speech. Based on abstaining from false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech—these are called the four purities.

Regarding seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, one speaks of what was seen, heard, sensed, and known; the opposite of these four is likewise understood. These are the eight noble modes of speech (*ārya-vāk*).
Question: What is meant by "seeking [truth]"? Answer: When someone asks a question, one does not hope for a false answer; therefore, the eight noble modes of speech fulfill the inquiry.
Regarding the object of pursuit, the third [of the four means of attraction] is beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), which extends to establishing [beings] in peace.

The commentary states that beneficial conduct is of an intrinsic nature; it cannot be practiced through exhortation unless preceded by pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*). All instances of exhortation constitute the practice of beneficial conduct.
Beneficial factors are all of the nature of selfhood (*svabhāva*).
The commentary states that they can cause one to obtain (*pratilambha*) pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and liberation (*vimukti*).

Regarding the annotation on all beneficial conduct (*hitakriyā*), it is also first divided into two: first, for sentient beings who are not yet matured, there is the benefit of being able to bring them to maturity.

[The practice of] conduct. Second, the beneficial conduct that brings about the liberation of sentient beings already matured. The subsequent text opens this into three [types]; the present passage refers to this.

The first consists of such activities as lawful commerce and agriculture; the second is the renunciation of the household life to practice alms-seeking and so forth—both of which involve the departure from desire and the attainment of pliancy in the present life;
and the third is the benefit of rebirth in the heavens and so forth. Within the latter category of benefits, the Tibetan manuscript of the treatise omits [the following].

Question: Zuan’s commentary states that there are present benefits, such as those who possess virtue obtaining fame and reputation; how could there not also be future benefits? Among future benefits, he mentions leaving the household life and so forth;
yet, are there not also present benefits such as being praised by humans and devas? If this were not the case, it would fail to constitute benefit for both lifetimes.
How then does this differ from the distinct ripening of suffering and pleasure in the two realms of rebirth? Answer: This [commentary] follows what is coarse and manifest.
"Associating closely with evil friends... (up to) holding wrong views and slandering [the Dharma].
The two phrases "difficult to practice" and "beneficial conduct" constitute a single unit. These three types of persons are difficult to exhort and guide;
therefore, the subsequent words of explanation are applied throughout this section. As for "planting," it should follow the reading "zhí."

The commentary states that [the practitioner] constantly gives rise to the eight envelopments (*paryavasthāna*). The sub-commentary proceeds to seek the practice for the purpose of causing one to leave these eight envelopments behind; the subsequent words "all can be opened and understood" are applied throughout this context.

As for the eight envelopments, they are: lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), sleep (*middha*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), remorse (*kaukṛtya*), and stinginess (*mātsarya*).
Envy. Question: What is meant by "pursuing what is sought"? Answer: For one who seeks liberation from the fetters (*paryavasthāna*), [the teacher] instructs them to abandon them.
[This concludes] the commentary on the ten unwholesome karmic paths, which is capable of bringing about awakening and understanding.
The two characters "constantly arising" (chángqǐ) are annotated [here]. However, they also pervade the two preceding types of beneficial conduct (*hitakriyā*).

Within the treatise there are nine [types], while these speak of ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*); thus, there is an opening and closing [of categories]. The three of body and four of speech are combined with the three of mind as one kind, and the drinking of alcohol is added;
therefore, nine types are formed. Since this does not depart from the original number, it is here called ten.
The commentary begins with "arousing the mind of great compassion" and concludes with "never regressing.
The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) also contains ten sections; here, however, only the latter five are presented, based on the internal purity of beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*).
The first phrase is the first: beneficial conduct through great compassion. The three phrases [following] are the second: beneficial conduct without weariness.
The sixth phrase is the third: beneficial conduct through humility. The fourteenth phrase is the fourth: beneficial conduct through purity and reality.
The final two phrases constitute the fifth: beneficial conduct without regression. These are called beneficial conduct based on internal purity. As for the preceding five, they are called...
Based on external pure beneficial conduct, there are five types: first, faultless beneficial conduct; second, non-reversing beneficial conduct;
third, gradual beneficial conduct; fourth, universal beneficial conduct; and fifth, appropriate beneficial conduct.

These five kinds cause others to be free from fault, prevent them from turning toward what is erroneous, proceed from the shallow to the deep, universally benefit all beings, and provide benefit according to what is suitable. This is called [external pure beneficial conduct].
This constitutes the fifth [category].
Regarding the fourth, "common purpose" (samānārthatā), up to the point where it says "consulting and receiving instruction on this matter":
the commentary notes that within this [section on] common purpose, there are no nine gates, because it follows directly from the preceding practice of common purpose. This is the text.

There are two parts. First, it is shown that one’s own practice is followed by others; second, it clarifies that when one does not practice oneself, one is instead held accountable. Within the first part, there are two sections:
first, it clarifies that others act in accordance [with the teaching]; second, it distinguishes the absence of any contradictory words.
The Commentary next describes the offerings to the Triple Gem.
Note 44 states: first, offering to the *śarīra* (relics); second, offering to the *caitya* (stupa/shrine); third, offering in the presence [of the object];
fourth, offering in the absence [of the object]; fifth, offering performed by oneself; sixth, offering performed by instructing others.

The sevenfold offering of wealth, the eighth, the vast offering, the ninth, the undefiled offering, and the tenth, the offering of right practice—how does this differ [from the previous classification], and what is its meaning?
Answer: In the subsequent commentary of the treatise, it clarifies that both systems are valid.

If the first two are expanded, they constitute twelve types. This implies that the former two refer to the objects [of offering]; since they are not separate from the latter [eight], they are thus included therein.

This is omitted. The discussion relies on both general and specific categories. First, based on the two objects, the two general categories are listed; subsequently, they are divided specifically into eight.

As for the "two-fold joint offering," because it is a combination of the specific, it is not listed separately. Since the details are provided within the commentary, they are therefore explained separately.
Commentary: First, regarding "facing the present" (至) up to "making offerings face-to-face.
As for *śarīra*, it is erroneously called *sari*. It refers to the physical body of the Buddha. The Treatise states:
"The form-body (*rūpakāya*), as well as the teeth and so forth, are all *śarīra*. *Caitya* is often translated as "stūpa. *Stūpa* means "high and manifest."
Commentary II: Regarding the other three times (up to) practicing non-manifest worship.
Note: This is based on merely imagining other realms and so forth.
Commentary III: Regarding the time of being present (up to) practicing manifest and non-manifest worship.

The commentary notes that the characters "duì" (face-to-face) and "xiàn" (manifest) are inverted; this refers to regarding others as the Buddha while they are present before one, and thus it constitutes an offering to both.
The sub-commentary states: "If after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa... [up to] the provisions for enlightenment."
The commentary previously explained the merit of making offerings by way of analyzing the causes; it then clarified that the karmic fruit of creating images is likewise great. Question:
The intent of the treatise is to speak of offerings not made in the presence [of the Buddha]. What is the meaning of this? Answer: Because the object of focus differs.

This statement is made with reference to a Buddha who has already passed into extinction. However, regarding those objects of veneration such as *caityas* (shrines) that are currently present before one, these are also called "present. (Lunzhi)
Direct Commentary: This is to clarify the attainment of the fruit.
The Sub-commentary (Sū) states that "in such cases" refers exclusively to making offerings to oneself.
The Annotation (Zhù) points out that "such" refers to caityas and the like; it means not even employing servants or slaves for this purpose.
Commentary (5): If one gives rise to a compassionate heart [up to] causing others to make offerings.
Note: Having not extensively bestowed one's own possessions upon others, and since there is nothing further remaining, others alone make the offerings.
Commentary 6: "Or both perform" (up to) "perform this offering. The note states:
"One's own practice and exhorting others," extending even to exhorting servants and so forth, also constitutes performing it together.
Commentary (Sū): 7. With incense, flowers, and so forth... [up to] practicing material and reverential offerings. Sub-commentary (Zhù): Question:
Regarding the phrase "inexhaustible wealth" (*akṣaya-dhana*) in the *Śāstra* text, what is its meaning? Is it not distinct from the eighth [category]? Answer:

It refers to the many meanings explained below; however, it is not because the duration is long. Since the following possesses three meanings and is thus termed "extensive" (*vistara*), this term "reverence" (*gaurava*)— [End of segment]
This refers to inquiries after one’s health and so forth.
The commentary (Sū) states that through material wealth and reverence, one performs vast offerings.

The sub-commentary (Zhù) explains that these involve broad objects, broad minds, and long durations, possessing seven characteristics: first, abundance; second, excellence; third, presence before one's eyes.
Fourth, non-manifestation; fifth, performing it oneself; sixth, instructing others; seventh, purifying the mind. The above follows the established order, compiling various interpretations.

"For a long duration" constitutes one [category], while "purifying the mind" belongs to the explanatory section that establishes the meaning. According to this broad interpretation, there are two types:

first, the breadth of performance (*abhisamskāra-vipulatā*); second, the breadth of dedication (*pariṇāmana-vipulatā*). If one relies on the previous explanation, the present text contains all three, and so forth.
This exceeds four. Furthermore, in interpreting the treatise regarding "manifest" and "non-manifest," the single character "ruò" (若) should be taken as forming a single meaning.
The same applies to performing the act oneself and instructing others to do so. However, this is then expanded by including long-term dedication with a pure mind, thereby constituting seven types.
This text contains five [sections], up to and including the "Transcending the Two.
The Commentary (Sū) on the nine [points] states that one should not be negligent (until) "practicing undefiled offerings.
The Note (Zhù) states that within this there are three; this is the first: the sixfold pure offering. These six do not exceed two: purity of mind.
Regarding the purity of objects: as can be understood from the text, the treatise specifies six types [of impurity]. First, making offerings without avoiding contempt.
Second, making offerings without avoiding indolence or lack of respect. Third, making offerings without treating them with disdain or casting them away.
Fourth, making offerings without distraction, negligence, or defilement. Fifth, making offerings without hypocrisy or false pretenses. Sixth, not using impure substances as offerings.

Now, the text explicitly mentions four [types], while "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the remainder. Furthermore, they do not follow a fixed order; within the category of "contemptuousness" (*paribhava*), three or four types may be subsumed separately, such that there are six kinds in total.
The commentary states: "Exerting one's own power to gather wealth (up to) making offerings.
This refers to the second section within "Freedom from Attachment," namely "Gathering Wealth Without Attachment. This section contains three parts; the first is "Gathering by One's Own Effort."
One attains [the visualization]. The visualization is transformed into three; within these transformations there are four: body, hands, voice, and implements, as can be understood from the text.

Furthermore, regarding these transformations, the commentary adds the character "xiang" (visualization), which refers to mental construction (*parikalpa*). This treatise places it within the section on sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
Regarding the term "resolute conviction" (*adhimukti*):
the commentary (*śāstra*) identifies Jambudvīpa [as the location]... up to "universally generating sympathetic joy.

This is annotated within the third section, which correctly analyzes sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). The treatise cites the "absence of material wealth" (*niṣkiñcana*), relying for the time being solely on this pure state; the intention is to clarify delusion (*moha*).
One may possess wealth, yet merely rejoice [in others' merit]. To give for oneself while rejoicing in others—this practice is not without merit.
Although the commentary mentions that little effort is required, one must nevertheless apply oneself with diligence to cultivation and study.

The commentary notes that there may be those who harbor doubts and are unwilling to practice this; therefore, these words were written. If one asks, "In asserting its superiority, to whom is it being compared?
[The answer is:
If there is even a moment [of practice]... up to... practicing the actual offering.

The commentary first clarifies the cultivation of mental recollection (*saṃjñā-bhāvanā*), and subsequently clarifies the cultivation of volitional action (*abhisamskāra-bhāvanā*); the latter three lines constitute this [latter section]. Within the former [section], there are two parts:

the first clarifies mental recollection, and the second distinguishes the observance of the precepts; these correspond to what follows below. Within the first of these, the treatise contains five sections:

1. the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*); 2. the four principles regarding suffering (*duḥkha-catuṣkoṭi*); 3. the excellence of *nirvāṇa*; 4. the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛtayaḥ*); and 5. patience (*kṣānti*).
Faith is signless. By practicing these five contemplations, one abides in the code of discipline (*vinaya*). The reason for not mentioning the others is that they must be actively maintained.

Within the subsequent cultivation of practice, there are also four gates: first, calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*); second, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*); third, the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); and fourth, the sublime matters.
Here, we address only the last one; the others will follow later.
The Commentary states that one should reflect on this [up to] "incomparable.
The Sub-commentary notes that this is a praise of its excellence.
The Commentary states that when practicing offerings [up to] "the locus of all meanings."
The commentary states that there are six kinds of superior intention (*adhyāśaya*): first, being a great field of merit; second, possessing great kindness and virtue;
third, being the most honored among sentient beings; fourth, being extremely difficult to encounter; fifth, appearing uniquely and alone; and sixth, being the basis for the welfare of all.
Here, "meaning" (*artha*) refers to benefit; this [Buddha] lacks the third [quality].
The commentary states that regarding the Dharma and the Saṃgha (up to this point), it should be understood accordingly as well.

The note [in the original] previously arranged these above; this synthesis of the commentary’s intent does not rely on the wording of the treatise itself, but rather pertains to the six types of mental disposition (*āśaya*).
Prior to the six types of intention and following the ten aspects, there is further textual material concerning the ritual for making offerings to the Dharma and the Saṅgha. The treatise states:
"By means of these ten aspects, one should know that this is called 'endowing all modes of worshiping the Tathāgata. Just as with the worship of the Buddha..."
Making offerings in this manner to the Dharma or the Saṃgha should be understood accordingly as being likewise. The meaning of the sections accords with the commentary;
the commentary captures the essential points, for the full explanation of the great fruits cannot be exhausted.
This passage is also connected to the six types of resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*). The treatise states:

"By means of these six kinds of resolute intentions, if one contemplates even a small portion regarding the Tathāgata, or regarding the Dharma of the Tathāgata, or regarding the Saṃgha, and offers worship, one still obtains immeasurable fruits of great merit; how much more so if it is extensive?"
The commentary states that one should next draw near to virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
The sub-commentary also contains forty-four [points]. Making offerings is internal, while drawing near is external; therefore, this is the proper sequence.
The commentary [continues] from "the precepts are without breach or flaw" up to "the characteristics of a virtuous friend."
The commentary contains seven questions: four concerning the virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and three concerning close attendance.
This answers the first [question], regarding the characteristics of the virtuous friend. The treatise enumerates eight characteristics: (1) abiding in the precepts; (2) extensive learning;
(3) cultivation and realization; (4) compassion; (5) fearlessness; (6) patience; (7) tirelessness; and (8) lucid eloquence. Now, he possesses all of these.
The commentary seeks the benefit and happiness of giving (up to) "what is done is not in vain.
The note states that this answers the second point, "what is done is not in vain": first, the prior desire to act for the sake of benefit; second, the actual desire to act therein.
Third, possessing power through skillful means; fourth, benefiting others without weariness; fifth, impartial great compassion.
[The commentary] from "the perfection of majestic deportment" up to "frugality and accumulation followed by relinquishment."
This third point establishes the basis for faith. The treatise presents five meanings: first, sublime and wondrous deportment; second, the perfection of tranquil deportment;
third, gravity and solemnity, such that the three karmas are free from agitation; fourth, freedom from hypocrisy, not acting to deceive others;

fifth, freedom from envy, characterized by patience and sympathetic joy toward excellence; and sixth, frugality, which involves relinquishing this very [lack of] frugality. Regarding the character "accumulation" (*zhu*) used in contrast to "frugality" (*jin*), it appears to be a scribal error in the treatise. Frugality...

The character [for "accumulate"] is pronounced with the initial *zhān* (in the *zhǎnqiè* system) or alternatively with *jiǎn* (in the *xiūjiǎn* system). Because both are difficult to employ, they result in the accumulation that constitutes stinginess (*mātsarya*), which is likewise difficult to employ.

It would be more appropriate to say "frugality" (*jiǎnyuē*). Alternatively, if the character *xù* (畜) is used without error, then "frugality" (*jiǎn*) is further joined with "accumulate" (*xù*) to provide a comprehensive explanation of the text.
When referring to having few stored vessels and implements, this character *xù* (稸) is appropriate.
The *Śāstra* states that one should "counsel and exhort so as to cause [the other] to remember," up to "may serve as a basis for trust.

The commentary notes that this answers the fourth point regarding the duties of a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). The treatise also sets forth five meanings: first, the ability to counsel and exhort;

second, the ability to cause [others] to remember; third, the ability to provide instruction (*avavāda*); fourth, the ability to provide admonition (*anuśāsana*); and fifth, the ability to preach the Dharma. The present mention of "basis for trust" refers back to these.
This is the third [point]. It is unclear what this refers to; one should say that because these things exist, they can serve as a basis for faith to be transformed.
The Commentary states:
"Whether sick or not sick... is called 'intimate attendance' (*upaniṣad*)."
This commentary notes that this answer constitutes the foremost way of approaching [the teacher]. According to the treatise, one may only approach [the teacher] when four characteristics are present:

first, swiftly establishing respectful faith; second, rising to greet and cultivate reverence; third, providing necessary articles as required; and fourth, following along and going oneself. This [text] possesses all of these;
two lines constitute each characteristic, with the final line serving as the conclusion. Regarding the fourth characteristic, the treatise states: "In the Tathāgata..."

If the meaning of the Dharma were to depart [from its source], it would follow and revolve according to one's own will; this is what is meant by "following and revolving. Now, I shall cite the following passage from the text itself regarding "going of one’s own accord":

going of one’s own accord to inquire after [the teacher’s] well-being, and going of one’s own accord to listen to the breath-meditation (*ānāpāna*). Previously there were seven questions, of which the first five have already been answered.

There are two further answers: regarding the Dharma-master, one should manifest five kinds of pleasing signs: first, the jewel; second, the eye; third, wisdom; fourth, [the Dharma]; and fifth, [the Sangha].
Virtue. Five are faultless. Seven arise from five sets of five points by not forming five kinds of divergent thoughts:

first, regarding the impairment of precepts; second, regarding the impairment of lineage; third, regarding the impairment of appearance, meaning ugliness and so forth; fourth, regarding the impairment of literary expression; and fifth, regarding the impairment of beauty.
These sixth and seventh [categories] have already been cited previously, and thus they are not included here.
Next, the commentary explains the cultivation of the immeasurables (apramāṇa), from loving-kindness (maitrī) through compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekṣā).
The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) likewise contains forty-four [sections]: three mirrors and four practices, as can be understood from the text.
The Commentary states that from "in the ten directions" up to "is called objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*).

To be entirely without conceptual discrimination is called "objectless compassion. To take suchness (*tathatā*) as its objective condition is called "objectless compassion"; this refers to the fundamental level.
The commentary states that for those who possess suffering (up to the point where it says) "the rest is the same as before.

Regarding the latter one [of the three immeasurables], which is benefit (*anugraha*):

this has two gates. The three beginning with the objectless (*anālambana*) and the four beginning with compassion (*karuṇā*), though differing in being conventional or ultimate, perceive sentient beings as the same;
their dharmas are likewise so. How could non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) be absent in the two vehicles? The commentary states: "The Bodhisattva, fundamentally..."

Because it is practiced for the sake of benefiting others, fundamental loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is established. The followers of the Two Vehicles do not do so; for them, it arises only through conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Following this, the commentary on the "Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment" (*Bodhipakṣyapada*) explains that there are fifteen aspects. First is the cultivation of shame (*hrī*) and remorse (*apatrāpya*); second is firm exertion (*sthāma-dhṛti*); third is being without...
1. Weariness; 2. Knowledge of the various treatises; 3. Knowledge of the world; 4. Cultivation of the four reliances;

The five gates. This constitutes the first cultivation of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*).

There are four bases for this state of shame: first, failing to do what ought to be done; second, doing what ought not to be done;

The Commentary states: "One should look within one's own body... [up to] cultivate and give rise to a sense of shame."

This commentary clarifies their essential nature. They are divided into two: internal and external. To revere what is virtuous and reject what is non-virtuous is called *hrī* (shame) and *apatrāpya* (embarrassment).

Because of these, one feels shame regarding the four aforementioned matters. Although the term for *apatrāpya* is translated as "arrogance," it does not mean being haughty; rather, it refers simply to the absence of reverence.
The commentary next explains the cultivation of firm power (up to) maintaining one's own nature (*svabhāva*).

Enduring suffering and being courageous constitute the third.

Following the commentary on observing the world, the preceding two gates have been transcended. With a mind free from weariness and well-versed in all treatises, the fifth [gate] shall now be explained; one must be well-versed in them.
Regarding the world:

[the passage from] "the corruption of lifespan and the corruption of sentient beings" up to "weariness and compassion" contains errors in the previous sectioning (*ko*). This is because certain sections were divided into ten, which also appears to be erroneous. Now, based on the text...
The *Lunke* (Treatise on Categories). This treatise has two sections: first, understanding the world;
second, conforming to the world. Within the first section, there are four categories: first, the sentient world; second, the vessel world; third, the contemplation of the eight aspects of activity;

and fourth, the contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Now, only three remain; this is the first. "Turbidity" (*nirmala*) refers to being defiled and impure, not conforming to former traces.

That which is base and evil, and loathsome, is called turbidity (*kaṣāya*). The first [turbidity] is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), which constitutes the essence of the turbidity of life (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*).

The five factors—lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and laziness (*kausīdya*)—constitute the essence of the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). If one relies on [the perspective of] simultaneous occurrence, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) constitute its essence.

Excluding views and the aforementioned five [factors], the remaining afflictions (*kleśa*) constitute the essence of the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). The five views, together with improper [attention], [also constitute it].

"Knowledge" refers to the essence of the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*). The four objects (*viṣaya*) and five aggregates (*skandha*) constitute the essence of the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kāṣāya*).
The commentary states that one contemplates the formation and destruction of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) to cultivate the perception of impermanence (*anitya-saṃjñā*);

this is the second [section]. Below are eight contemplations concerning suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, as well as the gratification (*āsvāda*), the disadvantage (*ādīnava*), and the escape (*niḥsaraṇa*) regarding craving.
Together with renunciation, these constitute eight [factors]. This is the third [section]. This is omitted here for brevity. The Commentary states:
"Observing one's own internal body... until not being dogmatically attached."
This is the fourth note. [It states that] persons lack selfhood; only dharmas exist as provisional designations, and thus they are without self.
Regarding the treatise on dharmas, it previously relied upon the aggregates (*skandha*) and bases (*āyatana*); now it relies upon the six elements (*dhātu*).
The commentary states that his years and virtue were venerable and honored...
[up to] ...like the notion of male and female. The sub-commentary (note) below follows worldly convention. If one relies on the topical outline (*lunke*), the treatise has four sections:

first, the practice of loving speech (*priyavāda*) that transforms others by conforming to their sentiments; second, from "whether known or unknown" onwards, the practice of benefiting others by transforming them according to their capacities; third, transformation...

Thus, one practices giving in accordance with the minds of sentient beings. The fourfold integration acts according to the requirements of the occasion through shared activity. This section has two parts: first, a specific explanation;
second, a general explanation. This is the specific explanation, which contains three further clarifications regarding the three types of persons, as can be understood from the text.
As for what is called "together" (*jù*), it refers to both age and virtue.

Now, upon examining the treatise, the sections concerning being ill or not ill occur prior to the phrase "whether recognized or unrecognized."
The commentary on "avoiding the fourteen defiled karmas" (up to) "embracing the four spiritual friends" notes that this is also beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*).
It involves avoiding defilement and embracing what is wholesome. Regarding the mention of "fourteen," the *Chuan* (Commentary) to the *Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra* states:

There are four [unwholesome actions] of body and speech: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying. There are four evil causes: greed, hatred, delusion, and fear. There are six ways that wealth is depleted:
addiction to alcohol, gambling, profligacy, infatuation, attachment to music and song, and evil friends. Regarding the phrase "concealing [the truth] in the six directions": [it refers to these six].
Parents are the east; teachers and elders are the south; wives and children are the west; relatives and friends are the north;

servants and laborers are below; those of high virtue are above. One’s mind should not be arrogant or haughty toward them; abiding therein is called the "Treasury. As for the four types of evil friends:

first, the friend who is like a relative but evil—appearing submissive outwardly while being malicious inwardly; second, the friend of sweet words—whose speech is compliant but whose intent is contrary; third, the respectful and obedient [evil friend]...
A bad friend is one whose mind is compliant [with wrongdoing] and who does not offer admonition. There are four types of bad friends: those who engage in the affairs of various evil associates.

As for the four types of good friends: first, they restrain one from what is wrong; second, they are compassionate and sympathetic; third, they benefit others; fourth, they share the same purpose. Of these, the middle two differ only in that the former expresses compassion while the latter bestows happiness.
The commentary states that dividing the property equally [up to] "without being off by even a hair's breadth" is an act of giving (*dāna*).
This has three meanings. The section beginning with "having examined carefully" refers to the third meaning.

Below the commentary on the four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), there must be nine sections; here, only one is indicated, while the remainder are deferred with the phrase "and so forth" (*yāvat*).
The general meaning below this is to distinguish the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), which consist of fifteen sections. The treatise merely indicates them thus.

According to the preceding and following parts of the treatise, all that is cultivated serves as the cause for enlightenment and is therefore a factor conducive to enlightenment; hence, it says "and so forth," which conveniently implies "up to."

Regarding the karma of the thirty-two marks and the sublime wisdom of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is stated in the fiftieth chapter, "The Establishment of Ultimate Yoga": "What is the sublime wisdom of all aspects? ...

It should be understood that herein, whether it be the Tathāgatas regarding those phenomena that lead to a collection of what is meaningless, or regarding those phenomena that do not lead to a collection of what is meaningful..."
Alternatively, regarding those phenomena that lead to a collection of meaningful things and those that do not lead to a collection of meaningless things—
within all such phenomena as these— the non-erroneous knowledge is called the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
If the Tathāgatas possess non-erroneous knowledge regarding those phenomena that lead to a collection of meaningful things among all phenomena, it should be understood accordingly.

This is called the Tathāgata’s wondrous wisdom (*jñāna*). Within this very context, if one were to combine the "knowledge of all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the "wondrous wisdom" into one, it would be termed the "wondrous wisdom of all aspects" (*sarvākāra-jñāna*). Some commentators place this section under the "Aids to Enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*);

however, placing it here below as part of the general exposition of the main text likely does not reflect the intent of the commentary (*ṭīkā*). If this passage were definitively assigned to this specific chapter, what [would be the consequence]?
There is a passage concerning the karma for the thirty-two marks and so forth; this should be reflected upon.
The commentary (*śūtra*) states that [the Buddha] causes [the practices of] body, speech, and mind (up to "all to manifest")—this note follows the text below.
This appears at the end of the forty-third chapter, the Chapter on the Four Means of Attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). Generally speaking, it also occurs across seven chapters.
There are nine gates; this is the first, the gate of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The treatise presents three meanings: first, active manifestation (*samudācāra*);
second, supremacy (*paramatva*); and third, purity (*viśuddhi*). Here, the first [meaning] consists of the active manifestation of the first two types of karma.

Within supremacy, there are again two meanings: first, vastness (*audārya*), and second, non-defilement (*anāsrava*). Vastness further has three aspects: first, [the vastness of] sentient beings... [text fragment].
There is no distinction between the two things; there is no distinction between the three times. That it is universally for all sentient beings is the first [point].
That it is at all times is the third. That one cultivates every aspect is the second. Regarding the absence of defilement, there are four further points:
first, joy; second, not harming others; third, seeing merit; and fourth, being without expectation. In the text, the character for "expectation" (悕) [is used].
The treatise begins with the character "xi" (希). The character "děng" (等) [in the title] includes by extension qualities such as not seeking recompense;

this was indicated in the preceding heading. Following the momentum of this textual flow, subsequent headings are introduced. This commentary, however, proceeds from the perspective of *dāna* (giving), as these elements mutually illuminate one another.
The general meaning is simply that these are the dharmas studied by Bodhisattvas; with the exception of the first two periods, all are what Bodhisattvas should correctly practice.
Regarding "Training" (*śikṣā*) and "the factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*): this meaning can be understood through the three textual divisions.

The third is called the "Division on the Factors of Enlightenment" (*Bodhipakṣavibhāga*), because it distinguishes the ten factors of training while also including the training in conduct. Below this, within the section on training, there is a major structural division:
first, the individual analysis of various practices; second, the comprehensive categorization and selection. One may examine this in detail according to the preceding essential summary.

One should study these up to the point of reaching the King [of Dharma]. Furthermore, the seven types of aspiration (*āśaya*) mentioned in the subsequent text—such as all of these—are called the "dharmas to be studied" (*śikṣitavya-dharma*).
This entire section, which cites these six perfections (*pāramitā*), necessarily constitutes a single unit that comprehensively explains everything to be studied by all Bodhisattvas;
thus, it may also be termed a "factor of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*). The seven aspirations mentioned below are specifically the aspirations (*āśaya*).
Chapter. [This connects to] the following "Chapter on Abiding. At the beginning of the "Chapter on Abiding," there is a general introductory passage; the preceding text may be sought therein.
The commentary states that the contemplations of impurity and so forth are all as explained in the Sūtra.

The commentary states that these are practiced together with those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), yet their underlying intentions regarding non-contemplation and so forth differ. The previous classification appears to be erroneous;

this text actually belongs to the forty-fifth section, within the ninth gate, among the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*). It is appropriate to treat them as identical here. The treatise says:
Regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), one understands them as they truly are, yet does not realize them. Or, the characters do not differ.
In the subsequent section of the treatise, the two types of cultivation are explained in detail. Within the character "yu" (與), one perceives their common meaning. The treatise states:

One universally and as-it-isly understands the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment in the Śrāvaka vehicle, and likewise understands all thirty-seven factors of enlightenment in the Mahāyāna as they truly are.
One is able to abide in the contemplation of the body within one's own person, yet does not conceptualize the body as having an intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
(And so forth. Because it is like that, it is distinct [from the Śrāvaka path]. Although the distinct cultivation is the same, one certainly does not realize [the fruit] prematurely.

the remainder are applied accordingly across various chapters. Since this is a general discussion and not restricted to this chapter alone, the aspiration is presented first. Fifth.
