The sub-commentary explains that conditioned phenomena are provisional, while emptiness is the reality. Their essence is actually non-existent. The character "already" (已) belongs to the preceding phrase.
The commentary states that as appropriate (until): it is explained as having the meaning of "basis" (*āyatana*).
Within the word "only" (*kevala*), it is revealed that [this] is not ultimate reality. Otherwise, what would be negated?
The commentary further states that although this is based on worldly convention (until): the sequence is thus.
This commentary relies on the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) to explain their sequence; it should be understood accordingly based on their respective objects (*viṣaya*).

Alternatively, they may be explained in combination, yet it must still be stated that the faculties come first and the objects follow: "seeing" refers to the eye; "inquiry" refers to the ear; "anointing with incense" refers to the nose;
"receiving food" refers to the tongue; "attending to needs" refers to the body; and "discriminating" refers to the mind. It is like a guest who arrives: one must first see them.
...up to the final differentiation of high and low.
The *Shu* (Commentary) states that from the eye and ear up to the mind, these are the eight consciousnesses.

The *Zhu* (Annotation) does not mention the eight consciousnesses here; how then can this be reconciled with the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*? [The five consciousnesses] follow...

Regarding the faculties (*indriya*): mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) pertains to both [the faculty and its object], because it functions in accordance with them. The seventh and eighth consciousnesses pertain to neither.

Some claim that the six consciousnesses also do not involve separation or conjunction because they lack physical form; this is incorrect. One may only say that they are described in relation to the location of their respective faculties, as they are said to be "within" them and because they are the locus of their support (*āśraya*).
To claim that the faculties are cited to manifest the consciousnesses does not accord with this text, for the text explains each of them separately.

The commentary states that the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*) is not fixed. This note regarding "the stage of fruition" refers to mastery (*vaśitā*), namely the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth, because it is accepted that such functions [operate] there.

Whether [the stages] are treated as distinct or combined is not fixed. There are those who claim that consciousness alone acts as the basis for function; this specifically contradicts the present text. If [consciousness] does not act as the basis for function, then...
In that case, the attainment or non-attainment of cause and effect would be identical; why then say it is "indeterminate"? The Sub-commentary (*Sū*) states:
"The functions of the eyes and ears are superior, thus they receive the name 'supernormal' (*abhijñā*). The Note (*Zhù*) explains:

"They are called 'superior in function' because their cognition operates through separation from the object (*parokṣa-jñāna*). This is based on the stage of the cause (*hetu-avasthā*). If based on the stage of the fruit (*phala-avasthā*), the five sense faculties [are so designated].

All [the faculties] are established. Those who claim that the characteristic of dharmas consists in the destruction of the faculty’s sprout specifically contradict this text; they should instead say that it does not exist because it has not yet attained mastery.
The commentary states that "transformation [bodies] are not real" and exist only in the Desire and Form Realms.

The note on the preceding phrase excludes what is not [real], clarifying that this [discussion] distinguishes the actual [roots]. "Not transformation [bodies]" refers to the lower phrase concerning the realms;

this distinguishes the actual faculties. The statement that they "pervade the Desire Realm" includes the explanation of karmic retribution. "Cultivated [faculties] exist only in the Form Realm. This passage broadly distinguishes their pervasiveness.

The section on the "gates" is as follows. Alternatively, this may serve as a general gate concerning the connection to the realms (*dhātu-bandhana*), with subsequent sections providing a detailed classification of similar categories.
Or, the first sentence may constitute a separate gate.
The sub-commentary [states]: "The various consciousnesses of the lower stages (up to) have varying degrees of superiority and inferiority in their functions."
The commentary below relies upon the middle [section]. There are these four powers; since these all borrow from consciousness, there are also the conditions of karma and the power of dharmas.
The cultivation across the various stages is unequal in terms of superiority and inferiority, as explained according to the five positions.

As for the sequence of nine, eight, seven, and five conditions mentioned below, the commentary notes that these differ from the preceding [explanation]. Since it explains the various conditions upon which the dependent consciousnesses rely—namely the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*)—it does not constitute the main text.
These are not included in the previous four; there are nine others: first, space (*ākāśa*); second, light (*āloka*); third, the faculty (*indriya*); fourth, the object (*viṣaya*); fifth...
(1) Attention; (2) seeds; (3) discrimination; (4) defilement and purity; (5) the fundamental [consciousness]. The latter three correspond respectively to the six, seven, and eight consciousnesses.

Eye-consciousness arises from nine conditions; ear-consciousness arises from only eight. Nose, tongue, and body consciousnesses arise from seven; the latter three [mental consciousnesses] arise from five, four, and three [conditions] respectively.
The fleshly eye possesses all nine; the ear possesses eight, excluding light. The three consciousnesses of the nose and so forth possess seven; furthermore, they exclude...

The *ākāśa* [element] is as described above; the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is the same. For the sixth consciousness, there are five [conditions], excluding both the defiled and the pure, because these are themselves the faculties (*indriya*).

Furthermore, it excludes conceptualization (*vikalpa*), because that is its own essential nature. For the seventh consciousness, there are three conditions, excluding the fundamental [consciousness], because that is itself the faculty.

Therefore, for the eighth consciousness, there are four conditions; however, its object is added back in. Regarding the exclusions for the final three [consciousnesses], their essential natures are the same, and thus they follow the previous principle.
It is said: "Excluding the mind" means there is a distinction. For instance, the seventh [consciousness] is also excluded from being a basis because it is not its own self-substance (*svabhāva*).

Regarding the exclusion of the defiled and pure [factors], they instead constitute its self-substance. The eighth [consciousness] excludes the defiled and pure [factors] and instead constitutes the faculty (*indriya*).
Here, only five are mentioned and not four or three; this is in reference to the six consciousnesses. This is because it follows the Hīnayāna, which speaks of six [consciousnesses] and two [natures].
The *śāstra* states that derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) refers to shadows, shapes, and manifest actions, up to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The commentary (*bhāṣya*) cites three categories of matter: the thirty-one subtle types and the thirteen manifest types, namely blue, yellow, red, white, light, and shadow.

Light, darkness, smoke, clouds, dust, mist, and space constitute the single category of manifest color (*varṇa*). There are ten types of shape (*saṃsthāna*): long, short, square, round, coarse, [fine, high, low, even, and uneven].

Subtle, tall, short, straight, crooked, and so forth—there are eight types of manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*): taking up, putting down, contracting, extending, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
Furthermore, each of these has [sounds that are] agreeable, disagreeable, and those which are contrary to both; within sound there are also those that are non-clinging and those produced by both.
Moreover, there are sounds that are agreeable, disagreeable, and contrary to both, as well as speech that is noble and that which is ignoble.
Furthermore, there are those produced by causes and those established by worldly convention; these include the pervasive conceptualization of sounds, totaling twelve types.

Within odors, there are additionally the categories of pleasant, unpleasant, and neutral, totaling six. Regarding the three lower [steps], they involve lifting the foot. However, tangibles and mental objects (*dharmas*) are likewise not listed separately.
The commentary begins with five [points], the first two of which concern the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*).
Below the note, there are six sections. First, the section on the three categories: the first five sense organs (*indriya*) lack *niṣyanda* (outflow) results. Second, the section on the three realms:

because in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is the color-form that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*). This does not discuss the mental faculty (*manas*); now, regarding the formless realm as well...

There is maturation (*vipāka*). Regarding the three categories of manifest (*vijñapti*) and non-manifest (*avijñapti*): ten are exclusively non-manifest; four pertain to the gate of the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*), which depends solely on their intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*);

if one follows the manifest, then form (*rūpa*) and sound (*śabda*) pervade all three natures. Five depend on the gate of formation (*nirmāṇa*): that which is based on a substance (*dravya*) is direct, while that which is separated from a substance is indirect;

alternatively, they are distinguished as "complete" or otherwise according to the realms (*dhātu*) and so forth. Because these do not differentiate the actual essence (*svabhāva*), they are termed "provisionally formed. Six.
The gates of the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) are as easily understood as usual.
The commentary on the twenty verses states (up to): "Like sentient beings born by transformation (*upapāduka*).

The upper mention of "transformation" refers to those who are the primary audience (*yathā-adhikāra*). The lower mention of "transformation" refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). The upper transformation...

Regarding the instruction for others: if one neglects the transformation of those below while seeking birth above among sentient beings, one will be reborn in the four modes of birth below. The following serves as an illustration:
just as the intermediate state (antarābhava) body is not a truly existent sentient being, yet is provisionally designated as such to refute the view of nihilism.
The Commentary states that this explains the Buddha [as such] (up to the point of) abandoning the grasping at a self.

The Sub-commentary states: "In order to eliminate the grasping at a self, [the Buddha] forcibly designates a 'place' within that which is beyond words, just as one speaks of the 'intermediate state' (*antarābhava*).

Question: Since the intermediate state truly exists, why is it called an "intentional terminology" (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*)? Answer: That which does not manifest as a physical form is called intentional terminology; it is not that it lacks a shape.

The characteristic is called "intentional meaning" (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*). If that were so, then all explanations of the four modes of birth (*yoni*) and the nine types of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*), and so forth, would necessarily be intentional.

Answer: The facts are indeed the same; however, these [other categories] are cited because they are not directly perceived (*aparokṣa*). They are the shadow of the intentional meaning, and furthermore, they serve as correct examples because the four modes of birth and so forth are primary.
Moreover, that intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) is not a separate, distinct retribution (*vipāka*), for it is precisely the fundamental existence (*pūrvakālabhava*).
The commentary states that the followers of the Two Vehicles do not understand [this] (up to the point where they) cling to it as being truly existent.
The note below this section enters into the sūtra; however, this refers back to the clinging to the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and does not refer to transformation-birth (*upapāduka*).
The Commentary now clarifies that which is grasped (until the point where it concludes that there is no locus).

The main body of the Note contains the characteristics of the non-existence of all three natures. Two phrases refer to the *parikalpita* (imagined nature), and two phrases refer to the *paratantra* (dependent nature).

The expression "non-existence" (*wu*) consists of two characters; both names and their definitions are raised together, rather than being a redundant negation. If it were a redundant negation, it would instead imply existence.
Alternatively, "non" (fei) may be a scribal error for "existence" (you), or it may be "true" (zhen). Or perhaps the character "non" has been omitted entirely.

Or "real" (shi) may be a mistake for "empty" (kong); this can be understood by examining the preceding text concerning the aggregates (skandhas). Alternatively, it may refer to that which is grasped as an object of attachment.
It is called "unreal" because it does not exist within dependent origination; however, as with the text on the aggregates, this is easy to understand.
The two lines constitute the perfected nature, and the two lines constitute the summary—both can be understood accordingly.
The Commentary on the Great Sūtra explains [the passage] up to "the sphere of phenomena is empty," noting that because names have no reality, they are the characteristic of emptiness.
The Commentary on the Sūtra states: "There is no eye-element, and so forth, up to no mind-consciousness-element."
The commentary on the sutra relies on the eye-element and the form-element, as well as the eye-consciousness-element and the form-consciousness-element; these six and three are paired respectively.
The sub-commentary praises this, saying: "In this sutra, within emptiness, there are no eighteen elements."
The commentary explains the three natures individually; some explain them as "true emptiness," both as previously stated.
The sub-commentary (*shū*) states that regarding those who speak of "superior emptiness" (up to the point where it says) "by analogy with the sixteen intermediate elements."
The commentary on this passage is as appropriate as it should be; it is also treated in this manner.
The sub-commentary states that because it is conventional, it is said to "exist," yet [it does so] because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is empty.
The five or four phrases [of the commentary] have the same general meaning as before.
The Commentary (*śūtra*) says, as appropriate, [up to] "it is called a *dhātu*.
The Sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) states that this is established by way of convention; the reflection is not real.
The Commentary [continues] from the previous section on the sequence [up to] "the sequence is thus."

The commentary states that this sequence is based solely on the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The objects and consciousnesses are associated with the faculties, which differs from the previous arrangement.
As for the statement that "the element of consciousness arises accordingly," this refers to its enumeration as being associated with the faculties, rather than according to their distinct locations.
The commentary states that "the discerning [consciousness] apprehends objects" up to the point of "the characteristics of the six consciousness-elements.
The sub-commentary explains this by grouping them as "three and six," because their categories of meaning are identical; thus, their function is such, rather than following a sequential order.
The commentary states that because the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma depends upon the capacities and inclinations of his audience, this section contains two gates.

The first is based on the opening and closing [of categories], wherein there is mutual variation between expansion and brevity. The second is based on the enumeration of dharmas; although the names are brief, the content is extensive.

This is for the sake of those who are deluded regarding the three [categories]. For those with understanding, these belong to the preceding [section]: the aggregates (*skandha*) are for those deluded about the "basis" (*āśraya*), the sense bases (*āyatana*) are for those deluded about "form" (*rūpa*), and the elements (*dhātu*)...

Distinguishing the ignorant consciousness: I now fear that it belongs to the following section, which is a brief exposition within a broader context. This is because the preceding section merely presents the brief and the broad.
The commentary refutes the notion of "I" as the sustainer (up to the point where one) clings to it as being real.

The commentary refutes that substantial self; it then provisionally designates [the aggregates] as "realms" (dhātus) based on their capacity to sustain [the self]. The followers of the Two Vehicles then cling to this.
The *Śāstra* states that "that which is clung to is entirely non-existent," and this [passage] concludes by confirming that non-existence.

The commentary also possesses the three emptinesses. The first phrase refers to the *parikalpita* (imagined); the second phrase refers to the *paratantra* (dependent) and *pariniṣpanna* (perfected). The *paratantra* is mentioned merely in relation to the *pariniṣpanna*, not as an object of grasping;
or it is mentioned in relation to being free from verbal designations (*abhilāpa*).
The Commentary on the Sūtra states: "From 'no ignorance' up to 'also no exhaustion of old age and death. The Sub-commentary notes:

Previously, only the non-existence of the aggregates, bases, and elements was taught. That here, within this dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the term "exhaustion" is also mentioned is because it serves as the direct antidote;

the preceding three [truths] are remote. Among the Four Noble Truths, this refers to Cessation (*nirodha*) and the Path (*mārga*). The same applies to wisdom (*jñāna*) and attainment (*prāpti*). Above.
According to what is appropriate: if it is superior to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), then "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*) has the meaning of emptiness; yet it is also precisely that which serves as the antidote.
Furthermore, as explained below, the Commentary (*Śāstra*) praises this, stating: "The term 'superior emptiness' [extends] down to 'there is no proximate observation'."
The commentary notes that with respect to the preceding three categories, these are termed "proximate.
The sub-commentary (*shu*) states: "Below, there is no proximate contemplation" (up to the point where) the twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) is explained.
The commentary restates the subject of what has arisen for a separate explanation: "To whom does this contemplation belong? The meaning of the preceding text should be understood accordingly.
The same applies here. The *Shu* (Commentary) further states that ignorance [is non-existent]... up to "now it is said for whom it is non-existent.

The *Zhu* (Annotation) is identical to the previous three sections; it asserts that it is truly non-existent. It is incorrect to claim that the previous section was intended merely to cite evidence. The final sentence belongs to [the following].
"Below. This is also not [the case]. One should say: "This is the dependent origination of liberation. The subsequent text below explains that liberation is likewise inexhaustible.
[The commentary] says "exhausted" means "non-existent" (until) "there is no exhaustion of old age and death."
This commentary explains that which is inexhaustible; that which can exhaust [all things] is itself emptiness. Even the discourse on emptiness is non-existent, and its name is likewise inexhaustible.

Combining this with what preceded, one should speak of "neither of the two. However, that [previous section] set aside the means of expression (*prapañca*), whereas the preceding [section] explained it by way of enumeration.
The Commentary on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (up to this point) now clarifies its reflection.
This note serves to resolve potential objections. Fearing that an external critic might ask: "In the first three and the final two [sections], you spoke only of dispelling substantiality;
why is it that here you further dispel emptiness as well? Therefore, this is clarified.
The Commentary states that "as appropriate" (meaning up to) "all have both direct and reverse [orders].
The Sub-commentary notes two direct and two reverse orders; these should be understood as follows.
The Commentary explains that regarding "contaminated [phenomena] in direct order," this is a statement concerning the repeated contemplation of phenomena.

The commentary briefly indicates the forward and reverse orders. Based on what contemplative wisdom does one practice the contemplation of sequential arising? This is called "contemplation according to the flow" (*pravṛtti-anuloma*), which is the initial contemplation.
Subsequently, during the stage of application, when the contemplation of the mind has become mature, one traces back the preceding causes, asking, "By whom [does this] exist?

and so forth; this is called "reverse contemplation" (*pratiloma*). Fundamental wisdom cuts the root at the very beginning, namely ignorance (*avidyā*); subsequently, through the wisdom of subsequent attainment (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), one contemplates again, starting from the suffering that precedes it in the reverse order.

Therefore, the sequence of these [contemplations] in both forward and reverse order is as follows. According to the *Chang* (Chapter), once one has attained the state of an Arhat (*aśaikṣa*) through the purification of the reverse order, only then does one perform this [contemplation].
Regarding the contemplation of the defiled forward order (*sāsrava-anuloma*), it extends up to being endowed with the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*).

The commentary states: "In the first case, the power of wisdom is inferior and cannot be traced back; thus, it does not yet correspond [to the full set]. If one relies on the cause as it is produced (*kṛtakāraṇa*), there are only eleven;
this [present case], however, relies on the observation of the essential nature (*tattva-darśana*), and therefore possesses all twelve."
The commentary states: "From 'first, ignorance' (up to) 'called decay, change, and final extinction.

The sub-commentary notes: "'Confrontation' means direct encounter. When the object is superior and agreeable, it is so called; for inferior and neutral objects, one should infer accordingly. The rest is as explained in treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Yogācārabhūmi*."
The Commentary states that this contemplation is pursued by delusion (*moha*). The Sub-commentary explains that "delusion" is none other than ignorance (*avidyā*).

All worldly phenomena are erroneous. The fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) follows karma; "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); the "six sense bases" (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) consist of the faculties and the outflows;

"contact" (*sparśa*) and "feeling" (*vedanā*) constitute the two [remaining links]; and the seeds that bring about fruition pertain generally to the aforementioned six branches. "Attachment" (*tṛṣṇā*) is the state of being addicted and clinging. It nourishes...
Grasping (*upādāna*) is the cause; karma and so forth are existence (*bhava*). The latter two [links] are easily understood.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "With birth as condition, there is old age and death" (*jāti-pratyayā jarāmaraṇam*).
The commentary notes that this establishes the sequence of the agent and the object as conditions for arising.
The commentary states that the five types, beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), are designated as the subsequent conditions.
This note explains that this refers to the seeds; it describes the arising of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in relation to the stage of future birth.
Regarding the commentary on the "contemplation of the reverse order of defilement" up to the "teaching of the established truths" (*vyavasthāpana-satya*): [the text continues].

The commentary states that looking forward to subsequent purity is the non-established contemplation (*apratiṣṭhita-vipaśyanā*), which is called "initial" and "practiced. Alternatively, it refers to the stage equal to consciousness.
The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains that from old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) [up to the first noble truth], one contemplates all the truths (*satya*) in succession.
In the commentary, the character "suffering" (苦) has been omitted below the character "death" (死). Alternatively, because its essence is identical [to that of death], it is not mentioned again.
This passage explains that each member of the dependent origination arises in relation to the four truths, resulting in forty-four [instances].
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states that one first observes [the links] in reverse order, starting from the link of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
This note addresses a potential objection; it may also be connected to what precedes it.
The Commentary explains that by means of three characteristics, the three [links] are not indeterminate.

This commentary relies upon the Suffering and Origin [Truths]. The factors (*aṅga*) are categorized into four groups: (1) the two factors of Origin constitute the five types of suffering; (3) the two factors of Origin constitute the two types of suffering.

For one who observes correctly, each factor is observed individually, and there are three aspects to this observation. When observing the final factor, at the time of observing its function as a cause, the various categories are treated collectively;

therefore, the subtle causes mentioned below—namely craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*)—are explained here. This is found in the ninety-third fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
If one follows the *Kechao* (Excerpts from the Commentary), it should state: "One contemplates its five branches by means of three aspects.
Why, then, does it say here only "contemplating old age and death"? Therefore, this refers specifically to contemplating the three causes and conditions of the branch of old age and death:

contemplating the first two as dependent origination (*paratantra*) and the last one as pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*). The former two are direct contemplations, while the latter involves removing the aforementioned two causes; what remains is...
Because there is nothing further [beyond it].
The commentary states that the causes and conditions for the arising of sensation are called "subtle" (extending to the point where) there is old age and death.

The *Fahua yishu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) mentions only two [stages], yet it first explains the coarse and subsequently explains the proximate. Here, it first explains the subtle, following from what preceded.
It is said that what is adjacent is "near" and what is separated is "distant. What is near is easily known and is termed "coarse";

what is distant is difficult to comprehend and is termed "subtle. However, if it can function as a condition, it is simply called a "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*). This refers to the "arising from two."
This refers to the two causes of the coarse and the subtle. The treatise states:

"The causal conditions that bring about the arising of the self-substance are also called 'arising,' and the self-substance that arises is also called 'arising. This passage likewise explains the aforementioned two causes.
The *Śāstra* states that future old age and death have coarse birth as their cause.
The *Commentary* (*Zhù*) provides a two-period analysis: because future birth does not yet exist, it does not speak of coarse birth;

because the craving and grasping of present old age and death have already ceased, it does not speak of subtle birth. Therefore, each speaks of only one. The *Yìdēng* further explains "each" [as follows].
It spans two lifetimes, discussing what has been and what will be; therefore, there are two for each.
The commentary (*śāstra*) excludes the substance of arising; from "the rest" to "the name is not indeterminate.
The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) judges this to be the "investigating cause" (*parimārga-hetu*), thus making seventy-seven. Taking four characters as a phrase, it is the "arising cause" (*janana-hetu*).

Regarding the "two causes": that which is referred to as "the remainder" consists of *īśvara*, *pradhāna* (primordial matter), and so forth; therefore, these are [the objects of] the parikalpita-svabhāva (imagined nature). This constitutes one member [of the dependent nature].
According to the ninety-third [sūtra], there is a subsequent passage that, by way of analogy, points to four members. The treatise states:

"Just as one contemplates old age and death, birth, existence, grasping, and craving—each through two kinds [of causes]—one should know that the same applies when observing them according to principle. This...
This refers to the *Fahua yideng* (Lamp for the Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), yet neither of these [works] contains it; thus, later students find it difficult to perceive the ten branches.
Question: What are the characteristics of the two causes of the birth-branch (*jāti-aṅga*)? Answer: This shall be explained below.
Although the *Śāstra* observes [the links from] old age and death (up to) not yet being satisfied, the two phrases of the commentary provide a general indication.
Regarding the branches up to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the two phrases are reiterated according to the world. As for "the future limit" (*aparānta*), it is because one must connect to present suffering;
the reason "the present limit" (*pratyutpannānta*) is not mentioned is that it is separated by craving and so forth. The above constitutes the full citation. Although [one] observes...
The five factors each have two causes. [The first] is for the sake of not being content; it does not merely repeat what preceded. [The second] takes craving and so forth as its cause;
this repeats the preceding while citing the illustrative text.
The Commentary further observes [up to] present suffering.
It notes that the accumulation of future suffering consists of craving, grasping, and becoming; this cause of future accumulation is precisely present suffering.
This suffering is itself the five branches beginning with consciousness.
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states that one should universally and retroactively contemplate [the links] down to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The *Ṭīkā* (Sub-commentary) notes that one contemplates the suffering manifested above; in each case, there should be two causes and conditions. This should be understood according to the principle.

The text of the *Śāstra* follows the previous pattern, having already exemplified birth (*jāti*) and so forth; it does not further state that these have two causes and conditions, but the meaning should be understood as such.
The Commentary observes the suffering of the future (up to) the existence of the suffering of the present life.
The Sub-commentary states that one will return [to the beginning]. Reiterating the initial observation: by whom is the suffering of old age and death in the future brought about?

One knows it is due to what is to be accumulated (*āyūhana*). This refers to the cause of accumulation; "accumulation" itself is the cause. Furthermore, one observes this accumulation: by whom does it exist? One knows...
When observing in this way through present suffering, one knows that present suffering arises from prior accumulation (*saṃskāra*). The Commentary states:

"One knows that it arises from what was previously accumulated; with consciousness as its limit, there is the suffering of the present life. 'Prior accumulation' refers to ignorance as the formative action (*saṃskāra*)."
The Commentary (*Śāstra*), having already known [the cause] from the past... [to] how this could exist;

the Sub-commentary (*Ṭīkā*), having already observed the time when the future causes were accumulated, simultaneously understood that present suffering arises from those past causes, which were previously accumulated.
It does not observe further: "How could this present suffering exist? This is the text of the Question Chapter.

It appears to be distinct. Yet it is said that ignorance and formations are not different from craving, grasping, and becoming; therefore, the commentary explains that this refers to the reason for simultaneously understanding [them].

The Sub-commentary notes that the section on "no death after" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* appears within the tenth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

This explains that each member [of dependent origination] is examined in terms of its origination; it regresses up to consciousness. [The question arises: by what does consciousness exist? It is known to exist by virtue of name-and-form; therefore, [it does not regress further].
Furthermore, one contemplates ignorance and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). Again, there are ninety-three [verses]. The subsequent passage below is like a bundle of reeds;

the preceding text, based on the treatise, clarifies the subtle cause of consciousness; as for its coarse causal conditions, "consciousness" refers to—

Regarding distant time, one also understands that it arises from what was previously accumulated and no longer further examines from whom consciousness exists.

feeling (*vedanā*), contact (*sparśa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and the coarse causes. These are the same as for craving, with only one [link] being gradually reduced. The subtle causes have already been understood.
Next, one contemplates the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Since its subtle cause has already been known, one contemplates only its gross cause, which is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

Having understood the point of the subtle cause, one then infers from the link of formations (*saṃskāra*) that it likewise possesses two causes and conditions—craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*).

When contemplating the gross cause, there are ninety-three [links]; they are like a bundle of reeds. One no longer separately contemplates the causes and conditions of the link of formations; for this reason, it is called "the limit" (*sama*).
Consciousness recedes. The preceding section analyzed the branch of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). This text continues until the observation of the branch of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

The treatise consists of exactly two sections; these should be examined in detail.

Subsequently, one abandons grasping and realizes the liberation of the mind. The chapter states: "Because ignorance ceases, there is liberation through wisdom;

whereas "extinction" clarifies the transition from prior existence to subsequent non-existence. Thus, the two meanings are distinct. There is no [intrinsic] activity and no [intrinsic] cessation.
It is not correct to categorize this as a question and answer based on these two natures. This is merely a self-examination;
the commentary understands that from the cessation of the unconditioned (*avijñapti*) [up to] the cessation of old age and death.

The three [aspects] were discussed previously; they serve to rectify oneself. Regarding the four aspects of cessation (*nirodha*): the complete extinction of such truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) without remainder is called "cessation" (*nirodha*).
Causing all suffering to be stilled without remainder is called "calm" (*śānta*). Such cessation and calm, being supreme and excellent, are called "sublime" (*praṇīta*).

Because it is eternally abiding, it is called "detached" (*niḥsaraṇa*) from bondage. Regarding the four aspects of the path (*mārga*): that which acts as an antidote is called the "path" (*mārga*). It is the true knowledge [of the way].

"Name" refers to the four truths (*catur-āryasatya*). "Activity" (*saṃskāra*) refers to that which functions in accordance with them. "Departure" (*niḥsaraṇa*) refers to that which leads toward *nirvāṇa*;
alternatively, it is called "activity" because it is directed toward cessation (*nirodha*), and it is called "departure" because it is free from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

Each of these has four aspects, neither more nor less, because the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) possesses four inversions (*viparyāsa*). The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) anticipates an external objection, saying: "Since each Truth has four aspects (*ākāra*), why are the four aspects of Suffering said to apply generally to the latter three Truths, while the other three [Truths] do not?"
It is not so. This is understood through this principle: because that which is remedied is pervasive, that which remedies it is also pervasive. The other three are not so.
The essential meaning of this passage is that what is pervasive is retained; that is to say, emptiness is retained, for it is precisely that which correctly dispels existence.
The Commentary states that this is the gateway for entering the ultimate truth, because only by [attaining this] does one truly enter the ultimate.

Based on the previous discussion of "nearness," this is also stated in reference to that which is absent. This refers to the absence of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), and does not pertain to the level of reality (*tattva-bhūmi*).
The commentary cites a verse which says: [up to] "consciousness arises without anything apprehended.

The note explains that the first half [of the verse] refers to the absence of the grasped (grāhya), while the second half refers to the absence of the grasper (grāhaka). The statement that they exist "in dependence upon consciousness" refers specifically to the mental afflictions (kleśa).

To say that [the object] is non-existent in dependence upon the objective sphere (*ālambana*) is to speak of its very essence. The meaning is this: while it is said to exist in dependence upon consciousness, the apprehended object (*grāhya*) is actually non-existent.
Since that object is non-existent, consciousness itself is also not existent.
The *ṭīkā* states that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is likewise free from the two graspings (*dvaya-grāha*).
Although the root text and the commentary differ in their phrasing, they are equal in meaning insofar as both are free from the two graspings.

While the verse text is general, why are the two subsequent sections distinguished? One should use the preceding verse to corroborate the preceding general statement. Having provided this specific explanation, [the author] further cites one...
The verse is also a general principle.
The commentary further contains a verse (up to the line) "the nature of non-attainment is equal.

The note states that the first half establishes the principle, while the second half serves as the conclusion. It says that the locus of consciousness is entirely due to outflows (*āsrava*); it is consciousness that grasps.
There is attainment. According to reality, however, there is none. Thus one knows that the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) are equally non-existent upon reaching the stage of non-attainment.

Nature is the principle of the cause; when the principle and wisdom are equal, how could one realize the subsequently attained [wisdom]? This meaning is universally applicable and free from hindrance. Alternatively, this may be "having attainment."
Based on the preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*), the seeds of grasping in other stages are excluded; that is to say, there are two types of grasping.

The commentary states that everything up to the preparatory stage is termed "other stages. This is because they are not yet clearly manifest, and thus are called "existent" in a semblance sense, rather than [in an absolute sense].

The image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is termed "possessing attainment" (*sopādāna*). Now, the refutation of its substantial reality does not pertain to the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), or it may be intended to distance [the object] from it;

thus, there is no fault in its removal. Alternatively, regarding that which is not yet clearly manifest, it is described as "having grasping" (*sopādāna*); this refers to the removal of the seeds (*bīja*).
The Commentary refutes the real grasper (upādātṛ). [This continues] until: "However, because it severs the grasper. Regarding this, there are two interpretations.

In the first, the non-existence of wisdom (*jñāna*) and the non-existence of attainment (*prāpti*) each negate one type of grasping. In the latter, the non-existence of wisdom and the non-existence of attainment each negate both.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that they "negate individually," this refers to the specific negation of their functions as contrasted with the subsequent negations. It is a specific negation.
This is the essence (*tattva*). Although it is said that both are negated, one still distinguishes between essence and function, negating each separately.

Based on this interpretation, one can easily understand both the subject and the object. How does wisdom negate the apprehended (*grāhya*) within itself? This is explained in the subsequent verse. However, it severs the grasper (*grāhaka*).
The grasped object also does not exist; therefore, the capacity of the grasper is negated, and both functions are simultaneously discarded.

This commentary explains that these [negations] all eliminate the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva). From the phrase "because the dependent nature is like an illusion" up to "there are entirely no two characteristics," [the text establishes this].
The commentary below separately explains the dependent and perfected natures; when combined with the imagined nature, they are collectively termed "emptiness.
Within this emptiness, there is no real wisdom to be attained.
Therefore, according to the three natures (as stated in the sub-commentary), everything is non-existent.
The commentary states that "obstructing and excelling emptiness" means there is nothing at all.
The sub-commentary explains that regarding "wisdom and the locus of wisdom," up to the point where it says "because one does not grasp at signs," the term "locus" refers to that which is attained;
neither is said to be non-existent. What is called "the Real" below refers to fundamental wisdom being signless (*animitta*).
This is the taking [of it]. It is the division seen by the eye. Because one does not grasp at marks (*nimitta*), there is nothing to be grasped.
The *Sūtra Commentary* says: "Because of non-attainment.
The *Zangshu* (Treasury Commentary) does not provide an explanation for the preceding phrase; rather, it serves as the fourth section to distinguish what is attained, based on the profound [meaning].

Commentary: Therefore, there is that which is attained by means of these words, yet it is not something attained by each preceding stage. To universally designate all dharmas as "non-attainment" serves to comprehensively establish what has been stated previously.
The Commentary states: Regarding the words "Supreme Emptiness" (śūnyatā-viśeṣa) [up to] "all are non-existent," the concluding notes provide a largely identical explanation;
however, it simply means that there is no substantial essence whatsoever.
Regarding the words "as appropriate" [up to] "the ten conditioned phenomena do not exist," the Commentary provides the explanation.

The "object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya) is precisely dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda). "Appropriateness" (sthāna) refers to what is logical; "inappropriateness" (asthāna) is its opposite. "Faculties" (indriya) refers to faith and so forth.
"Truths" (satya) refers to the Four Noble Truths. The remaining [categories] are explained by their names.

The Commentary states that from Śāriputra [up to] the preparatory practices of the near and far, although they have not yet turned their minds [toward Mahāyāna], this discourse concerns their spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and is termed "gradual enlightenment. This contemplation is taught so that they may not harbor attachments hereafter.

Consequently, this nature is not the same as those of the Madhyamaka or Yogācāra schools; it fully explains the ten [categories]. The three aggregates (*skandha*) apply generally to both the distant and the subsequent.
The three proximate [attainments] are all termed "preparatory" (*prayoga*). Some [commentators] link the fundamental [attainment] with the preparatory stage to divide them into three pairs;

however, this likely does not reflect the intended meaning of the text, as the fundamental stage was never previously excluded. The *Zangshu* (Commentary on the Pitaka) divides these into four sections across six gates.
The first three lines state that the phenomena (dharmas) open and close; this makes it impossible to distinguish whether they are viewed from afar or nearby.
The Commentary [states]: "From the fundamental seeds arising... until there is nothing at all."
The preceding passage states that Śāriputra gradually awakened to the Mahāyāna; therefore, this refers to his fundamental seeds, which thus pertain to both natures.
Consequently, the six types of skillfulness are now taught for him at the stage of true contemplation (*tattvadarśana*), as explained below.
Alternatively, this phrase may be connected with what follows to properly establish the means of removal, continuing from the preceding discussion.

The preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of the near and far [realms] are then termed the "fundamental" (*maula*). Since this applies to both the fundamental and the subsequent [stages], it is further stated as "two.
The intention is to refer to the initial arising; thus, the character "seed" (*bīja*) is added. Alternatively, these two characters were originally the character for "arising" (*jan*); consider this.

The first six immediately refer to the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and not the seventh, because the latter lacks the function of interruption. Or, it may be that the six are excluded, and they are called the "six truths."
Contemplation. Alternatively, it may be the character "entry" (入). The subsequent mention of the "six aspects" refers to the aforementioned aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth.
The commentary [explains] the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), comprehensively explaining the preceding "non-existence."

The preceding commentary explains the nature of pervasive imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); the following section distinguishes the dependent (*paratantra*) and perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) natures. Since the text states that all three natures lack fixed characteristics, they are understood as being unattainable;
this serves as a general explanation for the preceding section as well.
The commentary states that as the Great Sūtra says (up to) "there is also nothing to be attained.

The sub-commentary explains that this realization penetrates the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*), all of which are non-attainable. This is because *prajñā* is precisely wisdom that attains the middle way.
The esoteric intent of the sūtra has already been explained above and below.
The commentary on the sutra states: "From *bodhisattva* (until) *ultimate nirvāṇa*. The note says:

If one relies on the perspective of supreme emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), then the characters from the beginning up to "is" (*shi*) constitute the praise of the causal basis; the characters below "mind" (*xin*) constitute the praise of the benefit of abandonment.
"Ultimate nirvāṇa" is likewise that which is to be eliminated. If one relies on the perspective of suchness (*tathatā*), cause and effect are distinguished. This...
This is the praise of the cause; therefore, it is placed above the character for "mind" (citta). This is the praise of the virtue of relying on training; it is placed below the character for "mind.

It praises the attainment of superior benefits by relying on the second section: first, it praises the departure from suffering while still citing the subsequent neighbor [of the path], and later, it praises the perfect realization, manifesting true awakening (bodhi).
The Commentary states: Regarding the words "The Victorious Emptiness" (Śūnyatāvijaya) up to "the benefit of severing the defilements of the obstacles," the Sub-commentary asks:
For what reason do the structural divisions (*ko-p’an*) of the two schools differ? It answers: Because the two [positions] of the *Śūnyatāvijaya* are established as being mutually relative;
for example, because *nirvāṇa* is such that it cannot be discarded.
The commentary relies on what was previously stated (up to the point where) "those who are afraid" means they are terrified.

The sub-commentary first explains that which dispels [the fear], and subsequently explains that which is dispelled. It provides word-by-word glosses in response to difficulties; this may be understood from the text as it stands.

The commentary [states] from "not yet relying on wisdom and awakening" up to "ultimate nirvana," and the sub-commentary [states] up to "rejoicing in nirvana"—these all refer to those who have not yet awakened; for them, nirvana is like a dream-flower and the like.

The Commentary (Sū), from "relying on the Prajñā" up to "all things are distanced," provides annotations that proceed from the shallow to the deep, thereby dispelling [all attachments]. The Commentary,
from "as appropriate" up to "perfect realization," explains that one should speak accordingly.
The commentary on the text of these two sections is as previously indicated.
In the *Śū* (sub-commentary), this praises the benefits of cultivation during the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*) of the Bodhisattva.
The character "this" (*ci*) was omitted above; it has now been added. This single exclamation is pointed out as praising the benefits of the cause, all of which are dedicated.
"Bodhisattva. Ultimate Nirvana. It is praised that one shall be able to attain it. Based on this, it must be categorized as cause and effect.
[Commentary: "The Bodhisattva at all times... is named 'relying upon Prajñā.'"
This commentary explains the essence of the *prajñā* to be apprehended, which possesses the five preceding types. Cultivating them in successive order is called "relying on *prajñā*.
The sub-commentary states that while [the term] "hindrance" (*āvaraṇa*) refers to the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*), it here applies to both hindrances.
The preceding commentary is distinct; the latter commentary has the same meaning.
Regarding the note on "fear" (up to "arising from the defeat"):
this arising occurs prior to the stage of the provisions (*sambhāra*). This passage explains the causes and conditions for its arising; it is not [the case that...].

Regarding the essential nature [of these fears]: within the forty-seventh chapter, the "Chapter on Abidings," it is stated that in the "Abiding of Supreme Joy" (*pramuditā-vihāra*), one is free from the five fears.
This is the text from that source. If one were to extract their essential natures, the *Zuǎnlún* (Compendium of Principles) states in unison:

the fear of non-sustenance has as its nature the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and craving for the objects of livelihood (*upakaraṇa-tṛṣṇā*). The fear of ill repute has greed (*lobha*) as its nature. The fear of death has the view of self as its nature.
The latter two types both have delusion (*moha*) as their essence.
Regarding the commentary on "perversion" (up to the point where it says) "referring to 'self'":

the first three and the latter four are divided into general and specific categories. As for "perversion of mind," it receives its name by way of proximity; this excludes [the category of] perception (*saṃjñā*).
Because [the treatise] views the two [views of self and what belongs to self], as well as the remaining afflictions, as its substance;
the commentary [states] regarding the latter four types (up to "referring to the remaining afflictions"), this explains the first three.
The substance of perception (*saṃjñā*) is like that of name (*nāman*); "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) refers to the view among the four inversions mentioned below; "mind" (*citta*) should...
This refers to the outflow (*niṣyanda*) and the root [afflictions]. That is to say, below the characters, some characters were omitted due to doubt; they have now been added.
This commentary contains three types [of afflictions], namely the remaining afflictions (*kleśa*).

The commentary below lists the four inversions (*viparyāsa*). The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the inversion of taking what is non-self to be a self. The view of permanence (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) is the inversion of taking what is impermanent to be permanent.

The grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is the inversion of taking what is impure to be pure. The grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is the inversion of taking what is suffering to be pleasure.

Greed (*rāga*) pervades both purity and pleasure. In this text, the word "grasping" (*parāmarśa*) was omitted after the word "view" (*dṛṣṭi*); it has now been added. Thus, these are the four views regarding suffering.
Furthermore, its nature is craving.
Regarding the phrase "dream-thought" (*svapna-vikalpa*) [in the commentary]:
it is called "dream-thought" because it is a dream that is a thought; this refers to a dream consisting of conceptualization. This, in turn, encompasses the entire state of saṃsāra.
Regarding the preceding seven inversions (up to the phrase) "therefore they are called dream-like thoughts":

the commentary notes that these, in relation to the inversions, are themselves dream-like thoughts. One should say that the former [explanation] interprets them as being identical to the inversions, while the latter interprets them according to the distinction between cause and effect.
The *Śāstra* [states]: "Or, from the preceding various inversions (up to) 'is the fruit of birth and death.

The commentary notes that cause and effect are distinct; therefore, it is not a *karmadhāraya* compound. It may be treated as a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound, or as a *dvandva* (contradictory) compound."
The *Sū* (Commentary) states, "As if in a dream" (up to) "designating the name 'dream-like thought'.
The *Zhù* (Sub-commentary) relies on the second interpretation. It anticipates an external objection: "If birth-and-death is a dream, then both cause and effect are so;

why is it that regarding the cause, one does not speak of 'dream-like thought'? The general meaning of the *Sū*'s response is that the dream is manifest within the fruit [of experience], because it pertains to the objective sphere of the body (*kāya-viṣaya*). It should...
He further asks: "The fruit of birth and death is also a perversion; why speak of perversion only with respect to the cause?

There is no answer to this in the *Śāstra*, but one may provide an answer by analogy: "Because the causes, such as views and so forth, are augmented, it is only with respect to the cause that it is termed a perversion."
The Commentary states that "Vimala" (in Sanskrit) signifies the meaning of "the nature being serene.
The Sub-commentary provides separate explanations for these two characters, which are easy to understand from the text itself.
The Commentary further explains that apart from the nature of *tathatā* (suchness), there are four kinds [of purity] as taught.

The first two phrases of the commentary are concessive (*yady api*). It is inherently pure from the beginning; fundamentally, there is no dual essence, nor are there distinct characteristics. Or, regarding "no distinction":
even if one were to concede that it is described as manifold, there is still no distinction. This is like the removal of reality (*yathābhūta*) and so forth.

Alternatively, regarding "essence" (*tattva*) and "state" (*avasthā*), the following [phrase] negates the remaining three: "conditions" (*pratyaya*) are non-abiding because they are not [true] wisdom; "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*) refers to the latter two, because both cause and effect are exhausted.

The sub-commentary (Sūtra), from "I. Self-nature" up to "the true suchness (tathatā) of phenomena," provides this as the definition of the essence (svabhāva). According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, there are further ten meanings [of essence], as explained therein.
The Commentary states: "The two [aspects of] non-abiding (from 'non-abiding' up to 'pure *tathatā*').
The 'abiding place' refers to both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. Non-abiding in such places is precisely compassion and wisdom.
This nirvāṇa of non-abiding, characterized by compassion and wisdom, is always possessed [by the Buddha], capable of turning [the wheel of Dharma] like two wings."

The commentary [explains] "the *tathatā* revealed by [the state of] having a remainder of the three realms of existence" (*sopadhiśeṣa*) using the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) analysis. Alternatively, it refers to "the state of having no remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*), which is itself *nirvāṇa*, because in this revealed locus there are no other remaining phenomena.
Whether it is that which can cause [phenomena] to cease, or that which is absent, it is simply a *tatpuruṣa*.
In some places in the Commentary, from "based on the first" (至) to "attaining liberation together," the three annotations differ; their meaning is easy to perceive.
In this section of the Commentary, it is stated generally that [they] realize and witness *nirvāṇa*.

The Commentary (*Ṭīkā*) should treat this section and the subsequent text as an exegesis of the Sūtra, dividing it into three interpretations: first, a general interpretation of the common characteristics;
second, a specific correlation with the four stages; and third, a specific correlation with the three stages. This is also as in the New Curriculum (*Xinke*).

The Commentary states that from "or the bodhisattva" up to "the mind is without obstruction," the *sambhāra* (provisional equipment) and *prayoga* (preparatory application) stages are combined into one. Since, during the *sambhāra* stage, one has not yet eliminated the five fears, it is merely the manifest obstructions that are termed "obstructions.
In this *sambhāra* stage, one does not suppress the seeds of innate [afflictions] or conceptual [afflictions], but merely brings them into manifestation.
In the commentary on the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), [it says] "...there is no fear.
The note explains this as being because [the afflictions] are first severed and because they are suppressed in the present.
In the commentary on the stage of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), [it says] "...the dreams and illusions of birth and death."
This stage is noted because it is capable of bringing about the exhaustion of birth and death; according to the two preceding interpretations, cause and effect are separated.
In the commentary, this corresponds to the ultimate *nirvāṇa* of the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
This note praises the benefit of the cause; therefore, the term "should" is employed.
The commentary states that this is because the characteristics manifested in the four stages are explained in terms of their increase.

This note anticipates an external objection, asking: "Does not the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) also eliminate the five fears? [The response is: "It does, through the arising of right abandonment (*samyakprahāṇa*). This is a detailed analysis.

Because they are inverted. Since the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) have already suppressed them, what defilement would not be restrained? How, then, are the four stages (*catur-vīthi*) to be assigned? This [text] clarifies that point.
The meaning of "increasing" (*vṛddhi*) is as previously stated and has already been explained according to the text. As for the mention of "four," this is a general term.

The Commentary further states that because one abides in the Stage of Extreme Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi) up until the attainment of untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna), it is uniquely designated [as such] because one first attains the unimpeded [knowledges]. Nevertheless, as afflictions still manifest and function, it is not yet called "freedom from fear.
The three layers of skin, flesh, and [inner membrane] receive their names according to their relative depth.

The Commentary states: "In the effortless state of non-conceptualization (*anābhoga-nirvikalpa-vihāra*), because the fruits [of afflictions] have already been severed, the causes of fear for all afflictions do not manifest; since there is no further basis for them to arise, it is only then that one can be said to be 'detached.
The five fears are termed 'fruits,' yet they are already absent from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). By this principle, it should be understood that innate [afflictions] likewise cause fear."

The Commentary states: "From 'supremely perfected' up to 'inverted dreams and delusions,' [the phrase] 'giving rise to birth and death' is used because [these states] cause one to remain in saṃsāra. Within this context, the stage where [delusion] has already been severed is not mentioned, as it occurs in the subsequent clause."
The *shu* (commentary) identifies that which is abandoned as the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) and the three dwellings (*vihāra*).

The *zhu* (annotation), following this, concludes the text: "Do not divide it into four parts; rather, one should say that the first [part] explains the liberation from suffering, while the latter explains what is to be realized."
The first and second sections are divided into three parts; we shall revert to taking the first three. Within the initial explanation, the judgment is likewise based on this.

The commentary on the old ritual manual divides the mantra into four parts; furthermore, it subdivides the last section into three. I fear this may not accord with the original intent of the text.

first, a general demonstration of the benefits of the fruit; second, the manifestation of its superior capacity. This passage constitutes the former. The latter section is divided into two:

first, concluding that "this is the dharmārtha-dhāraṇī"; second, manifesting that by means of this, the *mantra-dhāraṇī* is taught. Within the former, there are two further divisions: first, clarifying the attainment of bliss.
The latter clarifies the abandonment of evil. Alternatively, this may be divided into two parts: first, manifesting the attainment of the fruit, whereby one obtains the two dhāraṇīs;

second, manifesting that based on this, one recites the secret mantra-dhāraṇī. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, clarifying the attainment of bliss; second, clarifying the abandonment of evil.

Within the first of these, there are two sections: first, manifesting the attainment of the fruit; second, revealing the four dhāraṇīs—or as some say, the two dhāraṇīs. According to the *Jie Kong* (Vajraśūnyatā), the mantra is...
The lower major section. As seen below in the main text, and also according to the new rubric, please examine this in detail.

the glosses, etymologies, and translations correspond exactly as they should be without difference. However, there are slight distinctions in the meaning of the three names thus obtained.

The commentary above explains this based on both principle and wisdom; this passage, however, relies solely on the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). This is the supreme emptiness.
This principle exists; it is still discussed in this manner according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*). If one relies on ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is already empty as previously established.
Now, this section on "Ultimate Emptiness" is again analyzed into two parts: first, the structural analysis (*ko-p’an*); second, the formal explanation.

The Śrāvaka excels by virtue of their spiritual name (*nāma*); their wisdom is inferior. The Pratyekabuddha excels by virtue of their brilliance (*vidyā*); they are somewhat superior. The Unsurpassed One (*anuttara*) surpasses them;
